sections.title: Analysis
sections.text: Once you have assembled your analysis dataset (Phase 12), you are ready to analyse. This section stays register-specific and practical : when to use what, which packages, and a minimal example - it does not teach statistical theory. For depth, see the Epidemiologist R Handbook, R for Data Science and the introductory R course hosted by the Danish Diabetes and Endocrinology Academy (DDEA) (see Learning resources).

sections.title: Analysis
sections.heading: Pages in this section
sections.text: Pick the pages that fit your study - not every study uses all of them. A usual order is: choose the analysis, describe the population (Table 1), fit the main model (regression, time-to-event or rates), then the sensitivity analyses and figures. Read the output-control box below before you start. Page Packages Choosing a statistical analysis stats (base R; choose test and model) Descriptive tables (Table 1) gtsummary , finalfit Figures for publication ggplot2 Regression glm / lm , survival::clogit (matched case-control) Time-to-event survival , survminer , tidycmprsk (Cox, competing risks) Rates and rate ratios (Poisson) glm (Poisson), MASS::glm.nb , Epi / popEpi (incidence rate ratio, person-time) IP weighting (IPTW and IPCW) WeightIt , cobalt (confounding + censoring/missing outcomes) Sensitivity analyses survival (robustness checks, negative control outcome, active comparator) Output control decides what you can compute, not just what you can send. Only aggregated results leave DST, and cells below the threshold (3 or 5 observations, depending on your project) may not be repatriated at all. That shapes the analysis itself: how finely you may stratify a table, whether a subgroup is worth running, whether a figure can show what you want. Plan for it here rather than discovering it at the end. The rules and the threshold are on Phase 14 - Export and repatriation.

sections.title: Build your study population
sections.text: Use this page to build your study population, once you know which registers your study needs and before you extract any covariates. You decide who could have entered the study at all (the source population), find the exposed people or cases, give each of them an index date, and exclude those who already had the outcome. When you are done you have a cohort: a table with pnr and index_date per person, which every later phase builds on (Phase 11 to Phase 13). Finding exposed people or cases in hospital data uses the LPR extraction pattern from Extract from LPR, so read that page first. What you do after this page depends on your study design, see the end of this page. What is an index date? Index date is the point in time that marks the start of follow-up for a given person. Exposed: the date the person received the exposure (e.g. surgery date, diagnosis date, first prescription dispensed) Comparator cohort: the index date assigned from the matched exposed person Everything that follows - outcome date, covariates at baseline, follow-up time - is calculated relative to index date. The definition of index date is crucial for study validity. Structural guidance, not verified code The examples show the shape of each step. They have not yet been run end to end on real register data , so treat them as a starting point: check the column names against your own delivery, and check the logic against your analysis plan.

sections.title: Build your study population
sections.heading: Step 1 - Define the source population
sections.text: Before you look for the exposed, decide who could have entered the study at all. That is the source population, and two things decide it: your data delivery and a residence criterion. Your data delivery sets the outer limit. DST only delivers data on the population your project is approved for. If your delivery is "persons in BEF 2005-2024", then a person who only lived in Denmark in 2003 does not exist in your extract at all - and no code can pull them in. Check your project guide first. The registers below can make the timing of residence precise within your delivery, but they cannot add people to it.

sections.title: Build your study population
sections.heading: BEF alone cannot decide residence
sections.text: BEF (the population register) is a snapshot: DST delivers it as quarterly pictures, each a status on the last day of the quarter (Nyt fra Forskningsservice 4/2019, PDF, Danish). Check which reference dates your own delivery has. That means BEF gets it wrong in both directions: Too many included: the person is in that year's snapshot, but had emigrated or died by your index date. Too few included: the person is not in that year's snapshot, but was genuinely resident on the index date. That happens if they had emigrated at the time of the snapshot and moved home later the same year. You can filter your way out of the first error, but not out of the second: a filter can only remove people from the pool BEF already found, never add the ones missing from it. So residence has to be decided on events, not on snapshots.

sections.title: Build your study population
sections.heading: Use BEF and VNDS together
sections.text: You need both registers, plus the death register: BEF: the population and demographics: who exists, date of birth and sex. Use all snapshots in your study window combined (the union), not one year at a time. VNDS (migrations): the events: immigrations and emigrations with dates. VNDS holds only migration events, so a person born in Denmark who never left has no rows in VNDS. Absence of events is the normal case, not an error. DOD (deaths): the date of death, applied on top. The rule is therefore a default with exceptions: resident since birth, unless VNDS says otherwise. For each person, find the latest VNDS event before the index date: Latest event before index Resident at index? Residence period starts "I" (immigration) Yes the event date "U" (emigration) No - no events Yes the date of birth That start date is what you measure a continuous residence requirement from (e.g. "at least 5 years in Denmark before index"). It is not the same as the earliest year the person appears in BEF: someone seen in BEF in 2005, but living abroad 2006-2012 and moving home in 2013, has only two years of continuous residence at an index date in 2015. Check these six things before you trust the rule. The event codes: run count(indud_kode) on your own VNDS. The guide uses "I" and "U" , but confirm the values in your delivery. Immigration before 1971: CPR only has complete immigration and emigration data from 1971 (see Further information). A person born abroad who immigrated before that has no events, and the rule above wrongly counts them as resident since birth. Greenland: a status of its own in CPR, not the same as emigration. Find out how moves there appear in your delivery. Disappeared people: people whose address is unknown to the authorities leave the population without an emigration event in VNDS, because DST counts them separately from emigrations (DST's documentation of the population figures), so the rule above counts them as resident; they drop out of BEF, which is one more reason to require presence in BEF as well. Short stays abroad: decide whether a short gap breaks "continuous" residence, and write the choice down in your methods. Register coverage is not residence: five years of residence only gives you five years of lookback if the registers cover those five years too. Another way: residence from the CPR address history Municipality codes can also be used to assess residence in Denmark. CPR keeps a running residence history: one period per address, with municipality code and dates. With it you can look residence up directly (was there a period spanning the index date?) instead of deriving it from BEF snapshots and VNDS events. CPR has complete information on municipality of residence in Denmark from 1971 and full address from 1977; Greenland is a separate series from May 1972. The residence history says nothing about whether the person is alive, so the date of death still has to be fetched separately. See Further information for the source. Do not read the gaps uncritically. A gap in the residence history can be either a genuine stay abroad or a missing registration, and the history alone cannot tell you which. Count how many people in your own cohort have a gap before you decide how to treat them.

sections.title: Build your study population
sections.heading: Code: the source population at study start
sections.text: Does each person have their own index date? Then the same rule applies, but it has to be used where the date exists, not here. The index date is not a property of the person: The exposed get their index date in Step 2 (the exposure date). Residence is therefore decided for them when you prepare the exposed on Comparison cohort. Comparison persons are only assigned an index date at the match itself, and the same person can be a candidate at several different index dates - and be resident at one but not the other. So residence is decided per (person, index date) at match time on Comparison cohort, never once and for all. So the source population here is at person level, while eligibility at index is at the level of person and date.

sections.title: Build your study population
sections.heading: Step 2 - Identify the exposed (or cases)
sections.text: You scan the register that defines your exposure. You do not have a cohort_pnrs list yet, so you query the entire register and filter on the exposure criterion. The exposure can be defined in several ways: Type Example Register Surgery / procedure (SKS code) Bariatric surgery KJDF10/KJDF11 lpr_sksopr (LPR2), lpr_a_procregistrering (LPR3) Hospital diagnosis (ICD code) Type 2 diabetes E11 lpr_diag + lpr_adm , lpr_a_diagnose + lpr_a_kontakt Medication exposure (ATC code) Metformin A10BA02 LMDB Clinical measurement / biomarker BMI > 35, HbA1c > 75 mmol/mol Laboratory results (HbA1c), clinical quality databases or project-specific data (BMI) Register names may vary on your project - see Overview of registers. The examples use read_register() ; it requires fastreg set up with the path to your registers - see Parquet and fastreg if you did not convert them from SAS yourself. Example A: exposure defined by a surgery or procedure (SKS codes) lpr_sksopr holds the procedure code ( c_opr ) and recnum , but not pnr or date; those are in lpr_adm . So you join the two on recnum to get person, date and procedure together, the same pattern as for diagnoses, see Understand LPR. Note that exposed holds only the operated individuals. The full cohort (exposed + comparison group) is built on Comparison cohort and saved as cohort - and it is cohort , not exposed , that the later phases use as cohort_pnrs . Example B: exposure defined by a hospital diagnosis (ICD-10 codes) This example pulls from LPR2 only. Decide which registers your exposure needs (LPR2, possibly the psychiatric LPR2 tables, and LPR3) and combine them as in Extract from LPR. If you leave out a register, you miss the cases that only appear there.

sections.title: Build your study population
sections.heading: Step 3 - Exclude prevalent cases
sections.text: People who already had your outcome before the index date must be excluded, otherwise they count as new cases even though they are not. The convention used throughout this guide: a diagnosis on or before the index date is prevalent ( <= ), and only one after it is an outcome ( > ). This applies to all designs, including a prevalence study without a comparison group, so it belongs here where you build the exposed cohort. Count how many drop out at each exclusion step, so you can describe the attrition and later draw a STROBE flow diagram (also called a participant or attrition diagram; see the STROBE checklist). The generic N-counting template is in Phase 6.

sections.title: Build your study population
sections.heading: Code: exclude prevalent cases with a function
sections.text: If the same check is needed more than once (e.g. also on a comparison group later, see Comparison cohort), wrap the logic in a function so the two checks do not drift apart. See Good coding practice. Planning a comparison cohort? Extract the outcome (and exposure) dates for the whole population here rather than just for the exposed, and reuse them: restricted to the exposed as above, and later for the comparison pool (see Comparison cohort). Filtering the diagnosis codes returns everyone with the diagnosis anyway, so it saves a second query against the registers. If that comparison group is matched with replacement, know what distinct(pnr) %>% pull(pnr) excludes. prior_outcome_pnrs() checks each row against that row's own index_date (the inner_join before the filter), but the final distinct(pnr) collapses the result to a plain list of people, so filter(!pnr %in% prevalent) drops every row for that pnr , not just the one where they had a prevalent outcome. If the same person is matched to a different case with an earlier index_date , where they did not yet have the outcome, that instance gets excluded too. That may be the conservative rule you want, but decide it on purpose. See the callout on repeated pnr on Comparison cohort for the general repeated- pnr problem this is one version of.

sections.title: Build your study population
sections.heading: Participant flow diagram (STROBE)
sections.text: The N counts you made in Step 2 and Step 3 come together in a STROBE flow diagram: a figure showing how many people were in from the start, how many were excluded at each step and why, and how many ended up in the study population. The diagram below also shows where the data comes from at each step (the numbers are simulated). How each step maps to the data: Source registers: the whole population's LPR data (you have no cohort list yet). LPR2 and LPR3 are opened lazily with read_register() , see Step 2 above. Step 2: you filter on your exposure codes and attach pnr + index_date . The result is exposed . Step 3 (exclusion): prevalent cases (people with the outcome before their index date) are found in the LPR diagnoses and removed. That is the n_before - nrow(exposed) shown in the exclusion box. Final study population: pnr + index_date per person, ready for Phase 11 - Extract variables. If you build a comparison cohort, Comparison cohort comes before the last step. Output control: the exclusion boxes show raw counts. Small numbers (e.g. an exclusion group with very few people) can be disclosive. What to do about them before the diagram leaves DST is in Phase 14 - A hidden number must not be possible to work out.

sections.title: Build your study population
sections.heading: Next step depends on your design
sections.text: Prevalence study / cohort without a comparison group: after this page you are done: you have your study population with an index date. Continue to Phase 11 - Extract variables and Phase 12 - Assemble and prepare the dataset. Cohort study with a comparison cohort: continue to Comparison cohort, where you build a match pool and risk-set match a comparison group. (Nested) case-control: continue to Case-control, where your "exposed" group above is instead your cases, and you sample controls who were at risk when the case had the outcome. Self-controlled or sibling design: the person, or the family, is their own control - see Self-controlled and sibling designs. Parents, siblings or a parent's characteristics: see Family links for how to link a child to its parents.

sections.title: Case-control
sections.text: Use this page when your study is a nested case-control study inside the register population. It comes after Build your study population, and it reuses the person table built on Comparison cohort, so you need Steps 1 and 2 there even though you will not match a comparison cohort. The group you identified is here your cases (those who developed the outcome), and their index date is the outcome date. For each case you sample controls: people without the outcome who were at risk exactly when the case had the outcome. When you are done you have a matched dataset of cases and controls with a matched-set id. Case-control is especially efficient when the outcome is rare, or when a covariate is expensive to extract for the whole cohort. The design choice between cohort and case-control is in Phase 1 - what type of study. Structural guidance, not verified code The examples show the shape of each step. They have not yet been run end to end on real register data , so treat them as a starting point: check the column names against your own delivery, and check the logic against your analysis plan. Confirm too that heaven::incidenceMatch() and Epi::ccwc() are available on your project. Classic case-control vs. nested case-control: what is the difference? Classic case-control: you find cases (with the outcome) and select controls (without the outcome) from the population, often without a defined cohort with follow-up behind it. Exposure is typically ascertained retrospectively (e.g. interview) - vulnerable to recall and selection bias, and choosing controls is hard. Nested case-control: the case-control study sits inside a defined cohort (e.g. a registry cohort followed over time). Cases are those who develop the outcome during follow-up; controls are sampled from those who were at risk (outcome-free) exactly when the case had the outcome (risk-set / incidence-density sampling). Exposure comes from registry data collected before the outcome → less recall bias. In register research at DST you almost always do the nested variant: the cohort already exists in the registers. Advantages: exposure is measured beforehand, and the odds ratio from incidence-density sampling estimates the rate/hazard ratio without a rare-outcome assumption. That is what this page shows.

sections.title: Case-control
sections.heading: The principle: incidence-density sampling
sections.text: Controls are selected by risk-set (incidence-density) sampling: for each case you draw controls who, on the case's index date (= the outcome date), (1) have not yet developed the outcome and (2) meet the inclusion criteria. A person can be a control for one case and later become a case themselves. That is correct in this design: excluding people who later become cases from the controls biases the estimate (Lubin and Gail 1984). It is the same mechanic as the matching in Comparison cohort - only the "event" has changed: here it is the outcome (case), not an exposure. So this page also reuses the person table from there.

sections.title: Case-control
sections.heading: Step 1 - Build the dataset for matching
sections.text: Identifying cases and excluding prevalent cases are done on Build your study population. Here you need one row per person and residence spell, with matching variables and the dates eligibility depends on. Reuse the pool from Comparison cohort, Step 2 (demographics + death date + first outcome date), and demographics and the migration events vnds_ev from Step 1 there, for the residence spells. For case-control, though: Exposure is not an eligibility criterion here: unlike the comparison cohort, where a control must be exposure-free at index. In case-control, exposure is what you study: you measure it for both cases and controls afterwards and do not use it to decide who can be a control. A control just needs to be outcome-free (and meet your other criteria) at the case's index. Who is a case, and when: the outcome date is the index date.

sections.title: Case-control
sections.heading: Step 2 - Sample controls
sections.text: Two routes. Both do incidence-density sampling; pick one. Route A: heaven::incidenceMatch() . The sibling of exposureMatch() from Comparison cohort, but the "event" is the outcome. Route B: Epi::ccwc() . Simple risk-set sampling from entry and exit times; not counter-matching). Confirm arguments with ?Epi::ccwc . Route B code: sample with Epi::ccwc() instead of heaven Same rules as in Comparison cohort: apply inclusion and exclusion criteria before sampling and to everyone (cases and pool), and set a seed . A control can be drawn for several cases, and a person can be a control before becoming a case; both follow from sampling from the risk set, so do not remove them. incidenceMatch() itself handles the risk-set time dimension via case.index + end.followup .

sections.title: Case-control
sections.heading: Analysis: conditional logistic regression
sections.text: The analysis itself belongs to Regression (Phase 13); here only briefly, so you know where this leads. Matched case-control data can be analysed with conditional logistic regression ( survival::clogit() with a strata() term per matched set), so the matching is respected; the odds ratio from an incidence-density design estimates the rate/hazard ratio. This is the standard approach for matched case-control studies. Before the analysis you attach exposure and covariates to the matched persons (from Phase 11/Phase 12). Measure exposure in a window defined relative to each matched set's index date (the case's outcome date), the same window for the case and its controls. The matched-set id is called case.id (Route A) or Set (Route B).

sections.title: Choosing a statistical analysis
sections.text: Use this page to find the test or model that fits your outcome before you start the analysis, and the R command for it. It is a quick pointer to the right test, not the final word: always check the test's assumptions and your analysis plan, and look things up if in doubt. Start with your question. First state your research question and null hypothesis - they drive everything else. In the R commands in the tables, x , y , group , m0 etc. are placeholders - replace them with your own variable and value names. Commands written as package::function (e.g. survival::coxph , epitools::riskratio ) come from a package that must be installed on DST; the rest are base R (the stats package, always available). Regression and time-to-event are expanded in Regression and Time-to-event. Prefer a flowchart? Antoine Soetewey's decision tree for choosing a statistical test is an excellent visual companion to the tables here - you click through data type, number of groups, paired/unpaired and distribution. Find the right test - three questions: 1. What data type is your outcome? Numeric (a number), binary (yes/no) or time-to-event (time until an event). This picks the tab below. 2. Are your data paired or unpaired? The same person measured several times or in 1:1 matched pairs = paired; otherwise unpaired. This picks the row in the table. 3. Are the assumptions for a parametric test met? If they are, use the parametric one; otherwise the nonparametric counterpart. This picks between the two rows in each block. New to the concepts? Expand them under Concepts in brief at the bottom. #### Numeric / continuous data Analysis type Paired? Purpose Parametric? Test Assumptions R Mean, one group Irrelevant Compare one group to a hypothetical value Parametric One-sample t-test Normal distribution; independent t.test(x, mu = m0) Nonparametric Wilcoxon signed-rank Symmetric distribution about the median; independent wilcox.test(x, mu = m0) Mean, two groups Unpaired Compare two unpaired groups Parametric Unpaired t-test Normal in both; (equal variance); independent t.test(y ~ group) Nonparametric Mann-Whitney (rank-sum) Independent; same distribution shape wilcox.test(y ~ group) Paired Compare two paired groups Parametric Paired t-test Normally distributed paired differences t.test(x1, x2, paired = TRUE) Nonparametric Wilcoxon signed-rank Symmetric paired differences; independent wilcox.test(x1, x2, paired = TRUE) Regression Unpaired General linear model for the mean Parametric Linear regression Linearity; normally distributed residuals; constant variance; independent lm(y ~ x) Mean, several groups Unpaired Compare several means Parametric One-way ANOVA Normal distribution; independent aov(y ~ group) Nonparametric Kruskal-Wallis Independent; same distribution shape kruskal.test(y ~ group) Relationship (correlation) Irrelevant Describe the relationship between two continuous variables Parametric Pearson correlation Linear relationship; normal; independent cor.test(x, y) Nonparametric Spearman rank correlation Monotonic relationship; independent cor.test(x, y, method = "spearman") #### Binary / dichotomous data Analysis type Paired? Purpose Parametric? Test Assumptions R Proportion, one group Irrelevant Compare one group to a hypothetical value Parametric Binomial test Binomial distribution; independent binom.test(x, n, p = p0) (exact); prop.test(x, n, p = p0) (approx.) Proportion, two groups Unpaired Compare two unpaired groups Parametric Chi-square / Fisher's exact Independent (Fisher for small counts) chisq.test(table) ; fisher.test(table) Paired Compare two paired groups Parametric McNemar Paired obs.; independent pairs mcnemar.test(table) Regression Unpaired Binary regression for relative risk Parametric Log-binomial regression Binomial; probability modelled by covariates glm(y ~ x, family = binomial(link = "log")) Regression Unpaired Binary regression for odds ratio Parametric Logistic regression Binomial; continuous covariates linear on the log-odds scale; independent glm(y ~ x, family = binomial) Regression Unpaired Binary regression for relative risk Parametric Modified Poisson regression Independent; robust (sandwich) standard errors m <- glm(y ~ x, family = poisson) ; lmtest::coeftest(m, vcov = sandwich::sandwich) Regression Matched sets Odds ratio within matched sets (e.g. matched case-control) Parametric Conditional logistic regression Continuous covariates linear on the log-odds scale survival::clogit(case ~ x + strata(match_id)) \ Chi-square, Fisher's exact, McNemar and the binomial test are called nonparametric in many textbooks (they assume no normal distribution). Here Parner's scheme is followed, where "parametric" means the test assumes a specific distribution - for these tests the binomial . An effect measure with a confidence interval for two groups (risk difference, RR, OR) is a descriptive measure, not a hypothesis test - compute it with e.g. epitools::riskratio() or epitools::oddsratio() . Log-binomial regression in the table = a glm with a log link, estimating relative risk (RR) instead of an odds ratio. Modified Poisson regression = a Poisson glm on the 0/1 outcome with robust standard errors, another way to estimate the relative risk (Zou 2004, doi:10.1093/aje/kwh090). Conditional logistic regression is explained in Regression. #### Time to event Analysis type Paired? Purpose Parametric? See Rates and rate ratios (Poisson) for when to choose it over Cox.

sections.title: Choosing a statistical analysis
sections.heading: Concepts in brief
sections.text: New to statistics? Expand for the concepts the tables build on. Which data type is my outcome? The data type decides which table you need: Numeric (continuous): a number, e.g. age, BMI or blood pressure. Binary (dichotomous): yes/no, e.g. whether a person got a diagnosis or not. Time-to-event: the time until an event happens, where not everyone reaches it during follow-up (censoring) - e.g. time to diagnosis or death. What is a normal distribution? A normal distribution is bell-shaped: most values lie in the middle, with few very small or very large ones. A skewed (or irregular) distribution does not - it may have a long tail to one side. !Two distributions (simulated data): a bell-shaped normal distribution and a right-skewed one. Most parametric tests (e.g. t-test) assume the data are roughly normal; if they are clearly skewed, that points to a nonparametric test. Check the shape with a histogram ( hist() ) or a Q-Q plot ( qqnorm() + qqline() ). Mean or median? The mean can be pulled by extreme values (outliers), while the median (the middle value) is more robust. In a right-skewed distribution the mean therefore sits to the right of the median: !Right-skewed distribution (simulated data) with the mean and median marked; the mean lies to the right of the median. Parametric tests typically work with the mean ; nonparametric tests use ranks/median and are therefore less sensitive to outliers and skew. Dependent vs. independent variable A dependent variable is your outcome - the result you are studying (e.g. weight loss). An independent variable is something you have measured that might affect the outcome (e.g. treatment, sex, age). In a study of two diets, weight loss is the dependent variable and diet an independent variable. (Don't confuse "independent variable" with "independent data" - see the next box.) Paired or unpaired data Unpaired or independent data: different, unrelated people in each group (e.g. one group gets diet 1, another diet 2). Recording e.g. sex on each person does not make it paired - sex and outcome are just two different variables. Paired/dependent data: the same unit is measured more than once (e.g. weight before and after a treatment) or forms 1:1 matched pairs. This decides whether you use a paired or unpaired test (see the tables). Paired and matched are not the same A 1:1 matched pair (one case + one matched control) corresponds to paired data and is analysed as paired. But if you match with several controls (e.g. 1:5 case-control) or have a matched cohort , there are matched sets with more than two members each - a paired test needs pairs and so does not fit. They are analysed instead with conditional logistic regression ( clogit + strata() , see Regression) or stratified/clustered Cox (see Time-to-event), which generalise the pairing idea to matched sets of any size. Parametric or nonparametric A parametric test or model assumes a particular distribution - usually the normal for tests on numbers, or the binomial for tests on proportions. A nonparametric test assumes no particular distribution and instead works on the ranks of the values (e.g. Wilcoxon); it is more robust to skewed distributions and outliers, but usually has slightly less power. Rule of thumb: if the parametric test's assumptions hold (see Assumptions below), use it; otherwise the nonparametric one. (Cox is called semi-parametric : it assumes no particular distribution for the survival time, but a fixed structure for how covariates affect the risk.) The nonparametric "twin" of each t-test Each t-test has a nonparametric counterpart, used when the normality assumption does not hold: One-sample t-test → one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank (tests the median against a value) Unpaired t-test → Mann-Whitney U (= Wilcoxon rank-sum ; two independent groups) Paired t-test → Wilcoxon signed-rank (paired measurements) Mind the names: Mann-Whitney U is also called Wilcoxon rank-sum - not the same as Wilcoxon signed-rank (the paired/one-sample one). In R both are wilcox.test() ; the difference is paired = and whether you give two groups or two measurements.

sections.title: Choosing a statistical analysis
sections.heading: Assumptions
sections.text: What each assumption in the tables means, and how to check it Every test rests on some assumptions. Some you can test or inspect in the data; others are design questions you must judge from how the data were collected. Here are the ones named in the tables: Normal distribution (t-tests, linear regression, ANOVA). That the values - or for regression the model's residuals - are roughly normally distributed. Check: visually with a histogram ( hist() ) and Q-Q plot ( qqnorm() + qqline() ); optionally a formal test ( shapiro.test() ), but it is oversensitive in large samples, so trust the visual most. With large samples, t-tests and means are also robust (the central limit theorem). Normally distributed paired differences (paired t-test). It is the differences (e.g. before minus after) that should be roughly normal - not each group separately. Check: histogram/Q-Q plot of the differences. Symmetric distribution (Wilcoxon signed-rank). The test assumes the distribution of the values (about the median) or of the paired differences is symmetric - not necessarily normal. Check: histogram of the values/differences; if it is clearly skewed, a sign test may be more appropriate. Equal variance (homoscedasticity) (unpaired t-test, ANOVA, linear regression). The groups (or residuals) have roughly the same spread. Check: boxplot per group; var.test() (two groups) or car::leveneTest() (several groups); for regression a residual plot via plot(model) . Note: Welch's t-test (R's default) does not assume equal variance, so it is rarely a problem there. Independent observations (almost all tests). Each observation contributes independent information - e.g. not several rows from the same person or other clusters. Cannot be tested in the data - it is a design / data-structure question. Inspect: do you have repeated rows per person, matched pairs or clusters? Then use a method that accounts for it (paired test, clustered standard errors - see Regression - or a mixed model). Same distribution shape (nonparametric tests: Wilcoxon, Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis). For the comparison to be meaningful, the groups should have roughly the same distribution shape. Check: compare density curves/histograms or boxplots per group (hard to test formally, so inspect visually). Binomial distribution (binomial test). A yes/no outcome counted over independent units with the same probability. Mostly a design question - judge whether the data fit it (independent people, same outcome definition). Adequate expected cell counts (chi-square). The test is unreliable if the expected counts in the cells are too small (rule of thumb: below 5). Check: look at the expected counts with chisq.test(table)$expected ; if some are small, use fisher.test() instead. Independent pairs (McNemar). The pairs are matched, and the pairs themselves are independent of each other. Design question - follows from how you paired. Independent (right) censoring (Kaplan-Meier, log-rank, Cox). That those who are censored (e.g. lost to follow-up) do not systematically have higher or lower risk than those still followed. Cannot be tested directly - argue from why people are censored (administrative end of follow-up = typically independent; loss to follow-up tied to health = problematic). Sensitivity analyses if needed. Proportional hazards (Cox regression). That a variable's effect (hazard ratio) is roughly constant over time. Check: survival::cox.zph() (Schoenfeld residuals) and log-log survival curves - see Time-to-event. This overview is based on notes from Erik Parner's statistics courses at Aarhus University - courses I warmly recommend. Further information Further depth in The Epidemiologist R Handbook : Simple statistical tests New to the underlying statistics (what a test, p-value or confidence interval actually means)? See Learning Statistics with R (Navarro) - a beginner-friendly walkthrough of the theory behind them.

sections.title: Comorbidity
sections.text: Use this page when your analysis plan has comorbidity at baseline as a covariate. It helps you decide between adjusting for individual conditions and adjusting for one combined measure, and whether to define a condition from hospital diagnoses, dispensed prescriptions or both. It then shows the extraction of diagnoses before index. It builds on Extract from LPR and Medication (ATC), and you end with one 0/1 flag per condition per person, saved as .rds .

sections.title: Comorbidity
sections.heading: Individual conditions or one combined measure?
sections.text: Which comorbidities to adjust for belongs to your analysis plan and typically follows from your DAG (directed acyclic graph, see Phase 1 - Choose your covariates using a DAG). There are two approaches: 1. Individual comorbidities as separate covariates, for example the specific diagnoses you identified as confounders in your DAG. You extract these as ordinary diagnosis variables, with the same LPR pattern as on Outcomes. This gives the most control and transparency, but you have to know in advance which conditions are confounders. 2. One combined measure of comorbidity burden: a count or an index built from hospital diagnoses, sometimes together with prescriptions. It is practical when many conditions are potential confounders, or when you want to describe the burden in Table 1. The Charlson Comorbidity Index is one such index; the code to compute it from LPR diagnoses is under Charlson Comorbidity Index below. The Nordic Multimorbidity Index (NMI) was developed to predict mortality; use it with care as a measure of comorbidity burden. Its authors describe it as a multimorbidity measure that can be used as a confounder summary score, but its predictors and weights were chosen to predict 5-year mortality. This guide therefore uses it for mortality risk and not as the combined measure in approach 2. See NMI for the reasons. With either approach, your own outcome must not be part of what you adjust for. If the outcome, or a strong predictor of it, is one of the conditions a combined measure counts, you partly adjust for the outcome itself. Check the list of conditions behind any index before you use it.

sections.title: Comorbidity
sections.heading: Diagnoses, prescriptions, or both?
sections.text: Whether a condition is defined from hospital diagnoses, from dispensed prescriptions, or from both is a design decision you make per condition, and it changes who counts as having it. Some conditions are captured well by LPR (the National Patient Register) on its own: the ones that reliably bring people to hospital, such as myocardial infarction or hip fracture. Others are mostly treated outside hospital. Hypertension is an example: people managed entirely in general practice never appear in LPR with an I10 diagnosis, but they do collect antihypertensives and so appear in LMDB, the prescription register. Both single-source definitions fail, in opposite directions: Diagnoses only miss everyone treated outside hospital: they look healthy. Prescriptions only catch everyone on the drug, including those taking it for something else. Antihypertensives are also prescribed for heart failure and angina, so a definition of hypertension from ATC (Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical) codes alone over-counts. If you combine the two, the halves normally need different rules: Diagnoses (ICD-10, from LPR) Medication (ATC, from LMDB) Typical window ever, or a lookback before index a recent window, e.g. the last year How many events count one recorded diagnosis usually more than one dispensing Onset date first qualifying contact date the dispensing rule is first met A single dispensing is weak evidence of treatment, because some people fill a prescription once and stop. The pattern for "at least N dispensings within a window" is on Medication. Whichever you choose, write the definition into your methods. Two studies that define hypertension differently are not measuring the same variable.

sections.title: Comorbidity
sections.heading: Extract diagnoses before index for your cohort
sections.text: Filter LPR to your cohort and to the time before index, then reduce to one row per person per condition. The code below keeps everything on or before the index date; add a lower limit if your definition uses a fixed lookback. read_register() assumes fastreg is pointed at your registers. Turning that event log into one 0/1 flag per condition per person is the any() pattern in Extract from LPR - from event log to one row per person. For a condition that also has a prescription half, flag users as on Medication and combine the two per person. Save the result as .rds and link it in Phase 12.

sections.title: Comorbidity
sections.heading: Charlson Comorbidity Index from LPR
sections.text: Two packages on DST compute the Charlson Comorbidity Index from LPR diagnoses: heaven::charlsonIndex() and EpiForsk::charlson_score() (see Algorithms & special packages). The example below uses charlson_score() . You extract the lookback yourself (often 5 years before the index date) and give the function every diagnosis in that window, not a code list: the function matches the codes to Charlson categories itself. Which diagnosis types to include is your choice; the example keeps types A, B and G (see Understand LPR for what each type means). The D-prefix ( DG30 etc.) is handled by EpiForsk and does not need to be stripped first. The lookback reads LPR2 (somatic and psychiatric) and LPR3, because LPR2 ends in March 2019 and an index date after that would otherwise miss most diagnoses. The LPR3 tables are filtered with lprindberetningssystem == "LPR3" as on Extract from LPR; read the warning about that filter before you use it. The window here runs up to, but not including, the index date; the general pattern above keeps the index date itself. Pick one and use it for every covariate. Person_ID = pnr alone is not enough if your cohort has repeated pnr . lookback above is correctly windowed per (pnr, index_date) , but charlson_score() itself only groups by the single Person_ID column you give it - it has no way to know about index_date . For a comparison cohort matched with replacement, that means diagnoses from all of a person's index_date windows get pooled into one Charlson score, silently reattached to every occurrence of their pnr . If this applies to you, build a single combined key first (e.g. mutate(pnr_index = paste(pnr, index_date)) ) and pass Person_ID = pnr_index instead, then split the two columns back apart from the result afterwards.

sections.title: Comorbidity
sections.heading: regmorbidity: many conditions from editable code lists
sections.text: regmorbidity is an R package in development for deriving many conditions at once from Danish register data. It is on GitHub only (not on CRAN), and parts of it have not been run on DST yet: read the package README for what has been tested before you rely on it. It computes no score and does not implement a published index. If you have code lists to contribute, get in touch. How the package is designed, if you are writing your own code Conditions live in plain CSV code lists, not in R code. One row per code, with columns for the condition, the vocabulary ( ICD10 or ATC ), the code and, for medication, the minimum number of dispensings and the window in days. One condition can therefore mix diagnoses and prescriptions, and the definitions can be edited and version-controlled without touching the code that runs them. Medication conditions take a configurable count and window , and the onset date is the date of the qualifying dispensing. Results are written to disk one file per condition , so a long run over the full register can resume after an interruption. The bundled code lists take Prior et al. (2016) (doi:10.1093/aje/kwv324) as their starting point. They are meant to be revised for your own study and are not an implementation of that paper's index.

sections.title: Comparison cohort
sections.text: Use this page when your study compares exposed people with a matched group of unexposed people from the population. It comes after Build your study population, where you identified the exposed and excluded prevalent cases (the object exposed with pnr , index_date and exposed = 1 ). Here you build the comparison group: people who are not exposed, resemble the exposed on the variables you match on, and were at risk on the index date they are assigned. When you are done you have full_cohort.rds with both groups, a matched-set id and the index date per row. If you would rather not match and instead adjust for confounders in the analysis, go to Without matching near the end of the page. Structural guidance, not verified code The examples show the shape of each step. They have not yet been run end to end on real register data , so treat them as a starting point: check the column names against your own delivery, and check the logic against your analysis plan. Confirm too that heaven::exposureMatch() is available on your project.

sections.title: Comparison cohort
sections.heading: Risk-set sampling: who can be a comparison person
sections.text: A comparison group gives you the counterfactual experience: what would have happened to the exposed had they not been exposed. The main rule: a comparison person is assigned the exposed person's index date and must be at risk on exactly that date: alive, resident in Denmark, free of your outcome and meeting your criteria. This is the core of risk-set (incidence-density) sampling , and it is what prevents immortal time bias (assigning someone follow-up time during which they could not possibly have had the outcome). A person can be a comparison person now and become exposed themselves later; that is correct (see the crossover fold-out below).

sections.title: Comparison cohort
sections.heading: What "risk set" means, and why the index date decides everything
sections.text: Study start vs. index date. Study start is the common date the study begins to look at data (e.g. 1 January 2010) - the same for everyone. The index date is a person's own start of follow-up: for an exposed person it is the exposure date, and a comparison person is assigned the exposed person's index date. It therefore varies from one exposed person to the next, and each comparison person is judged on exactly that date. Requiring "at risk" on the index date rather than at study start is what stops you including someone who had already died or emigrated by the time the exposed person was exposed. The risk set is a term from survival analysis: at each index date it is everyone still at risk right then - alive, outcome-free, under observation. Comparison persons are sampled from that set. An unexposed person stays in it until they themselves become exposed, then leaves it (and can become a case). Risk-set sampling captures that movement, because eligibility is judged on the index date rather than once and for all. !Risk-set sampling: on the case's index date (dashed line) comparison persons are sampled from those still at risk. A person who later becomes exposed can be a comparison person until their own exposure (crossover) and is then censored; someone who died or emigrated before index is not at risk.{fig-alt="Timeline with six people. A vertical dashed line marks the case's index date. People whose lifeline crosses the index date and are still alive form the risk set and can be sampled as comparison persons. One person later becomes exposed (crossover) and is then censored; another died or emigrated before index and is not at risk." width="100%"}

sections.title: Comparison cohort
sections.heading: The design choices
sections.text: Matching variables are typically sex and birth year, but can also be index date/calendar year, SES and municipality. Whether a person may be reused is decided below. Whether to match at all is the other decision, and it is a different route through the page - see Without matching after the four steps. Crossover: what to do with a comparison person who later becomes exposed In a risk-set design a future-exposed person is allowed to be a comparison person until their own exposure date. So do not exclude everyone who ever becomes exposed: that conditions on the future and can overestimate the effect (immortal-time or selection bias). Instead store a crossover_date = the date the person themselves becomes exposed, and decide how to handle it: censor at crossover, or let the person switch group. Crossover is explained briefly here; the censoring itself is done when follow-up time is calculated, in Link your extracts. General population or active comparison group: which to choose General population: maximal contrast, but a risk of confounding by indication (the exposed differ systematically from the background population). Active comparison: unexposed individuals WITH the same underlying indication (e.g. people with the same underlying disease but a different or no treatment). Reduces confounding by indication, but the group is smaller and may itself be selected, depending on how the indication is identified. Choose based on your research question; some studies report both. If you use more than one comparison group, they can share individuals - analyze each group separately against the same exposed, and do not pool them. Which variables to match on, and how many comparison persons per exposed Match only on what you want to adjust for by design (typically sex, age, calendar time). Avoid over-matching (matching on a mediator or on a consequence of the exposure itself). At best it just costs precision; at worst you risk introducing bias. Ratio (e.g. 1:5): more comparison persons give more precision, but with diminishing returns - each extra comparison person raises precision less and less, so at some point the gain is not worth the extra data. A large ratio + a narrow pool can also deplete the pool, so some exposed get fewer than the ratio. Measure and report how many (see Step 4). How many per exposed/case? Precision rises with the ratio, but the gain flattens after a few comparison persons per exposed. For matched case-control studies, Ury (1975) gives the efficiency of k1 controls per case relative to k2 as k1(k2 + 1)/k2(k1 + 1). Against an unlimited number of controls that is k/(k + 1): 80% with 4 controls, 83% with 5 and 91% with 10. Choose a higher ratio if the outcome is rare or the pool is plentiful. For a thorough review of sampling strategies for comparison cohorts, see Heide-Jørgensen et al. (2018), Clinical Epidemiology .

sections.title: Comparison cohort
sections.heading: With or without replacement
sections.text: When you sample comparison persons, decide whether the same person may be used more than once. The choice affects both the matching and the analysis afterwards, so decide it before you match. Default: sample with replacement (risk-set sampling). A person can be matched to several exposed (and themselves become exposed/a case later). In Heide-Jørgensen et al. 2018, sampling with replacement did not bias the comparators' outcome risk, whereas 5:1 sampling without replacement biased it in older, high-risk cohorts, and chronological sampling without replacement failed to fill the matching ratio. exposureMatch() and the manual loop below both sample with replacement by default. Without replacement (each person used at most once) is not recommended even when the pool is large. If you have a specific reason to use it, the manual loop has a WITHOUT_REPLACEMENT switch - then check the match rate in Step 4, and expect bias in older or high-risk cohorts. With replacement, use clustered standard errors in the analysis. Standard models assume each row is an independent observation. When the same person appears several times (reuse or crossover), that does not hold: the rows are correlated, and the model treats them as more independent information than they are. The result is confidence intervals that are too narrow (and p-values too small). The fix is clustered (robust) standard errors: you tell the model which rows belong to the same person (clustering on person id), so the uncertainty is computed correctly, or you use a model that handles it. It is expanded in Robust (clustered) standard errors. Package Used for Replacement heaven::exposureMatch() risk-set matching for a comparison cohort see note below + matchReport() heaven::incidenceMatch() risk-set matching for case-control see note below + matchReport() MatchIt::matchit() general matching (e.g. propensity score) explicit via replace = TRUE/FALSE Epi::ccwc() nested case-control sampling risk-set sampling, see Case-control manual loop full control with replacement by default ( WITHOUT_REPLACEMENT switch) That a control can be used for several cases is what replacement means (the control is "returned to the pool" and can be drawn again for another case). heaven::exposureMatch() has no argument to turn it off; the function does risk-set matching, where a not-yet-exposed person can be chosen as a control, and a future case can be a control until their own exposure (governed by end.followup ). Confirm the actual behaviour with heaven::matchReport() , which shows how often each control is used (and thus whether there really is replacement). Also confirm package names and arguments on your own project.

sections.title: Comparison cohort
sections.heading: Step 1 - Prepare the exposed for matching
sections.text: Identifying the exposed and excluding prevalent cases are done on Build your study population. Here you attach sex and birth date from BEF (needed if you want to match on age or birth year), derive the variables you need (e.g. age at index), and apply your inclusion criteria. The same criteria are applied to the pool in Step 2. Deriving a variable. A new column is computed from existing ones with mutate() . Age at index is the days between index and birth over 365.25 (a year is 365.25 days because of leap years): The same applies to other derived measures, e.g. mutate(bmi = weight_kg / (height_m^2)) . Compute it once and reuse it, so the matching age and Table 1 always agree - see Link your extracts. read_register() requires fastreg set up with the path to your registers - see Parquet and fastreg if you did not convert them from SAS yourself. How the 5-year residence requirement works, and why not the earliest BEF year The requirement is that the person has lived in Denmark continuously for at least 5 years up to their index date: years_resident >= 5 , where resident_since is the start of the current residence period. resident_since is the date of the latest immigration before index, or the date of birth if the person never left. The same requirement is used on the exposed (Step 1) and on the pool at match time (Step 3), so both groups are treated identically. Why not use the earliest BEF year? Because BEF is snapshots and says nothing about whether residence was continuous. Someone seen in BEF in 2005, but living abroad 2006-2012 and moving home in 2013, has an earliest BEF year of 2005 and would satisfy a 5-year requirement at index in 2015 - even though they have really only lived here for two years. A BEF-based lookback is also always bounded by YEAR_FROM and can therefore never look further back than your study window. The residence period from VNDS has neither problem. See Phase 10 - the source population for the rule and the six things to check before trusting it. bef is loaded lazily ( read_register() ), but bef_py is pulled into RAM with collect() - it is a concrete table we compute on, not a lazy filter.

sections.title: Comparison cohort
sections.heading: Step 2 - Build the comparison pool
sections.text: Now you build the pool that the comparison group will be drawn from. A member must satisfy two things: (1) be in BEF in the relevant years (i.e. resident in Denmark), and (2) meet your inclusion and exclusion criteria. The criteria depend on dates from several registers (death, emigration, exposure, outcome), so you join several tables to assemble the pool. The focus now shifts from the exposed to the whole population. On Build your study population the exposure definition gave you data for the exposed only. A comparison person can be anyone in the background population, so the variables that decide eligibility - demographics, death date, migration events, exposure date, outcome date, lookback - must be available for the whole population. That is why bef_py / demographics were pulled for everyone in Step 1, and why the dates here are extracted for the population too. The time-varying criteria (alive, exposure-free and outcome-free ON the assigned index date) cannot be filtered out here - they are decided at match time in Step 3: in Route A via end_fu (the date a person stops being eligible as a control), in Route B via the eligibility filters in the loop. So in this step you make sure the pool carries all the dates needed to apply them. The pool is built on top of demographics from Step 1 (the same BEF extract, not pulled again), with everything eligibility depends on: death date, exposure date and outcome date (so the outcome before the assigned index date can be excluded for the comparison person, exactly as for the exposed). Residence and lookback are instead decided from the migration events ( vnds_ev ) at match time, because the answer depends on the index date. The dates are extracted for the whole population with the same patterns as Extract from LPR. The comparison person must be exposure-free on the index date, not "never exposed". Attach each person's FIRST exposure date to the pool, and decide eligibility at match time with exposure_date > index_date . This automatically excludes an exposed person at their own index, but allows a future-exposed person to be a comparison person for an earlier index date (correct - they were unexposed then). Removing everyone who is ever exposed conditions on the future and introduces bias.

This is not a separate step but a rule: all inclusion and exclusion criteria (age, residency, prevalent outcome) must be applied to BOTH the exposed and the pool, each relative to its own/assigned index date, BEFORE you sample. Excluding after matching changes the population the exposed are matched to and introduces selection bias. See Heide-Jørgensen et al. 2018 on correct comparison-cohort sampling.

sections.title: Comparison cohort
sections.heading: Step 3 - Match the comparison group
sections.text: Always set a seed before sampling, so the matching is reproducible. Route A and Route B do the same single step; pick one. A package like exposureMatch() replaces only the sampling loop. Everything else (prepare the exposed, build the pool, exclusions, assemble and validate) you do either way. If you take Route A, skip the manual loop and the performance fold-out.

sections.title: Comparison cohort
sections.heading: Route A: heaven::exposureMatch()
sections.text: Route A is the one to start with for most studies. exposureMatch() is built for a comparison cohort: a case is a person who becomes exposed at index, and a control is one who is not yet exposed at the case's index. ( incidenceMatch() is the sibling for case-control; riskSetMatch() is the internal engine under both.) First we combine the exposed and the pool into ONE table ( all_persons ) in the format exposureMatch() needs: an event indicator (1/0), a case.index date and an end.followup date. exposureMatch() gives each row one continuous at-risk interval, so the table has one row per person and residence spell (a person who emigrated and came back has two rows). This prepares the match pool; the sampling itself is only the function call afterwards. (The manual Route B uses exposed and pool directly and does not need this assembly.) Why one row per residence spell. exposureMatch() gives each row one end_fu , i.e. a single continuous risk interval. With one row per person, someone who emigrates in 2008 and moves back in 2010 would leave the risk set in 2008 and never re-enter. With one row per spell they are at risk until 2008 and again once they meet the 5-year residence requirement after their return (from 2015), which is the same rule Step 1 and Route B apply on each index date. Each row also ends at death, so nobody can be drawn for an index date after they died or emigrated, including people who become exposed later. The residence rule itself is the one from Step 1, with the limits described in Phase 10 - the source population. What can exposureMatch() handle itself? A great deal: it matches exactly on terms , and via case.index + end.followup it handles the risk-set time dimension - who was still at risk at the case's index. end.followup is the date a person stops being eligible as a control (death, emigration, own exposure, i.e. crossover, or outcome), so the function handles crossover and competing risks. Time-dependent comorbidities can be matched with date.terms . Only quite unusual criteria require the manual loop. Argument vs. value. In a function call, the argument's name is on the left of = (fixed, defined by the function, cannot be changed), and the value you give it is on the right (usually the name of one of your columns, in quotes). E.g. event = "event" : the argument is called event , and we set it to our column "event" . Note the difference between transmute(event = 1L) (here we create a column called event ) and exposureMatch(event = "event") (here we point the function's argument at that column). The arguments here: ptid = row id (here one per person and residence spell), event = 0/1 indicator, terms = matching variables (must be factor/character; categorize e.g. age), data = the dataset, n.controls = controls per case, case.index = the case's index date, end.followup , date.terms (here the entry date) and seed . What an argument is, is explained in the Function guide. See a function's arguments and help in R: type ?exposureMatch or help(exposureMatch) , use args(exposureMatch) for a quick list, or place the cursor in the function name and press F1 in RStudio. For CRAN packages (e.g. MatchIt , Epi ) there is also an online page with vignettes. heaven is on GitHub (tagteam/heaven) - confirm availability and arguments on your own project (argument names have varied between versions). The design choice behind matching is in Phase 1.

sections.title: Comparison cohort
sections.heading: Route B: manual risk-set loop
sections.text: Route B code, for caliper matching or criteria Route A cannot express It also shows what exposureMatch() does under the hood. The manual loop gives full control, but you handle every step yourself, so there are more places it can go wrong; Route A is the safer starting point. Route B is needed when Route A cannot express what you need, e.g.: Interval / caliper matching: exposureMatch() only matches exactly on fixed factor variables (e.g. same birth year). If you want to match within an interval around the case's value - e.g. birth year ±1, age ±2 years or BMI ±5 - that cannot be written as exact matching, so you have to loop yourself. (You can put e.g. age into groups and match exactly on the group in Route A; only a rolling ± around each case's value needs the loop.) Matching criteria computed relative to the case: criteria that date.terms / duration.terms cannot express. Custom sampling: e.g. counter-matching or special replacement rules, or your own per-matched-set variables. The package is not available: heaven is missing on your project. For standard register matching (sex, birth year, calendar time, alive/resident/outcome-free/exposure-free at index, comorbidity timing) Route A is enough. Chronological order. We sort the exposed by index date ( arrange(index_date) ), so the earliest-exposed person gets comparison persons first. This mirrors the real time sequence: each exposed person is matched against those who were at risk on exactly its index date. With replacement (the default) the order does not change who can be drawn; it only matters with WITHOUT_REPLACEMENT = TRUE , where the earliest exposed use up candidates first - which is why chronological sampling without replacement can fail to fill the ratio (Heide-Jørgensen et al. 2018). Route B on a large pool: pre-split it by sex and birth year for speed With a pool of millions of rows it is expensive to filter the whole pool in every iteration (= one pass of the loop, i.e. one exposed person at a time). Pre-split it into a named list keyed by sex + birth_year , and pull only the neighbouring birth cohorts per iteration (birth year ±1). It is the same logic as the loop above, just faster. Only with WITHOUT_REPLACEMENT = TRUE : remove the chosen ones from their strata after each sampling ( pool_split[[k]] <- filter(pool_split[[k]], !pnr %in% chosen$pnr) ) to speed up later iterations. If you keep person-year rows (one per BEF year) to require a BEF record in the index year as a residency proxy, add the BEF year to the key.

sections.heading: Step 4 - Assemble, validate and save
sections.text: Route B only. Route A already assembled cohort at the end of its code, so skip this block. With the manual loop you put the exposed and the comparison group together yourself: Both routes. Compute age, check the result and save it: If the count(pnr) check above printed a number greater than 0, pnr alone is no longer a safe join key for anything measured relative to the index date. Much of this guide shows the simple case with one row per pnr in cohort . With replacement, that is no longer true: the same pnr can carry several different index_date s, one per matched set it was drawn into. A downstream left_join(..., by = "pnr") - for outcomes, diagnoses, medication flags, SES variables, anything measured relative to index_date - will then silently mix values across that person's different index dates: no error, no NA , just a value from the wrong window attached to the wrong row. The fix: give cohort a stable row id before you extract anything else, and use it (or pnr + index_date together, as the complete recipe in Link your extracts does) as the join key from here on, instead of pnr alone: Socioeconomic variables works through this pattern end to end - why a plain pnr join goes wrong and how to carry the id through every subsequent extraction - use it as a template regardless of which variable you are attaching. If the count(pnr) check above printed 0 (no person drawn more than once), none of this applies: pnr alone is a safe join key throughout the rest of the guide, and you can ignore this callout entirely. bind_rows() here, and the left_join() you use next to attach outcomes and covariates, are explained in Link your extracts. Keep the matched-set id ( match_id in the manual loop; exposureMatch() calls it case.id ). It tells you which comparison persons belong to which exposed person. This matters when the analysis must respect the matching: stratified or conditional analysis (e.g. stratified Cox by matched set, or conditional logistic regression in case-control), or at least clustered standard errors. Without match_id you cannot run a correct matched analysis. See Phase 13.

sections.title: Comparison cohort
sections.heading: Without matching: an unmatched comparison group
sections.text: A comparison group does not have to be matched. Matching and adjustment are two ways to handle the same confounders: Matching (design): you balance the groups on e.g. sex, age and calendar year before you look at the outcome (that is what Step 3 does). The cost is that a matched variable can no longer be studied as an exposure of its own, and a narrow pool can be depleted. Adjustment (analysis): you take a broader unexposed group without matching and instead control for the same variables in the analysis. If you "just" want a comparison group that is not matched on anything: 1. Define the eligible unexposed group with the same inclusion and exclusion criteria as the exposed (alive, resident, outcome-free and exposure-free at their index). This is still the pool from Step 2. 2. You need no matching function: just combine exposed and unexposed with an exposed indicator (1/0). 3. Assign a start of follow-up (index) to the unexposed, so follow-up begins at a comparable point. This is the hard part: do it so you avoid immortal time (e.g. using calendar time as the time axis, or assigning index dates from the exposed persons' distribution). 4. Adjust in the analysis for the variables you would otherwise have matched on (sex, age, calendar year, SES ...) - either as covariates in a regression model or with weighting (IPTW). See Phase 13. Neither matching nor adjustment removes confounding from variables you have not measured. Choose based on your study: matching balances strong confounders at the design stage and is easy to communicate; adjustment retains all information and lets you study more variables. You can also combine the two (match on a few, adjust for the rest).

sections.title: Comparison cohort
sections.heading: Checklist before you trust the matched cohort
sections.text: Every one of these is something you cannot repair after the fact: At risk ON the assigned index date (not just at study start) - otherwise immortal time bias. Exclusion BEFORE sampling and on both groups (exposed + pool). Exposure-free ON index, not "never exposed": do not exclude everyone ever exposed (crossover). Exclude prevalent outcome in both groups, each relative to its own index date. set.seed() before sampling: otherwise the matching is not reproducible. Compute age ONCE ( /365.25 ) and reuse the variable, so matching age and Table 1 agree. One row per person: deduplicate (duplicate person-year rows produce duplicate matches). Avoid over-matching: match only on confounders. With replacement (or crossover) → clustered standard errors in the analysis. Several comparison cohorts can share individuals - analyze each separately, do not pool them.

sections.text: You have full_cohort.rds : one row per person (per matched set, if drawn more than once) with pnr and index_date for both groups (exposed and comparison group). Use it in all subsequent extractions: cohort_pnrs thus contains the pnr's for both exposed and comparison persons, not just the exposed. Extraction of outcomes and covariates must cover the entire study population. sections.title: Want to help?
sections.text: Use this page if you have code, knowledge or a correction that other register researchers could use. It lists what the guide is missing most, and the two ways to send it: by email or as a pull request on GitHub. "We" are the people who maintain the guide at Steno Diabetes Center Aarhus. Many researchers have solved the same problems, each in their own project, without the code or the experience ever being shared. Two kinds of contribution help most: knowledge (recurring problems, methods and packages we should cover) and code (concrete, reusable solutions). Nothing needs to be finished: drafts and good pointers help too.

sections.title: Want to help?
sections.heading: Share your knowledge
sections.text: Where do register researchers keep hitting the same things? Point us in the right direction: #### Recurring problems Which pitfalls do you meet again and again? (immortal time, exclusion order, prevalent vs. incident, time-varying confounding ...) - so we can describe them in one place. #### Epidemiological methods Designs, bias and analysis approaches specific to register data - and how to explain them simply for beginners. #### Packages that already exist Do you know an R package that solves a register problem? (e.g. heaven , Epi , MatchIt , EpiForsk , comorbidity ...) Then we point to it instead of reinventing. Do you know the "stamdata" register? The National Centre for Register-based Research works with an external dataset of that name, and we have no description of it. If you know what it contains or how it is obtained, we would like to hear from you.

sections.title: Want to help?
sections.heading: Share your code
sections.text: Concrete, reusable solutions. It does not need to be validated - we are happy to work on from a draft: #### Ethnicity Deriving ethnicity/origin and generations from BEF/IEPE. #### Medication and medication use Exposure measures from LMDB: DDD, weighted use, PDC/MPR, insulin dosing, lag time and long-term prescriptions. Medication (ATC) explains why dispensings are not intake, but stops short of the code. #### Family linkage Linking parents, children and siblings, e.g. to carry exposures or covariates across generations. We have a recipe for parents, siblings and adoption - code tested on a real project welcome. #### Socioeconomic classification Education, income and employment, e.g. following the SEPLINE guidelines for socioeconomic position. We have a starter page - validated code welcome. #### Time-varying variables Variables that change over follow-up - blood tests, BMI, weight. We have a starter page - worked examples from real projects welcome. If you have something else that solves a general problem in register data, get in touch as well.

sections.title: Want to help?
sections.heading: How to contribute
sections.text: Two ways - pick whichever suits you: Email us (easiest): saras@clin.au.dk. Send code, a draft, or just an idea - we'll add it. You need neither git nor GitHub. Open a pull request on GitHub (if you're comfortable with it): The guide's source files live in a GitHub repository: github.com/steno-aarhus/registers-guide. Every page in the guide is a .qmd file, and the website itself is built automatically from them. A pull request is a proposal of concrete changes to those files that we can review and merge. How do I send a pull request? (step by step) A pull request is only a proposal - it is never merged automatically. We are notified, review the change, and merge it only once we have approved it. An outside contributor can therefore propose a change but cannot alter the page directly; only people we have explicitly given write access can merge. So nothing goes live behind our backs. 1. Create a (free) GitHub account if you don't have one. 2. Find the file. Every page is a .qmd file in the repository root, and the filename is shown in the address bar : the page at .../understand-lpr.html is the file understand-lpr.qmd (the part before .html is the .qmd name). 3. Click the pencil icon ("Edit this file") on the file. If you don't have write access (outside contributors don't), GitHub automatically makes a fork - your own copy of the project - and your changes are saved there, not in the original. 4. Commit ("Commit changes") and click "Create pull request" . To add a brand-new page instead, use "Add file" → "Create new file" at the top of the file list - that is sent as a pull request too. 5. We review , comment if needed, and merge when it's ready - and the website updates automatically. Everything can be done in the browser; you don't need to install git. If you prefer email, that's perfectly fine.

sections.title: DARTER pitfalls
sections.heading: 1. How far the parquet files reach
sections.text: Most registers are as of 2026 updated to end of 2024 . Check each register you use against your study period with the general coverage check. If a register stops too early, exposed people and comparators whose events fall after its end date look like nothing happened to them, which affects censoring and matching with no error message. If the parquet file does not cover your study period: You need to extract data from the raw SAS file on DST. Contact your data manager - they can help with raw data access and conversion. Deaths are the known case: dod is not in cleaned-data on DARTER. See Register paths and datastores for how to read it.

sections.title: DARTER pitfalls
sections.heading: 2. Surgery and procedures
sections.text: Procedure codes are split across two registers by period: lpr_sksopr (parquet-registers) - procedures and surgery 1996--2018, joined to lpr_adm via recnum procedurer_kirurgi (parquet-external) - 2019 and onwards, joined to lpr_a_kontakt via dw_ek_forloeb dw_ek_kontakt is NA for all rows in procedurer_kirurgi . Use dw_ek_forloeb - not dw_ek_kontakt - to fetch pnr from lpr_a_kontakt , or better, use lpr_a_procregistrering , which also exists on DARTER and joins on dw_ek_kontakt like lpr_a_diagnose does. The full column list, why the key is empty, and the fallback code are in Register paths and datastores.

sections.title: DARTER pitfalls
sections.heading: 3. LPR3: DARTER's LPR2 stops a quarter early
sections.text: The general guide filters lpr_a_kontakt and lpr_a_diagnose to lprindberetningssystem == "LPR3" to avoid counting LPR2 contacts twice (see general pitfall 13). On DARTER, that filter currently drops a real quarter of contacts, not just duplicates. DST's LPR2 files end 31 March 2019 (the regions switched their reporting to LPR3 on 2-3 February or 2-3 March 2019), but DARTER's lpr_adm / lpr_diag delivery available under cleaned_data currently stops 31 December 2018 , a full quarter earlier (confirmed directly, not DST's documented date). The LPR2-tagged rows still sitting in lpr_a_kontakt for January-March 2019 are the only record of those contacts anywhere in this delivery: filtering to lprindberetningssystem == "LPR3" removes them entirely, not just de-duplicates them. Direct measurement confirms the loss is bounded to that one quarter: practically no rows carry an LPR2-tagged start date after 31 March 2019, so this is not an open-ended problem spanning years. Do not just drop the lprindberetningssystem filter to get the missing quarter back - that also brings back the real 2017-2018 duplicates the filter exists to remove. The fix is a date cutover: keep genuine LPR3 rows, and keep LPR2-tagged rows only for the window DARTER's lpr_adm does not cover yet. The 2017-2018 LPR2-tagged rows stay excluded in both tables (their kont_starttidspunkt is before lpr2_cutoff , so step 2's filter() removes them, and step 3 only keeps what step 2 kept) - only the January-March 2019 gap gets pulled back in, diagnosis codes included. This is also self-correcting: once an updated delivery lands and lpr_adm_last_date reaches 31 March 2019, step 2's LPR2 branch stops matching anything and both tables quietly become equivalent to lprindberetningssystem == "LPR3" again - no need to remember to remove this code later. get_lpr_diagnoses() in DARTER - overview and pipeline already uses this cutover. If you have copies of LPR3 code in your own scripts, you must add it manually.
