sections.title: Register paths and datastores
sections.heading: Critical notes
sections.text: lpr_sksube has no procedure code on DARTER. The parquet holds three columns and no more: DST documents this register with c_opr , c_oprart , c_osgh and c_tilopr for every year 1999-2019, the same shape as lpr_sksopr . None of them are here, so the table can tell you that a procedure happened and on what date, but not which procedure. There is no filtering trick that recovers them. If you need examinations and non-surgical treatments, ask for the columns to be added to the delivery. Surgical procedures are unaffected: lpr_sksopr has c_opr and d_odto as documented. Deaths: dod is not in cleaned-data. On DARTER, cleaned-data only has dodsaars , which stops at the end of 2001 (general pitfall 1). dod (Døde i Danmark), the register to use for censoring at death, sits as a raw SAS file instead. You do not need a separate extraction on DARTER: the raw file reads directly. Do the range check. The file is named dod2024 , and the row above says 1970-2024, but nobody on the DARTER team has confirmed the start year of this extract . If it turns out to begin in 2001, and your study period reaches further back, you need dodsaars for the early years as well: Only do this if the range check says you have to. If both files cover 1970-2001, stacking them puts every pre-2001 death in twice, and distinct() then keeps whichever came first rather than the one you meant. lpr_adm / lpr_diag on DARTER stop 31 December 2018 , a quarter before DST's own LPR2 files end (31 March 2019; the regions switched their reporting to LPR3 on 2-3 February or 2-3 March 2019). The simple lprindberetningssystem == "LPR3" filter therefore loses January-March 2019; see pitfall 3 for the check and the fix. Laboratory results: use laboratorieproevesvar_ and only that source; see pitfall 4. [] procedurer_kirurgi - the pnr join is not solved. This is a delivery of LPR3 surgical procedures from Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's Forskerservice (see the end of the warning below); it is not a DST register, and it does not appear in DST's register list. Like every procedure table it carries no pnr : it identifies procedures, not people, so you have to join to a contact table to get one. On DARTER neither route works cleanly. Column Type Contents procedurekode character SKS procedure code - match on this (e.g. "KJDF10" ) dato_start Date Procedure date dw_ek_kontakt character The intended join key - but NA for every row here dw_ek_forloeb character Course-level key - usable, but many NA proceduretype character "P" = procedure, "+" = add-on code procedurekode_parent character Parent procedure code dato_slut Date Procedure end date lprindberetningssystem character LPR reporting system procedureregistrering_id character Internal registration ID The empty keys are by design, but the pattern here is still wrong. Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's guide to LPR3 for researchers states that LPR3 has four real join keys - dw_ek_helbredsforloeb , dw_ek_forloeb , dw_ek_kontakt and dw_ek_procedureregistrering - and that in a table where more than one of them could apply, "only the key that is relevant to join on is filled in" . A procedure attaches either to a single contact or to a whole course, and the other key is deliberately left empty. So NA on one key is not a defect. What does not fit is the proportion: the same guide says there will be "relatively few rows with course procedures" in procedurer_kirurgi , yet here dw_ek_kontakt is NA on every row, which is the opposite of what the register should look like. That points at the extract rather than at LPR3. The two keys are not the same level either: dw_ek_kontakt points at one contact, dw_ek_forloeb at a whole course, which can span several contacts. Swapping one for the other changes what a row means. The documented route for course-level procedures, if you do not have the forloeb table, is to join on dw_ek_forloeb in the contacts table . That gets you to a person, but at course level, not contact level. So there is still no verified way to attach pnr to a single LPR3 procedure through this file. Use lpr_a_procregistrering instead: it is the real DST register, it joins on dw_ek_kontakt , and DST even flags rows with no contact in flag_proc_uden_kont . Column names differ: procedurer_kirurgi lpr_a_procregistrering procedurekode proc_kode dato_start proc_starttidspunkt (datetime) dw_ek_forloeb dw_ek_kontakt (a working join key) Confirm lpr_a_procregistrering is in your delivery before you rely on it. Two more things from the same source, worth knowing before you plan around this table. procedurer_kirurgi is not a DARTER invention: it is Forskerservice's own table name, and it holds surgical procedures only. Non-surgical ones, including indication codes, are in a separate table called procedurer_andre . And add-on codes get their own rows, with procedurekode_parent and proceduretype_parent saying which procedure they belong to, so counting rows counts add-ons as procedures. DBSO: The identifier column is cpr in raw parquet - rename it to pnr before you join. OSDC: a classified diabetes population is already computed and lies ready on the project, so you normally do not run the algorithm yourself - but you can, if you need to change the definitions. read_register("osdc") finds it, but only once fastreg has been pointed at the project folders (see loading templates); without that it will not resolve the name. Both routes are described on Diabetes population (OSDC); the package itself is documented at steno-aarhus.github.io/osdc.

sections.title: Assemble and prepare the dataset
sections.text: You arrive at this phase with separate RDS files: your cohort from Phase 10 and the variables you extracted in Phase 11 - outcomes, socioeconomics and comorbidity (plus demographics from Phase 6 if relevant). You leave with one analysis-ready dataset ready for Phase 13 - Analysis. Before you can analyse, you need to: 1. Shape each extract into one row per person (most registers are in long format with many rows per person) 2. Assemble them into one analysis-ready dataset with left_join() That is what this phase is about. The technique for step 1 is either group_by() + slice() or pivot_wider() - the choice depends on what you want out of the register. Step 2 is a left_join() onto the cohort, so everyone in the cohort is kept.

sections.title: Assemble and prepare the dataset
sections.heading: What is an analysis-ready dataset?
sections.text: An analysis-ready dataset has one row per person and one column per variable - what we call wide format : pnr index_date exposure censor_date followup_years outcome age sex nmi 001 2015-03-01 1 2022-07-14 7.4 0 58 2 12 002 2016-11-20 0 2019-11-20 3.0 1 63 1 7 The example uses a cohort study with exposure , outcome and followup_years - the column names every Phase 13 page uses (the full list, including time_days and status_code , is built in Link your extracts). For a prevalence study the column structure will look different - typically without follow-up time, but with a cross-sectional date and covariates measured at that point. The techniques in this phase (joins, pivots, group_by() + slice() ) are the same regardless of study design. The registers you extract from - LPR, LMDB, BEF - are almost always in long format with many rows per person. This phase shows how to reshape and assemble them.

sections.title: Assemble and prepare the dataset
sections.heading: What have you already saved?
sections.text: Each extraction from Phases 6, 9 and 11 should be saved as its own RDS file - one register, one topic. Example of what you typically have: File Contents Key columns full_cohort.rds Cohort with index date pnr , index_date , exposed , sex , foed_dag extract_hip_fracture.rds First hip fracture diagnosis pnr , event_date (NA = none) extract_nmi.rds Mortality risk (NMI) at baseline pnr , index_date , nmi extract_ses.rds Socioeconomic variables pnr , index_date , education_cat , occupation_cat , income_cat Date of death and emigration have no file of their own here: Link your extracts reads them from DOD and VNDS when it attaches them. The goal of this phase is to assemble them into one dataset with left_join() - one new column per file. The cohort is the backbone: each extract is joined on via pnr (or pnr + index_date when the value is measured at index) and adds its columns - all cohort members are kept, and people with no match get NA . Assemble only what you need. It is tempting to keep all columns "just in case". Do not. Always end with select() and explicitly choose the columns the analysis requires. A dataset with only the necessary columns is far easier to debug and understand.

sections.title: Assemble and prepare the dataset
sections.heading: Two tools for shaping data
sections.text: The two central operations in this phase are pivots and joins - they sound similar but do fundamentally different things: Pivots Joins What it does Reshapes one table - changes the form, not the content Combines two tables - adds columns from another table Input One table Two tables with a shared key (typically pnr ) Output Same data, new shape Wider table with columns from both Used for Long → wide format ( pivot_wider ) or wide → long ( pivot_longer ) Assemble cohort + outcomes + covariates into one dataset Rule of thumb: Use pivot when you want to change the shape of one table. Use join when you want to combine two tables.

sections.title: Assemble and prepare the dataset
sections.heading: This phase's pages
sections.text: Two core pages take you from separate extracts to one analysis-ready dataset: 1. Long ↔ wide format: get each extract down to one row per person . Understand the difference between long and wide format, and use either group_by() + slice() (one representative value per person) or pivot_wider() (several time points side by side). 2. Link your extracts: join the extracts on pnr ( left_join() , inner_join() , semi_join() , anti_join() ), stack two versions of the same register vertically ( bind_rows() ), validate the join, and calculate follow-up time and event variable. This is where the final dataset is assembled. The order is deliberate: reshape first, then join . You cannot join predictably until each extract has one row per person. Two optional add-on pages you only take if your project needs them: Missing data: how to understand and handle missing values, including multiple imputation. Time-varying variables: what to do when a variable changes during follow-up (and when you do not need to do anything).

sections.title: Check your delivery
sections.text: DST's variable lists describe a register. Your project gets a delivery : a copy of the registers that someone ordered, converted and placed on your project's drive. The two can differ. Columns can be missing, keys renamed or empty, years cut off, and registers left out of the parquet folder. None of this causes an error. Your code runs, and the result is quietly wrong. Use this page once you can open and inspect a register (Phase 7 - Inspect your data) and before you build a cohort: spend an hour running the six checks against your own delivery. When you are done you know which registers, columns, keys and years you can rely on, and what to ask your data manager about. Each check comes with an example of what it catches. The examples are examples. Each one is a problem that turned up in one real project's delivery. They show what can happen, not what is in yours. Another project, or a newer delivery for the same project, may look completely different. That is the reason to run the checks yourself rather than rely on anyone's list of known issues, this one included. All the code reads registers with read_register() from fastreg. Without fastreg, use open_dataset("path/to/ /") instead; the rest is the same. To list the columns, the code fetches zero rows and reads their names, because colnames() on a lazy arrow table after rename_with() can come back empty (see Inspect your data).

sections.title: Check your delivery
sections.heading: 1. Does each register reach the end of your follow-up?
sections.text: Check the first and last year or date of every register you use against your study period. The code is in Inspect your data. In one delivery, the LPR2 contact register lpr_adm stopped on 31 December 2018, a full quarter before DST's own LPR2 files end (31 March 2019; the regions switched their reporting to LPR3 on 2-3 February or 2-3 March 2019). Contacts from those three months existed only in the LPR3 tables, so the standard LPR3 filter quietly removed them. See Extract from LPR for how to check where your LPR2 stops.

sections.title: Check your delivery
sections.heading: 2. Does each register have the columns DST documents?
sections.text: Compare the column names in your delivery with DST's variable list for that register (Overview of registers links to each one). If a column you need is not there, no amount of filtering will bring it back. Ask your data manager whether it can be added to the delivery. In one delivery, lpr_sksube (examinations and treatments) had only three columns: recnum , d_odto and year . DST's variable list for it has 11 variables, among them the procedure code c_opr . The table could say that a procedure happened and when, but not which procedure.

sections.title: Check your delivery
sections.heading: 3. Are the join keys named as documented?
sections.text: Joins fail, or join nothing, when a key has a different name than the code expects. Look for the key columns before you write a join. In one delivery, the psychiatric LPR2 tables used v_cpr instead of pnr and k_recnum / v_recnum instead of recnum . See Overview of registers for how to rename them only when your delivery needs it.

sections.title: Check your delivery
sections.heading: 4. Are the join keys actually filled in?
sections.text: A key column can exist and still be empty. Count the missing values in every key you plan to join on. Some missing keys can be by design: in LPR3, a procedure attaches either to a contact or to a whole course, and the other key is left empty. A key that is missing on every row is not by design. In one delivery, a project-specific LPR3 procedure table had the contact key dw_ek_kontakt empty on every single row, so joining it to the contacts returned nothing. The general LPR3 procedure register, lpr_a_procregistrering , had the key filled in and was the way out.

sections.title: Descriptive tables (Table 1)
sections.text: A Table 1 describes your study population: age, sex and other baseline variables, usually split by exposure. It is almost always the first table in a register-based paper. This page builds one from the analysis-ready dataset with the gtsummary package, adds a crude incidence rate per group, and writes the table to a file you can take through output control. Paths and variable names in the examples are generic - replace them with your own. gtsummary - and huxtable , if you want to export to Excel - must be installed in your R environment on DST; if they are not, contact your data manager.

sections.heading: Starting point
sections.text: You start from your analysis-ready dataset with one row per person (Phase 12), or one row per person and index date if your comparison group was matched with replacement.

sections.title: Descriptive tables (Table 1)
sections.heading: Build the table with tbl_summary()
sections.text: tbl_summary() summarises the variables you point it at. With by = you split the table into columns by a group (e.g. exposure). How tbl_summary() picks the statistics, and what each argument does tbl_summary() detects the variable type itself from the column's contents and picks a suitable statistic: factor and character variables - and numeric variables with fewer than 10 unique values - become categorical and are shown as {n} ({p}%) (count and percentage); other numeric variables become continuous and are shown as {median} ({p25}, {p75}) (median and quartiles, i.e. IQR); variables coded 0/1 , yes/no or TRUE/FALSE become dichotomous and are shown with only the one ("yes") row. statistic = is therefore optional. Omit the line entirely and you get exactly the default display above. It is only included to show how you change it - for mean instead of median, write all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd})" . In gtsummary the tilde ~ means "assign": what ~ value . E.g. age ~ "Age (years)" gives the age variable the label "Age (years)", and all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd})" sets that statistic for all continuous variables. all_continuous() / all_categorical() mean "all continuous" resp. "all categorical" variables, so the rule applies to all of them at once. digits controls the number of decimals (here 1 for the continuous variables). add_overall() adds an Overall column with all participants combined (both groups in one column), next to the per-group columns - handy for showing the total count and overall distribution. Omit it if you only want the groups. Should you add p-values? You can add a p-value column with add_p() . You can either run it afterwards on the finished table1 (as here), or insert add_p() into the chain above right after tbl_summary() - the result is the same. Note that hypothesis tests in a plain baseline table are often discouraged (with large register populations they do not test what people assume). Use them deliberately.

sections.title: Descriptive tables (Table 1)
sections.heading: Crude incidence rate (per 1000 person-years)
sections.text: Register papers often report the crude incidence rate per exposure group alongside Table 1: the number of events divided by the total follow-up time (person-years), scaled to per 1000 person-years. It needs outcome (1 = event, 0 = censored) and followup_years from your analysis-ready dataset (built in Phase 12). For a 95% confidence interval around one group's rate, put that group's events and person-years into poisson.test() (base R, exact Poisson interval): This is a descriptive rate with no adjustment. The number of events is a cell like any other, so check it against the small-cell rule before export. To compare the groups with control for confounding, see Rates and rate ratios (Poisson) for an adjusted rate ratio or Time-to-event, where a Cox model gives a hazard ratio.

sections.title: Descriptive tables (Table 1)
sections.heading: Export the table (for output control)
sections.text: Anything leaving DST must go through output control, and the rules are on Phase 14 - Export and repatriation. Before you write the file, check three things in the table: Small cells. Every count, including the "Missing" row, must be at or above your project's threshold (3 or 5). Hidden numbers. If you hide a count, the Overall column and the N in the header can give it back. See a hidden number must not be possible to work out. Median and quartiles. DST allows percentiles only when they cannot point to a person. In a large group that is not a problem; in a small subgroup, report mean (SD) or leave the row out. See min, max, median and percentiles. If huxtable or flextable is not available on DST, use the CSV route (base R, no packages needed) or contact your data manager.

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.text: Use this page as a checklist before you trust a result, and come back to it when a number looks too good or too small. It lists 13 mistakes that are easy to make with DST registers and hard to notice: most of them give no error message, and the result is just wrong. Each one says what goes wrong, how to check your own data, and what to do instead. If your code stopped with an error, go to Troubleshooting instead.

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.heading: 1. Four death registers - dodsaars stops in 2001
sections.text: Four registers have similar names, and the one whose name looks like "the death register" ended in 2001: Register DST's name Covers Use it for dod Døde i Danmark 1970-2025, ongoing Censoring at death dodsaars Dødsårssagsregistret 1970-2001, closed Cause of death, to 2001 dodsaasg Dødsårsagsregister 2002-2022, closed Cause of death, 2002-2022 dodsaarsager Dødsårsagsregister 2022-2024, ongoing Cause of death, 2022 on Names (in DST's own spelling) and coverage are from DST's register overview, read in November 2026. The date of death is in dod , which covers the whole period on its own. The cause of death is split across the three others, so a study spanning 1995 to 2024 needs all three, and none of them alone will tell you it is incomplete. dodsaasg and dodsaarsager both cover 2022, so check that deaths in 2022 are not counted twice when you stack them. If you censor on dodsaars , everyone who died after 2001 looks alive. There is no error and no warning. They stay in your risk set until the end of follow-up, so your survival curves are too good and your rates are too low. For a study running past 2001, use dod . Two things to check on your own project before you rely on this. Is dod in your delivery, and does it reach far enough back? Your project received the years it ordered, not necessarily all of 1970-2025. Check with read_register("dod") %>% summarise(min(doddato), max(doddato)) %>% collect() . Is it converted to parquet? On some projects dod sits only as a raw SAS file, so read_register() will not find it and you read it with haven::read_sas() instead. Ask your data manager for the path. Only if dod turns out not to cover your early years do you need dodsaars as well, and then you stack the two and rename so the date columns match. Do not do it by default: both registers cover 1970 to 2001, so stacking them can count those deaths twice.

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.heading: 2. RAM is shared - clean up after large extractions
sections.text: RAM (the server's working memory) is shared by everyone on the server. One oversized extraction slows the server for all users, and DST closes processes automatically when the memory is close to full (DST's guide on reducing RAM use, PDF in Danish), so it can also cost you your unsaved work. To find out which object is filling the memory, see Seeing your memory use from inside R: gc() for the session total and object.size() for the culprit. More habits (save often, partial loading, Task Manager) are in Mind your RAM in the shared environment.

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.heading: 3. rename_with(tolower) must be called on each register
sections.text: Raw column names vary by register and year: PNR , pnr , Pnr , V_CPR . If you forget it, semi_join(..., by = "pnr") stops with "Column pnr not found", even though the column is there under another spelling. The rule: every open_dataset() or read_register() call ends with %>% rename_with(tolower) as the first step in your pipe. See Extracting data step by step for explanation and example.

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.heading: 4. Date columns are not always in Date format
sections.text: Dates arrive in several formats. They look the same when printed but behave differently. Format Example What class() returns What to do Date 2020-05-15 "Date" Nothing - can be used directly Character "2020-05-15" "character" as.Date(column) Datetime "2020-05-15 14:32:00" "POSIXct" "POSIXt" as.Date(column) after collect() SAS integer 21990 "numeric" as.Date(column, origin = "1960-01-01") The rule: always check class() on a date column before using it in calculations. Filter a datetime column with a datetime, not a date A datetime and a date are two different types, and on a lazy table (before collect() ) the engines do not reliably convert between them. What follows was measured on one DST project server, on lpr_a_kontakt , with fastreg 0.14.1, duckdb 2.0.0, arrow 21.0.0.1 and duckplyr 1.2.2. Other versions may behave differently, which is the reason to run the count check below on your own server: filter(as.Date(kont_starttidspunkt) >= as.Date("2023-01-01")) on a table from fastreg::read_parquet_dataset() ran without an error but returned 0 rows, although millions of rows match. Others have seen a rapi error from the same pattern. The same line on a table from duckplyr::read_parquet_duckdb() stops with This operation cannot be carried out by DuckDB . Comparing the column with a datetime created before the pipe gave the same, correct count on both. Convert to a plain date with as.Date() after collect() , when the data are in R. After any date filter, compare count() before and after to confirm that the filter did what you meant: a filter that keeps nothing, or everything, is the warning sign. as.Date() on a datetime uses UTC unless you give it a tz . If the collected column carries another time zone (check attr(x, "tzone") ), a contact just after midnight lands on the previous day; as.Date(x, tz = "Europe/Copenhagen") keeps the local date.

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.heading: 5. BEF is a status snapshot - not a live register
sections.text: BEF is a status register: it records the population on a reference date, not continuously. DST classifies every register as one of four reference types: Status (a snapshot on one date, which is BEF), Statusperiode (population fixed on a date, values accumulated over a period), Forløb (rows with a start and an end date) and Hændelse (one row per event, with one date). The type tells you what a row means. BEF's reference date is the last day of a quarter (31 December for the annual file). Since 2008, BEF is also delivered quarterly (March, June, September, December). year == 2020 meaning 1 January 2020 is a project convention. In many projects BEF snapshots are renamed so that year == 2020 refers to the population composition as of 1 January 2020, but that does not follow from DST's delivery naming. Confirm the convention in your project guide. See DST's official BEF documentation: statistikdokumentation/befolkningen → A person is in a BEF file only if they were alive and living in Denmark on that file's reference date. DST's file BEF202012 is the status on 31 December 2020, so a person who died in June 2020 is in BEF201912 and BEF202003 , but not in BEF202006 or any later file. Which file your project calls year == 2020 depends on the convention above, so a filter on year cannot tell you who was alive on a given date.

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.heading: 6. The "a" in lpr_a_diagnose does not mean A-type diagnoses
sections.text: DST describes the LPR_A tables as an "LPR analyse model" in its release note from June 2025, which is the likely origin of the "a" in the table name. It does not mean that the table holds only A-diagnoses (aktionsdiagnose, the main diagnosis of a contact). LPR3 has two diagnosis types, and the table holds both: A (aktionsdiagnose, main diagnosis) and B (bidiagnose, secondary diagnosis). G (grundmorbus, underlying condition) is an LPR2 type and is not reported in LPR3. The six LPR2 types and their years are in Understand LPR. So you still choose the types yourself with a filter on diag_kode_type :
sections.code: lpr_a_diagnose filter diag_kode_type state types you want assume table only

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.heading: 7. Categorical codes are not consistent across registers
sections.text: The same variable can have different coding in different registers - different type (numeric vs. character), different values, or both. The case that costs most is ICD-10. LPR stores it with a Danish D in front ( DE119 ), the cause-of-death registers and the cancer register store the plain WHO code ( E119 ). A code list built for one matches nothing in the other, and the habit of stripping the D turns E119 into 119 . See ICD codes and the D-prefix. In practice you extract demographic variables (sex, age) from BEF and rarely need to compare the same variable in another register. But if you do, always check with table() and class() before using the variable:
sections.code: table register_a koen what are actual types class register_b

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.heading: 8. !! (bang-bang) forgotten in lazy evaluation
sections.text: When filtering with a local R vector inside a lazy query, dplyr first looks for a column with that name; only if there is none does it copy in the values of your R object. Usually that works. The trap is a name clash: if your local object has the same name as a column, the column wins and you get a wrong result or a confusing message. This guide puts !! in front of every local R object used inside filter() , mutate() etc. on a lazy Arrow or DuckDB table, typically code or year lists ( %in% !!codes , >= !!min_date ). To filter on pnr against the whole cohort, use semi_join(tibble(pnr = cohort_pnrs), by = "pnr", copy = TRUE) instead: it takes a local table directly and needs no !! . The full explanation is in Functions: overview.

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.heading: 9. nmi_count is not nmi
sections.text: If your dataset has both a Nordic Multimorbidity Index (NMI) score and a count of conditions, they are not the same variable and are not interchangeable: Variable What it is Source nmi Weighted score that predicts mortality: the Nordic Multimorbidity Index (Kristensen et al., Clin Epidemiol 2022). 50 predictors with individual weights; lung cancer counts e.g. 19 points, type 2 diabetes 2. See NMI page nmi_count Unweighted count of the number of conditions a person has been diagnosed with Calculated separately If you use nmi_count in your regression model instead of nmi , you are adjusting for something different than you think - and you get no error message.

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.heading: 10. Immortal time bias - exposure defined using the future
sections.text: Immortal time bias arises when a person is given follow-up time during which they could not, by construction, have had the outcome. There is no error and no warning, only an effect estimate that looks too good. It is easy to do with register data, because you define the groups looking back at what eventually happened. An example with made-up numbers. Question: does bariatric surgery lower mortality in people with type 2 diabetes (T2D)? You take everyone diagnosed with T2D in 2010, split them into a surgery group (had surgery at some point during follow-up) and a no-surgery group, and start counting follow-up for everyone at the diagnosis date. To land in the surgery group, a person had to survive long enough to be operated. Say the average wait from diagnosis to surgery is 2 years. Those 2 years are immortal : anyone who died in that window never reached surgery and so fell into the no-surgery group instead. The surgery group has been given about 2 years of guaranteed-alive person-time, labelled as surgery time. Group Deaths Person-years Rate (per 1000 py) Surgery (immortal time counted as surgery time) 24 12,000 2.0 No surgery (immortal time left out) 51 13,000 3.9 Surgery (time correctly aligned) 24 8,000 3.0 No surgery (immortal time moved here) 51 17,000 3.0 Correctly aligned, the 4,000 pre-surgery person-years count as no-surgery time, and the rates are identical (3.0): surgery does nothing. Counting those 4,000 immortal person-years as surgery time drops its rate to 2.0, leaves the no-surgery rate at 3.9, and makes surgery look 49% protective (rate ratio 0.51). The "effect" comes from the misaligned time zero, not from surgery. The fix is to align time zero: eligibility, exposure assignment and start of follow-up must coincide. Risk-set (incidence-density) matching: start each person's follow-up at the moment they become exposed, and assign each comparator the same index date (the core rule in Comparison cohort). Treat exposure as time-varying: the person contributes unexposed person-time until surgery, then exposed time after - never exposed time before they were exposed (see Time-varying variables). Defining a baseline covariate from post-index information is the same error (e.g. the OSDC diabetes type, see OSDC). Whenever a variable is built from the future, ask whether you are conditioning on the person having survived to see it. Background: Hernán & Robins, What If , §3.6 (target trial, time zero).

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.heading: 11. year is a folder name, not a date
sections.text: In a register converted to parquet with fastreg, year says which yearly file a row came from. Filtering on it is fast, because only the files for those years are read, but it does not tell you when anything happened. year == 2020 in BEF does not say which quarterly snapshot you have. When the timing matters, use the register's own date column ( hf_vfra in UDDA, d_inddto in lpr_adm , referencetid in BEF). The two uses look identical in the code. It is only a year at all if the register arrived as one file per year. Some registers arrive as a single file covering everything, and then every row carries the same year whatever its date. In the delivery this guide was written from, dodsaars spans 1970 to 2001 and says 2024 on every row, and lpr_a_kontakt is one file holding every contact that ended in 2017 or later, so counting by year puts LPR1, LPR2, MiniPAS (records from private hospitals) and LPR3 contacts in the same single year. Check with count(year) before you filter on it. One value means the column labels the delivery, not the data, and a year filter will return everything or nothing. Use the register's own date column instead, kont_starttidspunkt in lpr_a_kontakt . It is per register: lpr_diag in the same delivery really is split by year and filters correctly. Why four reporting systems end up in one file, and how to filter them, is explained in Understand LPR. How the year column is made is in Phase 4 - Reading a register that is split by year.

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.heading: 12. Published totals for the same thing do not agree
sections.text: Official publications can give more than one number for what sounds like the same thing, because the underlying population differs. For 2005, Hospital statistics 2005 reports 6,336,000 outpatient visits; the web-based Health data retrieval system reports 1,894,441 outpatient contacts for the same year, a difference of more than 3-fold. The first includes psychiatric wards and excludes private hospitals, the second does the opposite (Lynge et al. 2011, The Danish National Patient Register, Scand J Public Health 39(Suppl 7):30-33). Do not use a published aggregate as ground truth for your own extraction without checking its exact population. If your row count from lpr_a_kontakt does not match a number you found in a DST or Sundhedsdatastyrelsen (Danish Health Data Authority) publication, the mismatch may be the publication's population definition (which wards, which hospital types, which patient type), not a bug in your code. Check what the publication actually counted before assuming your extraction is wrong.

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.heading: 13. lpr_a_kontakt/lpr_a_diagnose are not pure LPR3
sections.text: The name suggests these tables hold LPR3 data only. They do not: LPR_A also carries older LPR1, LPR2 and MiniPAS (private-hospital) rows, reloaded into the same table and tagged by lprindberetningssystem , for contacts that ended in 2017 or later (DST's remark on LPR_A_KONTAKT). See Understand LPR for what that means for your extract. If you combine LPR2 ( lpr_adm ) and LPR_A without filtering, the same contacts get counted twice - once from each table. Filter both lpr_a_kontakt and lpr_a_diagnose to lprindberetningssystem == "LPR3" before using them alongside lpr_adm / lpr_diag : The filter can drop real contacts. Your own lpr_adm delivery can end earlier than DST's LPR2 files do (31 March 2019), in which case the simple filter above silently drops real, unique contacts along with the duplicates. See Extract from LPR for how to check your own delivery's coverage before trusting it. On DARTER specifically, see DARTER pitfalls, 3 for a worked fix. Check that lprindberetningssystem is in your delivery Deliveries differ between projects, and lprindberetningssystem is not always included: it has been reported missing from lpr_a_kontakt in a delivery where lpr_a_diagnose had it. Check both tables before you rely on the filter: If it is missing, ask DST to add the variable to your delivery.

sections.title: DST pitfalls
sections.heading: If the code stopped with an error
sections.text: Most pitfalls above are cases where the code runs and the answer is wrong. If you have a red error message, or a result that came back empty, go to Troubleshooting. To check a new delivery against several of these pitfalls at once, use Check your delivery.

sections.title: Export and repatriation
sections.text: This is the last step of a project: taking your results home from Statistics Denmark (DST), which DST calls hjemtagelse (repatriation). Read it before you build the tables and figures you plan to export (Phase 13), and use the checklist at the bottom before you upload. The data on the research machine are microdata: they stay there, and results leave only through DST's repatriation tool, after you have checked them against DST's rules. This page is an overview. DST's own rules take precedence, and they can change: read them before you export. DST: Rules for repatriation of analysis results (in Danish) DST: guidance on the data security rules, with worked examples (PDF, in Danish, April 2024) The Danish quotes on this page are from those two sources.

sections.title: Export and repatriation
sections.heading: What may leave DST?
sections.text: DST lets you take analysis results and other material home when three conditions all hold: nothing at the level of individuals (or their pseudonymised keys) is left in it, it is aggregated enough that no person can be identified or recognised "hverken direkte eller indirekte" (neither directly nor indirectly), and the file is of an approved type and goes through the repatriation tool. What can meet those conditions: Aggregated tables Figures built from aggregated numbers (see figures below) Analysis results, such as model estimates with confidence intervals Scripts. Program code is an approved file type and goes through the same tool. It must not contain microdata either: DST's guidance (page 10) names code with microdata written into a condition, such as a pnr value in a filter, and log files that list observations. What never leaves: Individual-level data in any form, also with pnr removed Small cells, see the threshold below Results that could identify a person, directly or indirectly Copied notes, screenshots or photographs of the screen. DST's rule names them: no microdata may be taken home by copying information down, or by "et skærmprint eller et billede af skærmen med din mobiltelefon" (a screenshot or a picture of the screen with your phone). See also DST's rules for working with microdata. Only the file types on DST's list may be repatriated (see the checklist below, and DST's page on permitted file types). R's own formats ( .rds , .RData ), Parquet and JSON are not on it, and renaming a file to get past the check is not allowed. A saved model object is also not an analysis result: a fitted glm object holds the data it was fitted on, row by row, and a coxph object holds each person's follow-up time, event and linear predictor. Export the coefficient table as .csv or .xlsx instead.

sections.title: Export and repatriation
sections.heading: Which cell size applies to you
sections.text: DST's baseline is at least 3 observations per table cell. Some registers are stricter: > "Der skal være mindst 3 observationer pr. tabelcelle [...]. For enkelte > registre kan der være strengere krav, for eksempel mindst 5 observationer pr. > tabelcelle. Hvis dette er tilfældet, vil det fremgå i DDV App, når du > bestiller data." In English: at least 3 observations per table cell; for some registers the requirement can be stricter, for example at least 5; if so, it is shown in DDV App (DDV is Danmarks Datavindue at DST) when you order the data. Check there which rule applies to your project. The rule applies at the finest level of the table: if you cross two variables, every cell of the cross-tabulation must hold the minimum. DST also says the number is a guide and the responsibility is yours: if you doubt that 3 (or 5) is enough to keep people anonymous, aggregate further. This page uses 5 throughout, because it is the safe side of both rules. If your project is on the baseline of 3, nothing here breaks: you are reporting more conservatively than required.

sections.title: Export and repatriation
sections.heading: A hidden number must not be possible to work out
sections.text: Hiding the small cells is not enough on its own. DST's rules also say that a hidden number must not be possible to work out again from the rest of what you take home: > "Observationer, som er blevet aggregeret eller på anden vis sløret eller > fjernet i en tabel, graf eller figur, må ikke kunne udledes ved tilbageregning > eller krydslæsning. Hvis dette er muligt, skal der aggregeres yderligere." In English: observations that have been aggregated, blurred or removed in a table, graph or figure must not be possible to derive by back calculation or by reading tables against each other. If they can be, aggregate further. In plain words: no subtracting your way back to a hidden number, within one table or across tables. The usual way it happens is a total. Take two rows of a Table 1 with an overall column: Age Overall Exposed (N = 282) Unexposed (N = 1,218) 70-89 165 35 130 90+ 18 1 17 Only 1 exposed person is aged 90+, so you hide that number. But the row still shows 18 overall and 17 unexposed, and 18 - 17 = 1. So you must hide a second number in the same row, the 17. Now the column gives the 1 back instead: the exposed column shows N = 282 and every other age group, so the missing 1 is what is left over. So a number in the same column must go too, and then one more to close the square: Age Overall Exposed (N = 282) Unexposed (N = 1,218) 70-89 165 .. .. 90+ 18 .. .. A reader can still see that the four hidden numbers add up to 165 and 18 across, and to what is left of each column. But that fits every split from 0 to 18 exposed people aged 90+, so the 1 cannot be found. The numbers you hide to protect a small one must not be small themselves. If you hid a 1 and a 3 in the same column, a reader could still see from N that they add up to 4, and 4 people is a small cell in its own right. Hide numbers so that the hidden ones in each row and each column add up to at least 5. Here they do: 165 and 18 across, 36 and 147 down. Usually the better answer is the one DST's rule itself points to: merge categories ("aggregeres yderligere"). Here a single 70+ group would leave nothing to hide. Where to look for numbers that give a hidden one back: Totals, overall columns and N in the header. Each of them makes a sum that one hidden number can be subtracted from. A row or column with a total needs either no hidden number or at least two, and the hidden ones together must come to at least 5. As the example shows, the second one often pulls in more. Percentages. A percentage is a number of people in disguise: 0.4% of 282 is 1 person. If you hide a count, hide its percentage too. The same people in two tables. If Table 1 shows 18 people aged 90+ and Table 2 shows the 17 unexposed among them, the two tables together give the 1 back. Check every table you take home together, and the ones you took home earlier. Subgroups and sensitivity analyses. If the main analysis has 120 people and a sensitivity analysis on almost the same people has 118, a reader knows that 2 people are in one and not in the other. When the difference is below 5, do not give both sizes exactly. One way is to round them, for example to the nearest 10; another is to give only the main analysis' size. The same goes for the exclusion boxes in a flowchart (Phase 10 - Build your study population). The mark you use for a hidden number. When you hide some numbers and show the rest exactly, a mix of marks gives the small one away: if it says <5 and the numbers hidden to protect it say .. , a reader knows which one is 1 to 4, and next to a total that narrows it down, sometimes to a single value. Give every hidden number in a table the same neutral mark, such as .. (a hidden 17 is not <5 anyway). Saying in the methods that counts below 5 are hidden is fine, since DST's threshold is public.

sections.title: Export and repatriation
sections.heading: Min, max, median and percentiles can point to one person
sections.text: A minimum or a maximum is one person's actual value, and a median or another percentile is often one too. DST's guidance (PDF above, page 6) allows max, min and percentiles such as the median only when there is no risk of identifying individuals: > "Ingen personer må derfor kunne genkendes i det hjemsendte output." In English: no person may be recognisable in the output you send home. The guidance tells you to look for outliers first and remove them if needed, and for max and min it requires that the observations at each end of the distribution lie close together, so that no one stands out. If in doubt, they must not be sent home. In practice: a median and quartiles of age in a group of several hundred people are shared by many and point to no one. A maximum income, or the range of a variable in a small subgroup, can point to one person. Leave min and max out unless you need them, and ask your data manager when you are unsure.

sections.title: Export and repatriation
sections.heading: Figures and curves
sections.text: A figure is judged as if it were the table behind it: > "For formater, der ikke indeholder tabelceller, såsom figurer eller grafer, > er en god tommelfingerregel, at de skulle have mindst 3 observationer pr. > tabelcelle, hvis de blev konverteret til tabeller." In English: for formats without table cells, such as figures and graphs, a good rule of thumb is that they would have at least 3 observations per cell if they were converted to tables. So every bar, point and histogram bin needs the minimum number of people behind it, and a plot with one mark per person (a scatterplot of individuals) cannot leave. DST's guidance (page 7) names three further things to watch: Outliers: a single extreme point or a long axis can show one person's value. Kaplan-Meier curves: "man fx med Kaplan Meier kurver skal være opmærksom på små populationer" (with Kaplan-Meier curves, for example, watch out for small populations). Each step in a curve is one or a few events, and the numbers in a risk table are table cells. Data stored inside the figure file: the file must not carry the observations the figure was drawn from. The guidance suggests PDF as one way to make sure. How to build figures that meet this is on Figures.

sections.title: Export and repatriation
sections.heading: Missing values (NA) are cells too
sections.text: A count of missing values is a cell like any other. If 1 to 4 people are missing on a variable, that count may not be repatriated. Merge it into another category, or hide it the way you hide any other small cell (and check that it cannot be worked out from the total). Agree the solution with your data manager if neither fits. Make a quick overview of missing values, so you see the small cells immediately instead of adding figures up in your head: table() hides NA by default; useNA = "always" shows the NA row. See Phase 7 - table() hides NA.

sections.title: Export and repatriation
sections.heading: How the upload works
sections.text: You upload from the research machine. On its remote desktop there is a shortcut called "Hjemtag Filer" (retrieve files), which opens the repatriation tool of DDV App in the browser. There are three steps: upload the files, check them, then download them to your own computer through DDV App. The tool scans each file for possible microdata. The scan is a supplement: DST states that it "kan ikke erstatte manuel kontrol" (cannot replace a manual check), so the check on this page is still yours to do. If a file gets a risk message, you must add a remark saying what the file contains. DST's control staff read it. Before the files are released you confirm that they follow DST's rules. Afterwards DST checks files with a risk message, files over 1 MB, files that could not be scanned, and a random 10% of the rest. Give the files names that say what is in them ( table1_baseline.csv , not output.csv ): it helps the person who checks the file, and it helps you find it again. If you are in doubt about a file, DST's instruction is not to take it home until you have aggregated further or asked. General questions go to DDVHjemtag@dst.dk, described with made-up numbers, never with real data.

sections.title: Export and repatriation
sections.heading: Checklist before uploading
sections.text: [ ] No individual-level data - only aggregated results [ ] All cells ≥ 5 observations [ ] No hidden number can be worked out from a total, a percentage, another table or an earlier export - merge categories, or hide more numbers so the hidden ones in each row and column add up to at least 5 [ ] Hidden numbers share one mark (e.g. .. ), so the small one cannot be told apart from those hidden to protect it [ ] Min, max, median and percentiles: no outliers, nothing that points to one person [ ] Figures: every bar, point and bin has at least 5 people behind it; no marks for individuals; the file does not carry the underlying data [ ] No count of 1-4 missing (NA): merge or hide it [ ] Descriptive filenames; no microdata in scripts or logs (no pnr values, no printed rows) [ ] File type is on DST's approved list, with the right extension: spreadsheets (xlsx, csv), text (txt), HTML, PDF, Word (docx), code (R, SAS, Stata), images (png, jpg, svg, eps and others), presentations (pptx). Not .rds , .RData , Parquet or JSON, and not a saved model object

sections.heading: After the export

sections.title: Extract from LPR
sections.text: This page has the code for pulling diagnoses out of LPR: for one outcome, for several outcomes at once, and as a reusable function, get_lpr_diagnoses() , that the later pages call. You need it whenever an outcome, an exposure or a comorbidity is defined by hospital diagnoses. When you are done you have one table with pnr , contact date and ICD code from LPR2 and LPR3 combined, and you know how to reduce it to one row per person. Read Understand LPR first. The code relies on what that page explains: the two periods (LPR2 and LPR3), the D-prefix, the diagnosis types (A/B/G) and the filter for retracted diagnoses. The extraction pattern itself (open lazily, filter, collect() ) is the one from Phase 5 and Phase 6, applied to each LPR period. The examples assume you already have a cohort: cohort , a data.frame with pnr and index_date per person, built in Phase 10. That phase comes later and uses the pattern you learn here, so read them in order and come back to this code once your cohort exists. They also use inner_join() and bind_rows() , explained in Phase 12.

sections.title: Extract from LPR
sections.heading: Before you run the code
sections.text: Check the column names in your own delivery. The examples use the names the registers typically have, but LPR_A renamed a number of them, and what you were given is not what the register contains. List them with arrow::schema() , and look the confirmed ones up in Overview of registers. Two facts from Understand LPR that the code depends on. Use the LPR_A files and filter them with lprindberetningssystem == "LPR3" (why), and expect a spike in diagnosis counts around 2019-2020 if your analysis counts diagnoses or looks at trends (why). Check that your LPR2 files reach the end of March 2019 before you rely on the lprindberetningssystem == "LPR3" filter. The filter solves one confirmed problem: lpr_a_kontakt also holds older LPR2 contacts, which would be counted twice if you did not filter them out. It does not guarantee that your combined series has no gap around the transition. DST's LPR2 files end on 31 March 2019, but the files in your own delivery can end earlier. Check it before you rely on a count that spans the transition: If that date reaches the end of DST's own LPR2 files (31 March 2019; the regions switched their reporting to LPR3 on 2-3 February or 2-3 March 2019, see Understand LPR), the filter is safe as written. If it does not, do not drop the lprindberetningssystem filter to get the gap back: that reintroduces the duplicates it exists to remove. One fix is a date cutover instead of a blanket filter. The same check applies to any other register that changed system or format during your study period.

sections.title: Extract from LPR
sections.heading: Private hospitals are in a separate register
sections.text: Private hospitals and clinics report to a separate system, MiniPas, which Sundhedsdatastyrelsen documents as a register of its own, MiniPas - LPR, covering 2002 onwards. At DST the corresponding registers are priv_adm , priv_diag and their satellites (2002 to 31 March 2019, DST's register overview). They are not part of lpr_adm and lpr_diag , and this page does not extract them. The exception is a small group of private or association-owned hospitals (mainly hospices) that report to LPR itself (Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's LPR documentation). If your study needs private-hospital diagnoses from before 2019, check that the priv_ registers are in your delivery. They do not appear by filtering LPR2 or LPR3 differently. lpr_a_kontakt holds MiniPas rows under lprindberetningssystem == "MiniPAS" , but only for contacts that ended in 2017 or later (DST's remark on LPR_A_KONTAKT), not the full register.

sections.title: Extract from LPR
sections.heading: One outcome or several: choose the route
sections.text: Which code you use depends on how many outcomes your study has: One outcome (or a couple): filter on your ICD codes inside the query, so only the matching rows are read. That is the worked example below. Several outcomes: pull all A and B diagnoses once into a table called all_dx , then filter that table per outcome. It is the same code with three small changes, see Several outcomes at once. You query LPR once instead of scanning the registers again for each outcome, and the function get_lpr_diagnoses() does it in one call. Either way the shape is the same, and it follows from how LPR is built: a hospital contact's pnr and date are in one table and the ICD code in another, so every extract is a join between a contact register and a diagnosis register, done once per LPR period and then stacked. The examples use read_register("name") (fastreg); without fastreg use open_dataset("path/to/ /") . LPR is one of the largest registers, so it must be in parquet: reading it from SAS pulls the whole thing into RAM. Convert first if nobody has: Parquet and fastreg. The code filters to your cohort with semi_join(tibble(pnr = ...)) rather than filter(pnr %in% ...) , because it pushes down into Arrow/DuckDB better and needs no !! - see semi_join() . You still need !! for a local code list inside filter() , e.g. substr(c_diag, 2, 4) %in% !!CODES . CODES must then hold three-character codes. The left side is always three characters, so a four-character code such as E119 silently matches nothing: filter on E11 and narrow afterwards on the full c_diag .

sections.title: Extract from LPR
sections.heading: Step 4: stack the three extracts
sections.text: This works only because all three steps produced the same column names: What must match, and what you choose. The register's own names ( pnr , recnum , d_inddto , c_diag , c_diagtype , dw_ek_kontakt , kont_starttidspunkt , diag_kode ) must be spelled exactly as they are in the register. The names on the left of = inside select() are yours: date_contact and icd3 are chosen here, not required. LPR2's date column is d_inddto and LPR3's is kont_starttidspunkt , so giving both the name date_contact is what lets bind_rows() stack them in step 4. Keep those harmonised names identical across the three extracts; the object names ( lpr2_dm ) can be whatever you like. Many codes? Build the regex instead of typing it: F-codes (dementia, depression)? Extend CODES_REGEX , e.g. "^DE1[0-4] ^DF0[0-3] ^DG30" , and do not skip step 3: contacts at psychiatric departments before 2019 are only in the psychiatric registers. A shorter version you may meet, and three ways it goes wrong on DST data A colleague may have shown you this shorter approach: It is shorter but has three pitfalls on DST data: 1. D-prefix error: "^S72" does not match "DS72..." , so it returns zero rows with no error message. Use "^DS72" (with D) or strip the prefix first. 2. left_join instead of inner_join : keeps all admissions from lpr_adm , including those with no matching diagnosis. Unnecessarily heavy on national registers. 3. No pnr filter: loads the entire population's data. Correct when building a cohort (Phase 10), not when extracting from an existing one.

sections.title: Extract from LPR
sections.heading: Several outcomes at once
sections.text: If your study has more than one LPR outcome, do not run the steps above once per outcome: that scans the registers again every time. Query LPR once, keep all A and B diagnoses in a table called all_dx , and filter that table per outcome. It is the same four steps, with three changes: 1. Drop CODES_REGEX and the grepl() line from every step. You are no longer filtering on codes at the source. 2. Name the results lpr2_dx , lpr3_dx , lpr2_psyk_dx and combine them into all_dx instead of dm_dx . Always include the psychiatric step here - all_dx is meant to serve outcomes you have not thought of yet. 3. Save it , so later scripts reuse it rather than re-querying: saveRDS(all_dx, "path/to/all_dx.rds") . The joins, the keys, the renames and bind_rows() are unchanged. The function get_lpr_diagnoses() further down this page does those steps in one call. Define the function first, then run: all_dx is large: it holds every A and B diagnosis for your whole cohort in RAM. On a big cohort, save it and work from the .rds , and free the memory with rm() + gc() when you are done (Phase 5).

sections.title: Extract from LPR
sections.heading: From all_dx to one outcome: first event per person
sections.text: all_dx has one row per diagnosis, so a person with five hip fracture contacts has five rows. An analysis dataset needs one row per person, with the date of their first qualifying diagnosis. The four lines from group_by() to ungroup() turn one into the other. From event log to one row per person shows the other way of collapsing. What slice(1) does. slice(n) picks rows by position, not by value: slice(1) keeps the first row of each group. It only means "earliest" because arrange(date_contact) put the oldest first. With arrange(desc(date_contact)) the same slice(1) gives you the latest contact instead. See slice() . Three things to check in this block: Keep the ungroup() : a grouped table stays grouped, and every later mutate() or summarise() then operates per person instead of on the whole table, without telling you. Ties are broken arbitrarily: if someone has two qualifying contacts on the same date, slice(1) keeps whichever row came first. That does not matter for a first-event date, since the date is the same, but it does if you also keep columns that differ between the two rows, such as the hospital or the specific ICD code. Repeated pnr in the cohort: step 4 collapses to one row per pnr , and the final left_join() is on pnr alone. If your cohort has repeated pnr (e.g. a comparison group matched with replacement), that join can attach one person's event to the wrong index_date . See the callout on repeated pnr on Comparison cohort. Excluding prevalent cases (people who already had the diagnosis before the index date) happens in Phase 10. Once you have done that, use cohort_clean in place of cohort above. Using duckplyr instead of dplyr? union_all() combines before collect() and needs identical column names and types, so rename the LPR3 columns to the LPR2 format first. Try it yourself: runnable example on synthetic data (local R, not DST) This example requires RStudio installed locally on your computer - not the DST server. The synthetic data package ( fiktive ) is not available on DST. Download R: cran.r-project.org · Download RStudio: posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop It uses open_dataset() on local synth_data/ folders; fastreg's read_register() is for a configured DST project, not ad-hoc local folders. The example extracts CVD diagnoses (ischaemic heart disease, ICD-10 I20–I25) from LPR2 and LPR3 combined - the same steps as above, runnable locally on synthetic data. It follows the one-outcome route: specific codes are filtered out before collect() . The synthetic LPR data is generated with fiktive , which you already know from Phase 6 - First extraction. Phase 6 saves bef and lpr_adm only. Run the block below for the diagnosis tables. It uses the same n , window, and seed, so lpr_adm matches. The path is relative to your working directory - check with getwd() . If you have already run the preparation block in Phase 6, synth_data/bef/ and synth_data/lpr_adm/ are already saved. This page still needs lpr_diag , lpr_a_kontakt , and lpr_a_diagnose from the block above. On this fixture senere_afkraeftet is never "Ja" , so the retracted-diagnosis filter below removes nothing. Keep it: that is the filter you use on real LPR3.

sections.title: Extract from LPR
sections.heading: get_lpr_diagnoses() - the whole pattern as one function
sections.text: Everything above is the same four steps with the code list swapped. Rather than copy them per outcome, wrap them once: get_lpr_diagnoses() takes the code list as an argument and returns the combined extract. Define it at the top of your script, or in a functions.R you source() . Use it when you have more than one or two outcomes: One place to fix when a register or a column name changes, instead of one fix per copy Each outcome becomes a single call rather than ~40 lines It keeps the diagnosis-type column ( c_diagtype ), so you can narrow the case definition for a sensitivity analysis later (see Diagnosis types) without re-querying LPR Read the four steps above first: when a column name in your delivery differs from the one the function assumes, you need to recognise which step it belongs to. Use the function. One call per extraction; only CODES changes: Two ways to call the function, depending on RAM. For a few codes, pass them via icd_codes : they are filtered before collect() , so only those rows are pulled, e.g. get_lpr_diagnoses(pnr_list, icd_codes = c("E11", "I50")) . For many different outcomes, pull everything once (omit icd_codes ), save with saveRDS() , free memory with rm() + gc() (Phase 5), then filter locally with readRDS() %>% filter(icd3 %in% ...) , so you do not scan the registers again for each outcome.

sections.title: Extract from LPR
sections.heading: From event log to one row per person
sections.text: get_lpr_diagnoses() (and the extracts above) return an event log : many rows per person, one per diagnosis. An analysis needs one row per person. Two patterns turn it into one row per person: A) One outcome with a date (e.g. time-to-event): filter to the codes, and take each person's first contact, the slice(1) pattern above. B) Many binary variables at once (e.g. comorbidity flags): build the flags, collapse with any() , and merge onto the cohort. any() returns TRUE if the person has at least one matching diagnosis in the window (0/1, not a count): It gives one 0/1 flag per comorbidity per person, ready to enter your model as covariates. (The same group_by(pnr, index_date) %>% summarise(any(.)) pattern is used on the NMI page, for example.) Step 2 groups on pnr and index_date , and step 3 rejoins on both. If your cohort has one row per person, that gives the same result as pnr alone. If a pnr is repeated (e.g. a comparison group matched with replacement), it keeps each row's flags tied to that row's own index date, see the callout on repeated pnr on Comparison cohort.

sections.title: Extract from LPR
sections.heading: Remove unwanted diagnoses
sections.text: A few codes record why a person was at the hospital rather than a disease of their own, and are usually removed from both outcomes and comorbidity: "Healthy companion": someone admitted as a companion to another patient, e.g. a parent, ICD-10 DZ763 . Related contact/observation codes with no disease: DZ032 , DZ038 , DZ039 . What to remove depends on your project and question: DZ03 (observation for suspected disease) is genuinely relevant in some studies and should be kept there. The pattern is adapted from the Plana-Ripoll group's code on OSF; verify against your own data.

sections.text: This page is the entry to Phase 11. You have built your cohort in Phase 10: a table with pnr and index_date per person. Here you extract the outcomes and covariates for those people, one register at a time, and save each extraction as its own .rds file. The table below sends you to the page for each type of variable. In Phase 12 - Assemble and prepare the dataset you link the files into one analysis dataset. Gather everything you need from one register in one extraction: all the BEF columns in one, all the LPR diagnoses in one, and so on.

sections.title: Extracting data step by step
sections.text: This page teaches the one pattern that every extraction in the guide follows: open a register as a lazy connection, filter the rows, select the columns, and only then fetch the result into R with collect() . Read it after Phase 4 - File types and loading, where you saw that parquet registers are opened lazily, and before you try the pattern yourself in Phase 6. When you are done you can read any extraction in the guide, and you can tell whether an object is data in R or still an unsent query. The reason for the pattern is size. read_csv() or readRDS() reads the entire file into memory at once, which works for your own small datasets, but BEF and LMDB have many millions of rows and would crash your session. A lazy connection lets you filter before you fetch, so only the rows you need reach memory.

sections.title: Extracting data step by step
sections.heading: The pattern: open connection → filter → select → fetch
sections.text: Think of a supermarket. You can either buy the whole shop and sort at home - or send a shopping list and only have what is on the list delivered. Lazy loading is the latter: you describe what you want, and only fetch the items at the end with collect() . Step 1 - open the register as a lazy connection. Pick the way that matches your project (the rest of the pattern is identical whichever you choose): #### fastreg (recommended) This assumes you have pointed fastreg at your registers with one options() call at the top of the script - see Point fastreg at your registers. That call is not repeated in the guide's examples: it belongs at the top of the script, once, not before each read. #### arrow (any parquet) Steps 2-3 - filter, select, then fetch. bef is now a lazy connection (no data has moved). The rest is the same regardless of how you opened it: Steps 1 and 2 are instructions only and cost almost no memory. collect() in step 3 is the only line that moves data. Why rename_with(tolower) as the first step? Column names in DST registers are not capitalised consistently ( PNR , pnr , Pnr ). With everything in lower case from the start, the rest of your code can use pnr everywhere. Add it right after read_register() or open_dataset() , before you filter or select.

sections.title: Extracting data step by step
sections.heading: Filter rows and select columns before collect()
sections.text: Calling collect() before you have narrowed the rows can crash your session, and because everyone shares the server's RAM, it slows the server for everyone else at the same time. The more you filter and select in advance, the faster and more stably it runs. Rule of thumb: filter() limits rows. select() limits columns. Use both before collect() , never after.

sections.title: Extracting data step by step
sections.heading: Very large registers: compute() instead of collect()
sections.text: On the very largest registers (LMDB, laboratory results), even a filtered result can be too big to pull into R comfortably, or you may need it as the input to several later queries. Then end the pipe with compute() instead of collect() : collect() compute() Where the result ends up an R data frame in R's memory a temporary table inside DuckDB What you can do next anything in R more dplyr verbs, then collect() Use it when the result is small and you are ready to analyse the result is large, or several later queries start from it compute() does not make the data disappear: DuckDB still holds the result in the server's memory until your R session ends. It only saves you from copying it into R as well, and from re-reading the whole register for every later query. So the rule above still applies: filter() and select() first. It works on the DuckDB-backed tables that read_register() and read_parquet_duckdb() give you. On an open_dataset() table (arrow), add to_duckdb() before compute() . Later: keeping only your cohort. Once you have built a study population, you will usually want only your cohort's people from a register. That is done with semi_join() against your cohort's pnr , and it first matters once the cohort exists (Phase 10). Never write an actual CPR number (pnr) in your code. Use only variable names and vectors. A CPR number identifies a person, and a script is the file you are most likely to show a colleague or bring home. What !! means, and when you need it Sometimes you filter on a list you defined in R yourself - typically a set of ICD or year codes: The lazy query is not executed by R, but by the database engine (Arrow/DuckDB), which runs separately from R and does not know your local variables. When the query is built, dplyr checks each name: if the register has a column called my_codes , it uses the column; if not, it looks up the R vector my_codes and copies its values into the query. So the code above usually works without !! too. The risk is a name clash: if your local variable has the same name as a column (e.g. a local year and the register's year column), the column silently wins. !! removes that ambiguity - it means: "this is an R object, not a column name - look up its values in R and use them in the query." Rule of thumb: if you refer to a column in the register, write the name directly. If you refer to an R variable you created yourself, putting !! in front of it is a recommended safeguard against a name clash. The other place this comes up is subsetting a register to your cohort's pnr . There you use semi_join() , which takes an ordinary local table and avoids !! entirely. See Extract from LPR.

sections.heading: Check: do you have data or just a connection?
sections.text: Many errors come from believing you have fetched data when you still have an unsent query. Ask the object what it is: What class() returns What it means What to do "tbl_df" "tbl" "data.frame" (and no "prudent_duckplyr_df" ) Data is in R Nothing - you are ready "prudent_duckplyr_df" "duckplyr_df" "tbl_df" "tbl" "data.frame" Unsent DuckDB query (from read_parquet_duckdb() , and from read_register() in fastreg 0.14.3 or newer) Add %>% collect() "tbl_duckdb_connection" ... Unsent DuckDB query (from to_duckdb() , and from read_register() in fastreg 0.14.2 or older) Add %>% collect() "FileSystemDataset" ... "ArrowObject" Arrow connection (from open_dataset() ) Filter/select, then %>% collect() "arrow_dplyr_query" Unsent Arrow query Add %>% collect() Which of the two DuckDB rows you get from read_register() depends on the fastreg version: up to 0.14.2 it opens the parquet with arrow and passes it to DuckDB, from 0.14.3 it uses duckplyr. Check yours with packageVersion("fastreg") . The duckplyr result says "data.frame" even though nothing has been fetched yet: look for "prudent_duckplyr_df" . As long as that is in the list, the data has not been collected. ( "Table" is an Arrow table that is already in memory, which you rarely meet in this guide.) RAM is shared: clean up with rm() and gc() after large extractions On DST all users share the server's memory. When the memory bar in RStudio turns red, it slows everyone's sessions. rm() removes the object from your active session - it can no longer be used in code and disappears from the Environment panel (top right in RStudio). gc() ( garbage collection ) does not affect your session - all your other objects are still there. R normally holds on to freed memory a little longer, because it is faster to reuse than to request new memory from the operating system. gc() makes R free that memory now, so it can be returned to the operating system and become available to other users on the shared DST server (how much is actually handed back, and when, depends on the system). You lose nothing - it helps your colleagues.

[] Parquet, Arrow and DuckDB: what each one is and when each is used You do not need to know these names to use the pattern above, but here is what happens under the hood. Parquet is a file format that stores data column by column rather than row by row. If you only want pnr and year , the computer reads only those two columns - not the rest. That is why it is fast. Getting your registers into parquet is covered on Parquet and fastreg. Arrow and DuckDB are the two engines that run your query against the parquet. Both are lazy and both end at collect() , so your code looks the same either way. If you hit an error about an "unsupported function" in Arrow, that is the coverage gap: switch to DuckDB with to_duckdb() , or collect() into R first and do the operation there.

sections.title: Family links: parents, siblings and parents' characteristics
sections.text: Use this page if your study needs to link a child to its parents, and from there to siblings or to a parent's characteristics. It is the first step of a sibling design, and also of any study that needs the mother's or father's education, income or diagnoses.

sections.title: Family links: parents, siblings and parents' characteristics
sections.heading: What the link is
sections.text: BEF has two columns for the link: mor_id and far_id , the person id of the mother and of the father. They come from the Civil Registration System (CPR). Three things about them are easy to miss. They are the legal parents, not necessarily the biological ones. CPR holds the legal relationship, and it keeps only the current one: "Danish legislation prohibits the CRS of keeping information on previous legal relationships. Thus, for example, for adopted children, the CRS contains information on the legal parents only" (Pedersen et al. 2006). Statistics Denmark (DST) is more careful still: "Parent child relations in CPR is an administrative relations, which cannot necessarily be sided be legal or biological parent-child relations" (DST, documentation of the Relatives statistics, accuracy and reliability). The Medical Birth Register records a different relation: "parents in the MBR are the (assumed) biological parents, whereas the parents registered in the Danish Civil Registration System are the legal parents and thus not necessarily equivalent to the former (unless a paternity trial has been resolved)" (Bliddal et al. 2018). See The mother at birth. A missing id means no link is registered. It does not mean the parent is unknown to the family. See the coverage table below. A parent can be of the other sex than the column. A co-mother is registered in the father's place, and DST marks that in FTBARN (see Adoption and other non-biological relations).

sections.title: Family links: parents, siblings and parents' characteristics
sections.heading: Coverage by birth cohort
sections.text: BEF takes mor_id and far_id from CPR. The shares below are for persons born in Denmark, from CPR as it stood in 2006 (Pedersen et al. 2006). They are the nearest guide to what your delivery holds, but count the missing links in your own data. Born in Denmark Link to a mother Link to a father 1950 8.0% 7.6% 1960 98.7% 95.7% 1970 99.9% 99.2% The same paper says the links for persons born in Denmark in 1969 or later are "considered to be 100% correct", and those for 1960-1968 "almost correct", because the links for 1969-1978 were checked against the parish registers (Pedersen et al. 2006). Why older cohorts have fewer links CPR started in 1968, and the parental links were first built from families living at the same address. Until 1978 a link was erased when the child moved away from home, when a parent moved, when the child had children or when the child turned 18. From 1978 links are kept permanently, and from then on they follow the legal relationship (Pedersen et al. 2006). You may also read that everyone born in Denmark in 1960 or later has a complete link to both parents (Pedersen 2013). That is about the Family Relations Database at the National Centre for Register-based Research (NCRR), which keeps only the links it deems valid. It is not a description of mor_id and far_id in BEF. For people born abroad the links are much rarer, because parent and child are not linked at immigration, and a parent needs a Danish CPR number to be linked at all (Pedersen et al. 2006; DST, Relatives , accuracy and reliability). In Pedersen et al., 29.8% of those born abroad in 1980 and 94.2% of those born in 1990 have a mother link. Expect a missing mor_id and far_id for most immigrants, and report the share. For newborns , the second parent can be missing for up to half a year after the birth, because it takes that long to register. DST names this as most common for births in the second half of a year and for unmarried parents, and advises against studying the relatives of newborns in the latest reference year (DST, Relatives , accuracy and reliability). Persons born before 1967 have too few registered parents and siblings, and for those born before 1935 the undercount may be very large (DST, Relatives , accuracy and reliability).

sections.title: Family links: parents, siblings and parents' characteristics
sections.heading: Step 1 - Take the link from BEF
sections.text: BEF is a snapshot register (see DST pitfalls, pitfall 5), so the same child has one row per snapshot, and mor_id and far_id can differ between snapshots or be missing in some of them. A parent can be added to the child after the first snapshots, for example. There is no single correct value, so you have to pick a rule and write it in your methods. The rule below takes, for each child, the first non-missing value from the snapshots at or after the child's birth. For a child born before the first BEF snapshot (December 1985) that is the link as it stood in 1985 or later. The rule is written as a function, because Step 3 runs it again for the siblings outside your cohort. A child with NA for both has no link in BEF. Count them by birth year before you go on, and report how many children each analysis loses on that account. A different rule, such as the most frequent value or the latest snapshot, is equally valid if you state it. What matters is that the rule is the same for every child.
