sections.title: Family links: parents, siblings and parents' characteristics
sections.heading: The mother at birth: the Medical Birth Register
sections.text: BEF holds the parents CPR has now. The Medical Birth Register (MFR) holds, for each birth in Denmark, the (assumed) biological parents (Bliddal et al. 2018). Sundhedsdatastyrelsen takes the link between mother and child from CPR ("udtræk fra CPR som giver den fornødne kobling mellem mor og barn", register declaration, section 0.7), and Bliddal et al. describe the identification of the mother for linkage as "virtually complete and ... of very high validity". MFR is the better source of the mother when: the child may have been adopted, because BEF then holds the adoptive parents; the child was stillborn or died soon after birth. MFR has every birth, live or stillborn (register declaration, section 1.1), and a child who died before the next BEF snapshot is in no snapshot at all; you need twins and other multiple births, which MFR records ( barnsnummer_flerfoldsfoedsel ). DST has no MFR table for births from 1973 to 1996. For those years FTBARN's mor1 , the first mother registered in CPR, is the nearest equivalent (see Adoption). Two limits: Births in Denmark only, and until 2018 only to mothers with a Danish CPR number (register declaration, section 1.2). From 2019 a birth counts even if the mother has no Danish CPR number, so check ErCPRnummerGyldigt_Mor before you join on the mother's number. The declaration says where the mother's link comes from, not the father's. Compare cpr_fader with far_id in BEF before you rely on it. MFR's column names, and a check of BEF against MFR Births Table Child Mother Father 1997-2018 mfr cpr_barn cpr_moder cpr_fader 2019 and later mfr_nyfoedte CPRnummer_Barn CPRnummer_Mor CPRnummer_Far

sections.title: Family links: parents, siblings and parents' characteristics
sections.heading: Step 2 - Check for adoption with FTBARN
sections.text: Do this before you build siblings. BEF only has the current legal parents, so an adopted child shares mor_id and far_id with its adoptive parents' other children, and Step 3 would make them siblings. BEF cannot tell you whether the relation is adoptive. FTBARN, the child file of the fertility database, can. It has one row per child from 1973 and, besides the parents ( mor1 , far1 ), two columns that mark the relation: mor_foed_adop for the mother and far_foed_adop for the father. DST describes them as marking whether information in the background registers (the Adoption Register, CPR and the Medical Birth Register) points to an adoptive or other non-biological relation. Codes 11 to 18 are a presumed non-biological relation, codes 21 to 23 a presumed biological one, and 30 to 39 cover children born abroad, children born before 1973 and relations with no sign of adoption or early registration. For the father's column DST's text gives 1991 instead of 1973 in the grouping, so the cut-off for fathers is unclear. The full list is in the value sets under FTBARN. Four points from DST's own documentation: It is presumed, not known. DST: "A biological relation can only be determined with a DNA test, which is not available in the background registers" (our translation). A child conceived with donor sperm or donor egg looks like a biological relation in the registers. Do not count adoptions with it. DST: "It makes no sense to count the number of adopted or biological relations from the variable" (our translation). Use it to select or exclude, not to estimate how many. Code 14 is not an adoption. It marks a parent of the other sex than the column, so a co-mother is registered in the father's column with code 14. Code 12 can concern the other parent. The child is in the Adoption Register, but the adoptive relation may be to the other parent. In FTBARN, mor1 is the first mother valid in CPR, and mor2 the latest one when it differs. The relation of mor1 to the child is in mor_foed_adop . No adoption markers for 2019-2023, and wrong ones in older deliveries DST changed the adoption columns in a correction of 30 October 2025. Version 2 of the fertility tables for reference years up to 2023 sets mor_foed_adop and far_foed_adop to unknown (99) for 2019 to 2023, because data are missing to form new adoption markers for those years. Version 1 held other values by mistake. For children born in 2019 to 2023 adoption therefore cannot be identified in FTBARN, and a delivery made before the correction has wrong values for those years (DST, FTBARN register history). Check the version column in your delivery. The code below sorts each parent into DST's groups. Codes 31 to 39, 99 and a missing value all become "unknown": a child in those groups is not non-biological, it is a child the registers cannot say anything about. State in your methods that the group is presumed biological, and how many children were "unknown".

sections.title: Family links: parents, siblings and parents' characteristics
sections.heading: Step 3 - Siblings
sections.text: Siblings are children with the same parent id, and the type depends on how many parents they share: Full siblings share both mother and father. Maternal half-siblings share the mother only, and paternal half-siblings share the father only. Do not count a pair as full siblings when one of the fathers is missing. The pair shares a mother, so it is at least a maternal half-sibling pair, and the father is unknown. The code below gives those pairs their own type ("maternal, father unknown"). Say in your methods how you handle them, and run the analysis both ways if there are many of them. The siblings you need are not only the ones in your cohort. If the exposed child has a brother who is not in the cohort, he is still a sibling. So first find everyone in BEF who has the same mother or father as someone in your cohort, and run the rule from Step 1 for them too. If your design needs biological siblings, use the groups from Step 2 to decide which children to keep, for example only children whose mother and father are both "presumed biological", and say so in your methods. The famnet package by Luke Johnston finds sibling pairs with fmn_siblings() , labelling each pair "sibling" without the split into full and half siblings above. It is on GitHub only, so it may not install on your project. See Algorithms and packages. For a sibling analysis you also need a family id for the strata. For full siblings the mother and father ids together identify the family. With half-siblings in the data, a person can belong to more than one family, so decide how the strata are formed and state it.

sections.title: Family links: parents, siblings and parents' characteristics
sections.heading: Step 4 - A parent's characteristic at the child's birth
sections.text: Use mor_id or far_id as the pnr of the parent, and look the parent up in the register that holds the characteristic, in the year that matters. That could be the mother's education, income or employment at the child's birth, or her diagnoses before it. The year rule is the one for any other person, so it is not repeated here. See When each dimension is measured for education, employment and income. Before you do this, check that the parent ids match the person ids in the registers you look them up in. Most non-missing mor_id values should appear as a pnr in BEF. If they do not, the ids are not comparable in your project and the lookup will return nothing. A parent who was not living in Denmark in the year, or who died before it, will have no row. That is a missing value in your analysis, so handle it as one (see Missing data).

sections.title: Family links: parents, siblings and parents' characteristics
sections.heading: What to write in your methods
sections.text: The source of the link (BEF mor_id and far_id , MFR for the parents at birth, FTBARN if you use it) and the rule for choosing between snapshots. That the link is the legal, administrative relation in CPR. The birth cohorts you include and the share with a missing parent link, by birth year, and how immigrants were handled. How half-siblings and pairs with a missing parent were handled. If you use the adoption markers, which codes you used and that the relation is presumed.

sections.title: Figures for publication
sections.text: Use this page when your analysis is done and you want figures for the paper: bar charts of counts, proportions with confidence intervals, and forest plots of model estimates, built with ggplot2 and saved to a file. You start from the analysis-ready dataset (Phase 12) or a fitted model (Regression, Time-to-event). On DST a figure is judged as if it were the table behind it, so you aggregate first and plot the aggregated numbers: a scatterplot with one point per person cannot leave. The rules are on Export and repatriation. Paths and variable names in the examples are generic - replace them with your own. ggplot2 must be installed in your R environment on DST.

sections.title: Figures for publication
sections.heading: Bar chart of counts
sections.text: Build the figure from your dataset. Here we count the number of people per group and draw a bar chart. With simulated numbers the figure looks like this: !Bar chart produced by the code above. The numbers are simulated. The key parts: aes() maps columns to the figure's axes ( x , y ) and e.g. fill (colour). geom_col() draws bars from values you have counted yourself (unlike geom_bar() , which counts rows for you). labs() sets the title and axis/legend text; theme_minimal() gives a clean look.

sections.title: Figures for publication
sections.heading: Customise the look
sections.text: A figure is built up layer by layer with + : you start with ggplot(...) and add a new line for each thing you want to change. What a function should control, you write inside its parentheses as an argument, e.g. labs(title = "...") . Because we saved the figure in the object p in the code block above, you can build on it with + : you write only what you want to add or change, not the whole code again. (This requires that you have run the first code block, so p exists in your session.) Each line is one layer. The order mostly does not matter, with one exception: a complete theme such as theme_minimal() resets every theme setting, so put your own theme(...) after it, or the legend goes back to the right. A few typical moves: Colour by a variable goes inside aes() (e.g. fill = outcome as in the example at the top of the page - made a factor there, since a numeric 0/1 would get a continuous colour scale); you then control the colours with scale_fill_manual(values = ...) or a ready-made palette ( scale_fill_brewer() ). If you instead want one fixed colour for all bars, write fill = "steelblue" inside geom_col() , i.e. outside aes() . Axes: scale_y_continuous(...) controls breaks; coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 100)) zooms to a min/max without dropping data ( lims() removes values outside the limits). Layout: coord_flip() makes the bars horizontal (good for many categories); facet_wrap(~ variable) makes one panel per group. Each function has many more arguments - look them up with e.g. ?labs or ?scale_fill_manual .

sections.title: Figures for publication
sections.heading: Figure with error bars (proportion and 95% CI)
sections.text: The bar chart above shows raw counts. In register work you will often rather show a proportion or rate with a confidence interval, so the figure also shows the uncertainty. Error bars ( geom_errorbar() ) draw the interval on top of each bar or point. Aggregate first again: one row per group with count, proportion and interval. Here we assume outcome is coded 0/1. With simulated numbers the figure looks like this: !Bar chart with 95% confidence intervals as error bars, produced by the code above. The numbers are simulated. The key parts: geom_errorbar() needs ymin and ymax ; we computed them as prop ± 1.96 · se and put them in the dataset beforehand. The interval here is a simple Wald interval . It works when the group is large and the proportion is not close to 0 or 100 %, but it becomes unreliable with few people or few events, and it can go below 0. Output control only asks for 3 or 5 people per cell, so a group small enough for this to matter can still pass. In that case use prop.test(x, n)$conf.int , a score (Wilson) interval, by default with continuity correction, or binom.test(x, n)$conf.int for an exact (Clopper-Pearson) one. Same pattern for means: to show a mean of a continuous variable per group (e.g. age at index), replace prop with mean(variable) and se with sd(variable) / sqrt(n) . The rest of the figure is the same.

sections.title: Figures for publication
sections.heading: Forest plot (estimates with 95% CI)
sections.text: A forest plot shows several effect estimates (hazard ratios or odds ratios) side by side with their confidence intervals and a vertical reference line at 1 (no effect). It is a common way to show the exposure estimate across models or subgroups. Plot the estimates you want the reader to interpret: the coefficients of the confounders in the same model are not effects of those variables, and showing them invites that reading (the "Table 2 fallacy", Westreich & Greenland 2013, doi:10.1093/aje/kws412). The code below pulls the estimates out of a fitted model with broom::tidy() and plots them. To show only the exposure, filter on its term. With simulated numbers the figure looks like this: !Forest plot (simulated data): hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals and a reference line at 1. The key parts: tidy(..., exponentiate = TRUE) converts the coefficients from the log scale to HR/OR ; conf.int = TRUE gives conf.low / conf.high (95% CI). The reference line at 1 is "no effect": if the interval crosses 1, the estimate is not statistically clear (here e.g. Low income ). scale_x_log10() puts e.g. HR 0.5 and HR 2 equally far from 1 - which is how ratios should be read. Control the order with factor(term, levels = ...) ; without it ggplot sorts alphabetically. Estimates and CIs are aggregated numbers. A model fitted in a small subgroup can still say something about a few people, so the subgroup's size and number of events are cells too.

sections.title: Figures for publication
sections.heading: Save the figure
sections.text: ggsave() writes the most recent (or a named) figure to a file you can send to output control. width / height + units ( "cm" , "mm" , "in" or "px" ) set the physical size; dpi = 300 is a good resolution for print. Choose .png (raster) or .pdf (vector, scales crisply) depending on the journal's requirements.

sections.title: Figures for publication
sections.heading: Check the figure before export
sections.text: Aggregating is not enough on its own. A bar or a point that covers very few individuals can still identify them, so check the group sizes behind every element of the figure the same way you would check the cells of a table. A single extreme value on an axis can show one person's value too. For Kaplan-Meier and cumulative incidence curves, see Time-to-event. DST's rule that a hidden number must not be possible to work out covers figures as well: a segment left out of a stacked bar can be read off from the bar's total height. See Export - a hidden number must not be possible to work out. Further information Further depth in The Epidemiologist R Handbook : ggplot basics ggplot tips

sections.title: File types and how to open them
sections.text: Use this page when you meet a file on the server at Statistics Denmark (DST) and need to know what opens it. It shows how a project folder is laid out, which R function reads each file type, and which of them read the whole file into memory at once (full loading) and which only open a connection (lazy loading). You need it right after logging in, before your first extraction, and later as a look-up. How to write a query against a lazy connection is the next page, Phase 5; converting registers to parquet and setting up fastreg is on Parquet and fastreg.

sections.title: File types and how to open them
sections.heading: What a project folder looks like
sections.text: A project on the DST server can be organised like this. The raw data DST delivers is under rawdata/ . The folder names under workdata/ shown here ( cleaned-data/ , parquet-registers/ ) are from one project, and yours may differ: The paths in the code examples follow this structure. Check your own folder names with File Explorer. Two things are worth knowing: rawdata/ is read-only: you cannot edit or write to the raw register data DST delivers. You work in workspaces/ , where each project member typically has their own subfolder ( [your-name]/ ) for scripts, intermediate results and output. Almost all the code in this guide assumes the registers are in parquet: if your project only has raw SAS files, converting them to parquet is the first job. See Convert SAS files to Parquet. How to name the scripts in R/ is covered in Good coding practice.

sections.title: File types and how to open them
sections.heading: Lazy or full loading: parquet is lazy, everything else is not
sections.text: Every file type below loads one of two ways. Full loading ( readRDS , read_sas , read_csv , read_xlsx ) reads the entire file into RAM straight away. Fine for your own intermediate results; it would crash your session on a whole register. Lazy loading (parquet) opens a connection instead, and fetches rows only when you call collect() . That is what lets you work with registers of millions of rows. How to write a query against a lazy connection is Phase 5 - Extracting data step by step. A full load of a large SAS file can cost you your session, and slows everyone else. On DST all users share the server's RAM, and DST automatically closes processes (RStudio sessions, jobs) when RAM is close to full, so an oversized read_sas() can lose you your unsaved work. If you use a SAS file repeatedly, convert it to parquet once: see Convert SAS to parquet for the procedure and Mind your RAM in the shared environment for the practical habits. DST's own advice is in Reducing RAM use in the shared environment (PDF, in Danish).

sections.title: File types and how to open them
sections.heading: Three ways to open parquet
sections.text: open_dataset() (arrow): you write the path to the parquet folder, e.g. open_dataset("path/to/bef/") . It works on any parquet, on any project. read_register() (fastreg): you write only the register name, e.g. read_register("bef") , because you have told fastreg once where the parquet lives (see Point fastreg at your registers; every read_register() example in this guide assumes that call has been made). It hands you a DuckDB-backed table, so more dplyr functions work without an extra to_duckdb() step. It requires that the registers were converted with fastreg. read_parquet_duckdb() (duckplyr): you write the path, like open_dataset() , but you get a DuckDB-backed table straight away, without the arrow-to-DuckDB step ( to_duckdb() ). Since fastreg 0.14.3, read_register() uses this same function underneath. It does not make it safe to filter a datetime column such as kont_starttidspunkt with a date: that rule applies whichever of the three you use (see pitfall 4). It needs an up-to-date duckplyr and duckdb : DST's pre-installed versions are old and come back after every server reset, so reinstall them at the start of each session. Whichever you pick, the rest of your code is the same: filter() , select() and collect() are written the same way, and you do not need to rewrite existing scripts to use a different one. The exact path depends on your project and server. Column names for each register are in Overview of registers. When the years do not have the same columns - union_by_name A converted register folder holds one parquet file per year (see Reading a register that is split by year), and they are read as one table. That works as long as every year has the same columns. It stops working when a register changes structure partway through, for instance a column that appears in 2022 but not in 2021. With read_parquet_duckdb() you handle that with an option: union_by_name = TRUE matches the files' columns by name instead of by position, and fills in NA for the years where a column does not exist. Without it, DuckDB expects every file to have the same columns and stops with an error when they do not. Do not switch it on by default. Without it you get an error that tells you the register changed structure, which you want to know before you analyse it. With it you get a column that is silently NA for some years, and an NA you did not expect is much harder to spot than an error. Use it once you know what changed and have decided to read everything anyway. You only need it for a folder of several files with differing columns. A single file, or a register whose years all match, does not need it. fastreg's read_register() and read_parquet_dataset() already combine the years by column name (with arrow's unify_schemas up to version 0.14.2, with union_by_name from 0.14.3), so with them you get the NA -filled columns, not the error.

sections.title: File types and how to open them
sections.heading: Reading a register that is split by year
sections.text: DST delivers registers as SAS files, often one per year. Converting them to parquet is a job the project does once, and fastreg writes the result partitioned by year, as /year=YYYY/part-XXX.parquet , so a converted register is a folder of yearly files. See Parquet and fastreg. You do not open those one at a time. Both open_dataset("path/to/bef/") and read_register("bef") read the whole folder, including the per-year subfolders, as a single combined dataset. So you pick years by filtering on the year column in the data: That column exists because of how the register was partitioned at conversion, not because DST supplies it, so its name can differ between projects. Check it in your own files. year says which folder a row came from, nothing more. It is not a date and it is not a DST variable. Because the files are split by year, filtering on it means the other years are never opened, which keeps a query against a very large register fast. Use it to limit how much gets read. Do not use it to decide when something happened. year == 2020 in BEF does not tell you which of the four quarterly snapshots you have, only which folder the row sat in. Whenever the timing matters to your research question, use the register's own date column ( hf_vfra in UDDA, d_inddto in lpr_adm , referencetid in BEF) and keep year for speed. The two uses look identical in the code, which is why this is also listed in DST pitfalls.

sections.title: File types and how to open them
sections.heading: RDS: the format you write yourself
sections.text: RDS is R's own format. It preserves types, factor levels and column names exactly. You save an intermediate result in one script and reload it in the next, so script 2 does not have to re-run script 1: Rarer formats (Stata, SPSS, Feather, RData) You rarely meet these in a DST cohort study: File type Package Function .dta (Stata) haven read_dta() .sav (SPSS) haven read_sav() .feather arrow read_feather() .rdata / .rda base R load() .rdata / .rda differs from .rds in that it can save multiple objects at once - but .rds is preferred because you control what the object is called when you read it back in. When to use each format (Parquet, RDS, SAS, CSV) The three formats you work with day to day: File type Used for Parquet The large registers (BEF, LPR, LMDB …). You load them lazily and filter before fetching data. RDS Your own intermediate results - datasets you save from one script and reload in the next. SAS Format tables and raw register data not yet converted to parquet. SAS - for format tables and unconverted register data: Loading a large SAS file is slow and takes the whole file into RAM, which is why projects convert their registers to parquet. Only use SAS for format tables and files without a parquet version. CSV - for exporting finished tables (e.g. at repatriation): Never save raw register data as CSV, only aggregated results. See Phase 14 - Export and repatriation for the rules.

sections.title: Find a variable
sections.text: Use this page when you know what you need but not where it is: which register has the variable, what it is called there, its R type and the codes it takes. You need it while you plan which registers to order and when you write code against an unfamiliar register. Search by column name, by what it means, or by register. Overview of registers goes the other way, from a register to its columns. Both pages are generated from the same schema, so they show the same information. For more than half of the columns no published source gives a data type, so the type shown is our assumption and is marked unverified (see below). This is a starting point, not an authority. The names, types and value sets here are collected from DST's and Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's published documentation, and they can be out of date or simply wrong. Codes change meaning, columns are retired, and what is documented is the register, not what your project ordered. Found something wrong? Open an issue or use the feedback box on this page. A mistake spotted once is a morning nobody else loses. What a result shows you Type is the R type you get after loading. Where it says unverified , no published source gives a type for that column, so the one shown is our own assumption: DST publishes data types for none of its registers, and only Sundhedsdatastyrelsen does, for the health registers. Confirm with sapply(class) before relying on it, especially for code columns, which lose their leading zeros if they arrive as numbers. Years is what DST or Sundhedsdatastyrelsen documents that they hold, not what your project was delivered. It is shown only when a column covers a different period from its register, which is the case worth noticing: a column that stops in 2003 is a silent hole in a series that runs to 2024. Same name, several registers is the reason this page exists. koen in BEF is a number, c_sex in LPR2 changed coding in 2005, borger_koen in LPR3 is text with an unknown value set. Three answers to one question, and the register pages show them one at a time. The value set is folded under each coded column: what U means in civst , what 3 meant in c_pattype before 2014. Working that out is normally the slow part, and where the codes are too many to list, the fold-out links to the classification instead. Under the register name you get how to join it, what period it covers, and a warning if it is closed. A column in dodsaars is fine for causes of death and wrong for censoring, and the search says so before you use it. Replaced by marks a column with a successor, like van_vtil . Using it alone leaves a silent hole in the middle of a series.

sections.title: Find your registers
sections.text: Use this page when you plan which data a study needs, or meet a variable and wonder where it comes from: a decision table from the question you have ("when did this person die?") to the register and key columns that answer it, and a table of the keys that link the registers. It assumes you can open and inspect a register (Phase 7 - Inspect your data). When you know which register to use, you find its exact column names, types and code examples in Overview of registers, or search for a single variable across all of them in Find a variable. The table says which register covers what at DST. Which of its columns and years your project actually received was decided when the data was ordered, so check your own delivery before you plan around anything here (Check your delivery).

Register Key column(s) Date of birth and sex BEF foed_dag , koen Whether a person has died - and when DOD doddato Whether a person has emigrated VNDS haend_dato , indud_kode A somatic hospital contact (until Feb/Mar 2019) lpr_adm d_inddto , recnum , c_pattype A somatic diagnosis (until Feb/Mar 2019) lpr_diag c_diag , c_diagtype , recnum A psychiatric diagnosis (e.g. schizophrenia, until Feb/Mar 2019) t_psyk_adm + t_psyk_diag d_inddto , c_diag , c_diagtype A hospital contact or diagnosis (2019+) lpr_a_kontakt + lpr_a_diagnose kont_starttidspunkt , diag_kode , diag_kode_type A dispensed prescription LMDB atc , eksd Education level UDDA hfaudd , year Household income FAIK famaekvivadisp_13 , familie_id Employment status AKM socio13 , year An incident cancer diagnosis The Danish Cancer Registry pnr - see variable list A primary-sector contact (GP/specialist) National Health Insurance Service Register: sysi (older) / sssy (newer) pnr - see variable list A laboratory result (e.g. HbA1c) laboratorieproevesvar_ pnr , NPU code, result value - column names differ between deliveries, see Laboratory results A surgical procedure / SKS code lpr_sksopr (LPR2) / project-specific (LPR3) c_opr , recnum (LPR2) - LPR3: see Overview of registers §5 An examination / treatment (ZZ code) lpr_sksube recnum - see variable list Birth outcomes / newborn facts (2019+) mfr_nyfoedte + 10 satellite tables CPRnummer_Barn , CPRnummer_Mor - see Overview of registers §Nyfoedte Birth outcomes / newborn facts (1997-2018) mfr cpr_barn , cpr_moder - see Overview of registers §MFR Birth outcomes / newborn facts (before 1997) ftbarn / ftforael / ftnaevn PNR - see Overview of registers §FTBARN Some diagnoses sit in both the somatic and the psychiatric register before 2019. Dementia is the typical case: most dementia diagnoses are made in somatic departments (neurology, geriatrics), so you need lpr_diag and t_psyk_diag . The regions switched their reporting from LPR2 to LPR3 on 2-3 February or 2-3 March 2019, and DST's LPR2 files end on 31 March 2019 - see Understanding LPR. What are SKS codes? SKS (Sundhedsvæsenets Klassifikations System, the Danish Health Classification System) is the Danish health-care classification. It holds the diagnosis codes, based on ICD-10, and the codes for operations and other treatments in hospital, e.g. KJDF10 for gastric bypass. The operation codes are based on the Nordic NOMESCO Classification of Surgical Procedures (NCSP).

sections.heading: Next steps

sections.title: First extraction
sections.text: On this page you run one complete extraction yourself, on synthetic register data on your own computer: pick a small population from BEF, pull their hospital contacts from lpr_adm , add two variables and save the result. Do it after Phase 5 - Extracting data step by step, which explains the pattern you use here; this page is the practice, not the explanation. When you are done you have a script with the four steps that most extractions in a real project repeat. These examples cannot be run on the DST server. The synthetic data package ( fiktive ) is not available there. You need R and RStudio installed locally on your computer: 1. Download R: cran.r-project.org 2. Download RStudio: posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop 3. Open RStudio, create a new script ( File → New File → R Script ), and copy the code there. With real register data you use the same pattern, on the DST server and with your project's registers. The data is synthetic, from fiktive (MIT licence, Sara Schwartz): fictitious persons with the structure and column names of DST registers. load_registers_schema() , generate_background_population() , and generate_registers() return tibbles. You save those with write_parquet() , and you practise open_dataset() on the files. (These local examples use open_dataset() ; fastreg's read_register() is for a configured DST project, not ad-hoc local folders.) The example extracts from lpr_adm - hospital contacts , dates only, with no diagnosis join. Pulling actual diagnoses brings in rules this page does not cover: the LPR2/LPR3 split, the D-prefix, and choosing diagnosis types. Those are in Understand LPR.

sections.heading: Preparation: install fiktive and generate synthetic data
sections.text: fiktive is not on CRAN - install directly from GitHub: BEF is quarterly from 2008, and year is an integer, so 2015 holds several rows per person. With n = 60 that year has 240 rows but 60 people, enough for the sample below. The path is relative to your working directory. "synth_data/bef/" is created in the folder R is set to work in - check which one with getwd() . To save elsewhere, use a full path: "C:/Users/yourname/projects/synth_data/bef/" . You can now practise open_dataset() exactly as on the DST server.

sections.title: First extraction
sections.heading: Step 1 - Define your study population
sections.text: Every extraction starts with a list of pnr values: the people you want data for. In practice this comes from your cohort script. Here we build a small practice cohort directly from the BEF register. slice_sample(n = 30) draws rows. Because BEF is quarterly, the same pnr can appear more than once, so distinct(pnr) comes first - that way you sample 30 people, not 30 rows. In a real project, cohort_pnrs is a vector you built in a previous script and reload with readRDS("path/to/full_cohort.rds") %>% pull(pnr) . The signs in filter() : , / & = AND, \ = OR, ! = NOT, plus == , != , > , >= , %in% . Examples and the parentheses pitfall are in Combining conditions in filter() . Recode BEF variables - what do koen, civst and reg mean? The BEF register stores koen , civst and reg as codes - not as text. This recoding translates them into analysis-ready variables: The code lists above are an excerpt, adapted from Anders Aasted Isaksen's dplyr practice vignette (MIT licence, Steno Diabetes Center Aarhus). The full vignette covers more variables and patterns.

sections.title: First extraction
sections.heading: Step 2 - Extract data from a register
sections.text: Now extract hospital contacts from lpr_adm for the cohort, with the pattern from Phase 5: open, filter, select columns, collect. What happened? open_dataset() opened a lazy connection - no data in R yet semi_join() and select() sent instructions to Arrow/DuckDB - still no data in R collect() executed the query and fetched only the necessary rows into R See Extracting data step by step for a detailed explanation of lazy evaluation. Test on a small sample first. Before running a heavy extraction on the full cohort, test the code on a few people or rows - this catches errors quickly without waiting. For example semi_join(tibble(pnr = head(cohort_pnrs, 10)), by = "pnr", copy = TRUE) , or head(100) %>% collect() while building the code. Put head() before collect() : the other way round fetches everything first.

Run getwd() to see which folder that is. On DST, saved files stay on the server. Save intermediate datasets in your project folder (for example datasets/ , see Log in to DST). sections.title: First extraction
sections.heading: Inspect the result
sections.text: Right after an extraction you should check that you got what you expected: If your extraction includes exclusion steps - e.g. "remove persons with an early diagnosis" - it is good practice to count N for each step. Replace raw and clean with your own variable names: These lines cannot be run with the synthetic practice data - they are a template for use when working with your own data and an exclusion sequence. The pattern is repeated for each exclusion step and forms the basis for a STROBE flow diagram (a standardised diagram showing how many were excluded at each step and why; STROBE is the reporting standard for observational studies, CONSORT is for randomised trials). The same attrition counting is used when you build the study population in Phase 10. This is a quick sanity check. The full toolkit for exploring data - summary() , table() , cross-tables and NA handling - is covered in Phase 7 - Inspect your data.

sections.heading: Source and adaptation
sections.text: Step 1 (cohort construction from BEF) is adapted from Anders Aasted Isaksen's dplyr practice vignette (MIT licence, Steno Diabetes Center Aarhus). The synthetic tables come from fiktive . Steps 2-4 and the checklist are written for this guide.

sections.title: Format tables
sections.text: Use this page when a register column holds codes and you need to know what they mean: municipality numbers, employment codes, education codes. It shows where DST's format tables are on the server, how to load one into R and join it onto your data, and how to pick the right file among the many with similar names. You need it when you build covariates and when you label a finished table. The join itself is explained in Phase 12 - Assemble and prepare the dataset. The format tables on the server are the authority, not this page. The examples and code lists here are a starting point. DST updates the format catalogue without this guide knowing, and a code can change meaning while keeping its number. Load the current table from E:/Formater/ and check the values in your own delivered data before you rely on a mapping. Several of the same code lists are also published outside DST, as classifications with a CSV download, which is the version Find a variable shows. DST's format tables are SAS files on the server that translate codes to text. A format table always has at least two columns: Column Contents Example START The raw code from your register 101 (municipality number) Label column The corresponding text label "København" You join the format table onto your dataset with START as the key - exactly like a dictionary lookup. Rows in your dataset without a match in the format table get NA in the label column - no error message. Always check with sum(is.na(data$label_column)) after the join.

sections.title: Format tables
sections.heading: Where are the format tables?
sections.text: The Star ( ) on the Windows desktop inside the DST server opens an HTML guide for finding the right table. DST's written guides sit here: The one worth reading is Brugen af SAS formater i Danmarks Statistik.pdf (\~2 MB, DST Consulting). It explains the naming systematics used below and has a section per topic - Uddannelserne, Brancherne, DISCO, Sundhed, Geokoder, DREAM. The same folder holds dated older editions (2012-2019) and a set of Allokering af formatbibliotek ( ).sas scripts for pointing SAS at the format catalog - those are for SAS users and are not needed from R. Two more folders one level up are worth knowing: They let you look up what a code means without loading anything into R - useful when you just need to check a single value. Subfolders are organised by topic - including: Education sits in two places, and the naming is confusing. DST's guide says the formats for the current classification, DISCED-15 (used from 2015), are in the format catalog called DISCED , while the catalog called Uddannelser holds the older classifications it replaced (Forspalte, ISCED1997 and DUN). Look in both SAS_datasaet/Disced/ and SAS_datasaet/Uddannelser/ before you pick a file; see Education level for how to tell them apart by name. Find the specific filenames in the folder yourself. The base path and subfolder structure above are confirmed on DST. But the specific filenames and column names further down the page (e.g. c_kom_v4_t.sas7bdat , KOM_V4_T ) are illustrative examples - naming varies, and you must find the right file in the relevant subfolder yourself. Use the Star guide / PDF guide to find the file, and names() / head() to see the actual column names.

The heaven package ships them as data, so you do not have to read a SAS format file at all: data(edu_code) : education codes with hfaudd mapped to categories in English and Danish, a 5-level grouping and ISCED codes. kommuneRegion(kommune) : converts a numeric 3-digit municipality code straight to one of the five regions (valid from 2007). It gives you the region , not the municipality name - for the name you still need the format table below. heaven is pre-installed on DST ( library(heaven) tells you if it is on your machine), and elsewhere it installs from GitHub with pak::pak("tagteam/heaven") (it is not on CRAN, so install.packages() will not find it). sections.title: Format tables
sections.heading: Education level (hfaudd)
sections.text: hfaudd is the four-digit code for the specific education . Its level - the thing almost every analysis actually needs - lives in a separate lookup, and the filename tells you exactly which lookup you are getting. These files are dictionaries, not data. A .sas7bdat in the format folders holds no people and no register records. It is a two-column translation table - one row per code, with the code and what it means - and they are tiny, a few hundred KB. You read one into R and left_join() it onto your own data, exactly like the municipality example above. Nothing about your cohort changes; you are only adding a column that says what a code stands for. What on this page has not been checked on the server. The naming rules below come from DST's own guide ( Brugen af SAS formater i Danmarks Statistik ) and DST's published DISCED-15 classification. The exact filenames in the education folders have not been listed and checked for this section, so treat every filename here as a pattern to look for, not a path to copy. Run list.files() on the folder first, as in the code below. How to read the file names. DST's guide gives the name for turning hfaudd into the main area as AUDD_HOVED_L1L5_KT ( $AUDD_HOVED_L1L5_KT in SAS, where $ marks the character version). The files you read from R carry the same parts, in lower case, with c_ or n_ in front and usually a version year: Part Means What to pick c_ / n_ the c haracter or n umeric version the one matching the type of hfaudd in your data, or simply c_ after converting hfaudd to text (see Character or numeric) audd / udd a fsluttet (completed) or igangværende/afbrudt (ongoing or interrupted) education audd for hfaudd (see why) 2015 , 2023 , ... which version of the format the newest only; it covers older years too (see Four things to check) hoved , type , niveau , fag which of the four DISCED-15 dimensions you group by (see below) hoved for short/medium/long, as SEPLINE does (see The four dimensions) l1l5 from level 1 (the four-digit code) to level 5 (the coarsest grouping) l1l5 to go from hfaudd to the two-digit main area (see The five levels) _k / _t / _kt what you get back: the code, the text, or both _k for analysis, _t for table labels (see Which variant to pick) Why there are several files for what looks like one lookup. DST's guide says it makes up to six variants of every format: character or numeric, each as _k , _t and _kt , "where possible". Seeing five or six files with the same stem is therefore normal. They hold the same mapping and differ only in the type they expect and what they return. [ Character or numeric: how to tell. ] Ask R what type hfaudd is in your delivery. head(0) returns the column types with zero rows, so no data is printed: The simpler rule that always works: convert hfaudd to text with as.character() and always use the c_ file, as the code further down does. Text is also the safer type for education codes, because some DISCED-15 codes start with a zero ( 0001 Ingen uddannelse), and stored as a number that code becomes 1 and no longer matches the lookup. [ hfaudd is a completed education, so you want an audd file, not a udd one. ] DISCED-15 distinguishes between the code for an ongoing or interrupted education ( UDD ) and for a completed one ( AUDD ) - DST documents the two separately - and there are format files for both. The name gives it away: hfaudd is højest fuldførte AUDD , the highest completed education. A udd lookup joined to hfaudd will match some rows, miss others, and never tell you. [ The four dimensions. ] DISCED-15 for completed education groups the same four-digit codes in four different ways, and each has its own format. Pick the one that answers your question: Dimension (Danish) Groups education by Top level, for example Use it for Hovedområde ( hoved ) the Danish main areas of education 10 Grundskole, 15 Forberedende uddannelser, 20 Gymnasiale uddannelser, 30 Erhvervsfaglige uddannelser, 35 Adgangsgivende uddannelsesforløb, 40 KVU, 50 MVU, 60 Bachelor, 70 LVU, 80 Ph.d., 90 Uoplyst short/medium/long education; what SEPLINE uses Uddannelsesniveau ( niveau ) level, lined up with the international ISCED 10 Grundskole til og med 6. klasse, 30 Gymnasiale og erhvervsfaglige, 50 KVU, 60 MVU / Bachelorer, 70 LVU comparing with ISCED-based studies; SEPLINE does not recommend its ISCED format for categorising, because e.g. 15 becomes ISCED 3 Fagområde ( fag ) subject, regardless of level 25 Humanistisk, 35 Samfundsvidenskab, 45 Naturvidenskab what field someone is trained in Uddannelsestype ( type ) type of programme 50 Bacheloruddannelser, 55 Professionsbachelor, 85 Voksenuddannelser og kurser ordinary vs adult education The same number means different things in different dimensions ( 50 is MVU in hoved and bachelor programmes in type ), so a code is only meaningful together with the file it came from. Record the filename in your analysis script. [ The five levels. ] Within a dimension, DST groups every education in a tree with five levels. Level 1 is the four-digit code you have in hfaudd ; each level above it is a broader group, and level 5 is the two-digit main area. The l1l5 in a filename means "give me a level-1 code, and I return its level-5 group". A file named l1l2 would instead return the level just above the code, which is still very detailed. For short, medium and long education you want the two-digit main areas, so an L1 → L5 file. Example: one education through all five levels Sygeplejerske, prof.bach. in the Hovedområde dimension, from DST's DISCED-15 AUDD classification: Level Code What it is L1 5166 Sygeplejerske, prof.bach. - the value in hfaudd L2 50893510 Sygepleje og sundhedspleje, MVU (eight digits) L3 508935 Sygepleje og sundhedspleje, MVU (six digits) L4 5089 a broader group within MVU (four digits) L5 50 Mellemlange videregående uddannelser, MVU An l1l5 file turns 5166 into 50 ; an l1l2 file would turn it into 50893510 . Note that the level-4 group has four digits, like an education code, so a four-digit value is not by itself proof that you are looking at hfaudd . [ Four things to check before you trust the result. ] Use the newest version, and only that one. The folders hold several versions side by side and it is tempting to think you need one per study year. You do not. DST's guide says the education statistics are updated every year with the newest codes backwards in time as well , so the latest version already covers the older codes. One file, for the whole study period. DISCED-15 or an older classification. From 2015 DST uses DISCED-15, which replaced Forspalte, ISCED1997 and DUN. A file with no dimension in its name (for example c_audd2015_l1l5_kt ) may belong to one of the older classifications, whose levels and codes are not the ones in the table above. Check the top-level codes with head() against the table before you use it. Character or numeric. c_ expects a character variable, n_ a numeric one. Pick the one matching your column, or convert - a type mismatch produces a join that matches nothing and fills the column with NA without any error. The unmatched count. A high number means a type mismatch or the wrong file ( udd instead of audd , or an old classification). Paths on DST. The E:/Formater/... path above is the same for everyone working on a DST research machine, so it should work as written - but check it yourself before you rely on it , and expect it to differ if you are on a hosted machine. DST's own guide gives the network path for both kinds of machine. The full guide is the PDF "Brugen af SAS formater i Danmarks Statistik" under E:/Formater/SAS formater i Danmarks Statistik/Vejledning mv/ . Why the level has to be looked up at all - and what it costs to guess it from the digits - is in Overview of registers. The full extraction, from opening UDDA to a categorised variable, is in Socioeconomic variables, which also covers the heaven shortcut.

sections.title: Format tables
sections.heading: Which variant to pick: _k, _t or _kt
sections.text: Every format comes in up to three output variants. DST's guide illustrates them with a municipality code turned into a region, using Copenhagen municipality ( 101 ): Suffix Returns Copenhagen ( 101 ) becomes _k the code only 84 _t the text only Hovedstaden _kt code and text together 84 Hovedstaden Use _k for the analysis variable. The code is short, it sorts correctly, and it does not change if DST rewords a label in a later version. You can filter and group on it directly ( %in% c("40", "50") ), and a model or a case_when() written against codes keeps working. Use _t for the labels in a finished table. Join it on at the end, when you build Table 1 or a figure, so the text never becomes something your code depends on. Use _kt for looking, not for analysing. It is the most readable while you explore, because you see what each code means and the values still sort by code. But "40 Korte videregående uddannelser, KVU" is code and text glued into one value: filtering on it means matching the whole string, and it breaks if the wording changes. Whichever you pick, the key is the same. All three join on START , the code in your own data. Only the returned column differs.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.text: Use this page to look up what a function in the guide's code does, when you meet it in an example and are not sure what it does or why it is there. It covers the functions for handling data (extract, clean, reshape, prepare), each with a plain explanation and a short example. Statistical models ( glm , coxph , lm ) are explained in Phase 13 - Analysis, where they are used. If you know the function name, search the page with Ctrl+F (Windows) or Cmd+F (Mac). Jump directly to Topic Section The pipe %>% The pipe Load register / open parquet file Data loading Filter rows Rows: filter and deduplicate Select or add columns Columns: select, add, transform Rename columns Column names Group, count and aggregate Groups and aggregation Join two tables Join - assemble tables Pivot (wide ↔ long format) Reshaping collect() and lazy evaluation Lazy query Dates and text Text operations · Numbers and dates Debugging Diagnostics and debugging The most important functions - start here If you understand the 6 functions below, you can read most lines of register data code. Function What it does read_register("name") Opens a lazy connection to a register (without fastreg: open_dataset("path") ) filter(condition) Keeps only the rows that satisfy the condition select(col1, col2) Keeps only the specified columns mutate(new_col = ...) Adds or changes a column left_join(other_df, by = "key") Joins two tables on a shared key collect() Fetches data from parquet into R's memory The order is intentional: read_register / open_dataset → filter → select → collect is the pattern that appears in almost every script.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: What is a function?
sections.text: Think of a function as a machine on an assembly line. You send something in one end, it does something with it, and you get something new out the other end. filter() is for example a sieve: you send a large table in, specify which rows you want to keep, and get a smaller table out. All functions in R are written with parentheses: functionname(what_is_sent_in) . What you write inside the parentheses is called the arguments . Many functions have named arguments of the form name = value : on the left of = is the argument's name (fixed by the function, cannot be changed), and on the right is the value you supply, e.g. ratio = 5 or na.rm = TRUE . You do not need to memorize them: ?functionname shows which arguments a function takes and what they do. Want to see what a function does? Place your cursor inside the function name and press F1 - the help page opens with description, arguments and examples directly in RStudio's Help panel. You can also type ?functionname or help(functionname) in the console, or args(functionname) for a quick list of arguments. For packages on CRAN there is an online page with documentation and vignettes (e.g. https://cran.r-project.org/package=MatchIt ). Some DST packages (e.g. heaven ) live on GitHub instead - use ?functionname for the arguments and confirm the package's availability on your own project.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: The pipe - %>%
sections.text: The most important symbol in all the code is %>% , "the pipe". What it does: the pipe passes the result from the line on the left forward as the first argument to the function on the right. The two ways of writing do the same thing: Both versions give exactly the same result. The pipe version is easier to read because you can follow the steps in order - and easier to debug because you can add or remove one step at a time. A line break after %>% is not required - it is only for readability. You can write the whole chain on one line ( bef %>% filter(...) %>% collect() ) or split it with one step per line. The only rule: if you break the line, %>% must sit at the end of the line, not the start of the next one. R reads line by line, so a trailing %>% signals "more is coming": The same applies to > and + in ggplot2. Analogy: Imagine cooking a meal. You chop the onions - and pass them on to the pot - which passes its contents on to the plate. The pipe does exactly that: it chains steps together so you can read the code from top to bottom like a recipe. %>% and > do the same job: two ways of writing the pipe. %>% comes from the magrittr package and is available via library(dplyr) . > is a built-in version introduced in R 4.1 - it requires no package. The two work identically in almost all situations. You will see both in R code online. The project uses %>% , but if you write > that is perfectly fine.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: open_dataset("path") <small>- arrow</small>
sections.text: What it does: opens a lazy connection to a parquet file or folder. Analogy: Imagine calling the library and asking them to find all books about cardiac surgery from 1990 to 2020. The librarian says "yes, I'll find those" - but they have not arrived yet. That is exactly what open_dataset() does: it tells the computer what you want, but the data has not been fetched into memory yet. The rest of your commands ( filter , select ) add further instructions, before you finally say "send them now" - that is collect() . #### fastreg (recommended) read_register() finds the path from your project config (set once) - see Parquet and fastreg. It returns a DuckDB connection. It can only find registers in fastreg's own format ( /year=YYYY/part-XXX.parquet ). If it does not know the name, list the available ones with list_parquet_datasets() , or point straight at the folder with read_parquet_dataset("full/path/to/folder") - see When read_register() cannot find the register. #### DST server (arrow) Replace the path with your own project's parquet folder; ask your data manager if you do not know it. #### Local synthetic data (fiktive) Generate and save synthetic data locally before use - see Phase 6 - First extraction. Used for all registers stored as parquet files: bef , lpr_adm , lpr_diag , lmdb , dod , dodsaars , vnds , udda , faik , akm , t_psyk_adm , t_psyk_diag , lpr_a_kontakt , lpr_a_diagnose and more. Arrow or DuckDB? open_dataset() returns an Arrow connection. Arrow is fast, but it does not support every dplyr function: if a step fails with an "unsupported function" error, switching to DuckDB usually fixes it, because DuckDB supports almost all dplyr verbs. Pipe through to_duckdb() : You do not need this step with read_register() (fastreg) - they hand you a DuckDB connection already, so the to_duckdb() conversion is built in. For when to use which, see Phase 5 - Arrow vs. DuckDB.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: collect()
sections.text: What it does: executes the lazy query and pulls data into R's memory. This is the point where the librarian actually brings the books to you. Call it late - after all filter() and select() steps - so only the necessary data is moved. The concept of lazy evaluation - why data is not in memory before collect() - is explained in detail on the page Extracting data step by step.

sections.heading: haven::read_sas("file.sas7bdat")
sections.text: What it does: reads a SAS data file into R. Used to load SAS files - e.g. DST's format tables or registers not yet converted to parquet. See File types and Format tables for practical examples. read_csv("path/file.csv") (from readr ) is the equivalent for a .csv file - a plain text table, not a register format, but common for a code list or a small file someone hands you outside DST.

sections.heading: arrow::write_parquet(df, "path/file.parquet")
sections.text: What it does: saves a data frame as a parquet file. Parquet is a particularly efficient file format for large datasets - it is far faster to read than CSV. Used when you want to save an R dataset as a parquet file, e.g. for use with open_dataset() or read_register() in another script.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: file.path(folder, "filename.rds")
sections.text: What it does: correctly assembles a folder path and filename into a full path. Analogy: Think of it as writing an address: file.path("C:/data", "results.rds") gives "C:/data/results.rds" . It is safer than just pasting strings together with paste0() , because it handles slashes correctly on all operating systems.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: file.exists("path")
sections.text: What it does: returns TRUE or FALSE - does the file exist? Used to give an understandable error message before the code tries to open a file that might not be there.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: dir.create(path, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
sections.text: What it does: creates a folder if it does not already exist. recursive = TRUE also creates any parent folders. showWarnings = FALSE suppresses the harmless warning you would otherwise get if the folder already exists.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: rename_with(tolower)
sections.text: What it does: converts ALL column names to lower case at once. Analogy: Imagine receiving a patient list from five different departments. One writes "CPR", another "cpr", a third "Cpr". It is the same thing - but the computer treats them as three entirely different things. rename_with(tolower) fixes it in one second: all names become consistent. Important: always call it right after open_dataset() or read_register() . If you forget it, semi_join(..., by = "pnr") will fail because the column might be called PNR .

sections.text: What it does: renames one or more specific columns.

sections.text: What it does: shows all column names in a data frame. Useful when you are not sure what a table contains. On a lazy connection names() is not always reliable - see arrow::schema() below.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: arrow::schema(lazy_table) <small>- arrow</small>
sections.text: What it does: lists the column names and their types of a lazy Arrow connection, without reading any data into RAM. Use it when you want to check what a register really contains before you write code against it - which you should, because a delivery only holds the columns your project ordered, and LPR_A renamed a number of them. For the DuckDB-backed objects that read_register() (fastreg) returns, use colnames() instead. Do not trust colnames() on a lazy Arrow query after rename_with() . It can return an empty vector silently, so a column that exists is reported as missing. The operations themselves are fine - it is only the name check that fails. (Seen on arrow 23.0.1 outside DST; not yet confirmed on the server.) Use names(collect(head(tbl, 0))) , which fetches the structure with zero rows.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: select(col1, col2, new = old, -remove)
sections.text: What it does: keeps only the columns you name. Analogy: You have a large Excel file with 50 columns. You only need 3. select() is like saving a copy with only the three columns you need. It reduces the amount of data pulled from the server, and is one of the reasons the code is fast. When renaming inside select() , the direction is new_name = old_name - the new name on the left, the existing column name on the right.

sections.heading: pull(column)
sections.text: What it does: takes one column out of a data frame as a plain vector, instead of a data frame with one column. Analogy: select(col) gives you a one-column spreadsheet; pull(col) gives you just the values, no spreadsheet around them. Use it when the next step needs a bare vector, not a table - e.g. before %in% , or after summarise() when you only want the single number out.
