sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: mutate(new_column = expression)
sections.text: What it does: adds a new column (or modifies an existing one), computed from the columns you already have. The number of rows is the same - mutate() adds information, does not remove rows. ( df is just the name of your data frame - call it whatever you like.) You can create several variables in one call , and a variable you just made is immediately available further down (here obesity_class uses the just-computed bmi ): Note that TRUE ~ "Obesity" as the last line would also catch every row where bmi is NA (a missing height or weight): case_when() treats a condition that is NA as not met, so the row falls through to TRUE . Use TRUE ~ for a catch-all such as "Unknown", not for a real category. Check the units first. BMI = weight (kg) / height (m)². If height is in cm , weight / (height^2) is wrong. Convert height to metres in a mutate() step before you compute BMI: case_when() has its own entry below. More examples of mutate() :
sections.code: dplyr mutate bmi weight height new column computed two existing ones obesity newly created usable right away obesity_class case_when several conditions first one wins normal overweight obesity missing matches none stays height_m height_cm then bmi correct icd3 substr c_diag icd code without prefix characters birth_year lubridate year foed_dag birth after collect see below

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: transmute(new_column = expression)
sections.text: What it does: like mutate() , but keeps only the columns you name - the rest are dropped. Handy when you want a clean table with exactly the columns a function needs.
sections.code: mutate event keeps all columns new transmute pnr only

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: case_when(condition1 ~ value1, condition2 ~ value2, TRUE ~ default)
sections.text: What it does: an advanced if-else with many conditions. Analogy: Think of a traffic light: is it red → stop, is it yellow → be careful, is it green → go. case_when() works the same way: conditions are evaluated in order, and the first condition that is true determines the result. TRUE ~ default is the "in all other cases" arm.
sections.code: mutate education_cat case_when edu_level short medium long unknown

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: if_else(condition, true_value, false_value)
sections.text: What it does: a simple two-way condition. Stricter than base R's ifelse() - both values must have the same type. 0L and 1L are integers in R. The L suffix is R's way of specifying that a number is an integer rather than a decimal ( 0 and 1 without L are double by default). if_else() requires both values to have exactly the same type - use either 0L / 1L (integer) or 0 / 1 (double), but not a mix.
sections.code: if_else is.na death_date person has died

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: coalesce(x, replacement)
sections.text: What it does: replaces NA values with another value. Analogy: After a left join, many persons will have NA in flag columns because they did not have that condition. coalesce(mi_flag, 0L) says: "if mi_flag is NA, set it to 0 instead". Used systematically after each left join that produces flag columns.
sections.code: coalesce mi_flag found absent

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: replace_na(x, replacement) <small>- tidyr</small>
sections.text: What it does: the same job as coalesce() above - replaces NA with a value - but written for use inside across() , where you are naming a function rather than writing out one column at a time.
sections.code: mutate across starts_with dx_ replace_na every column match found

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: across(columns, function)
sections.text: What it does: applies the same function to many columns at once inside mutate() . ~ coalesce(.x, 0L) is an anonymous function: ~ means "function of", and .x is the current column. It is equivalent to function(x) coalesce(x, 0L) - but shorter. across() calls this function once per column in nmi_variables . starts_with("prefix") picks columns by name pattern instead of naming them one by one - across(starts_with("dx_"), ...) applies to every column that starts with dx_ , however many there are. Common inside across() when you built the columns yourself with a shared prefix ( dx_ , rx_ ).
sections.code: mutate across all_of nmi_variables coalesce replace all nmi flag columns

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: rowSums(matrix, na.rm = TRUE)
sections.text: What it does: sums the values in each row across columns. Used in two places: 1. NMI score (Nordic Multimorbidity Index): sums the product of 0/1 flag columns and their individual weights → one weighted score per person, built to predict mortality. 2. Multimorbidity count : sums all 0/1 flags → simple count of the number of conditions per person.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: filter(condition1, condition2, ...)
sections.text: What it does: keeps only the rows that satisfy the conditions. Analogy: You have a patient list and only want to see women over 50. filter(koen == 2, alder > 50) is your sieve - everything else is removed. Signs for comparing a column with a value: Sign Means Example == equal to (two equals signs - a single = is assignment) filter(year == 2015) != not equal to filter(koen != 2) > · >= greater than · greater than or equal to filter(alder >= 18) < · <= less than · less than or equal to filter(alder < 65) %in% is in the list (see below) filter(icd3 %in% c("F00","F03")) Signs for combining several conditions: Sign Means Example , or & AND - both must be true filter(koen == 2, alder > 50) → women and over 50 \ OR - at least one true filter(icd3 == "F00" \ icd3 == "F03") → F00 or F03 ! NOT - invert the condition filter(!is.na(alder)) → keep rows where alder is not missing Pitfall - never mix AND and OR without parentheses. & binds before , so filter(alder > 50 alder < 18 & koen == 2) reads as alder > 50 (alder < 18 & koen == 2) . If you mean "(over 50 or under 18) and woman", add parentheses: filter((alder > 50 alder < 18) & koen == 2) .
sections.code: filter c_diagtype only main secondary diagnoses date_contact surgery_date post operative contacts icd3 s72 hip fracture codes

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: %in% - "is in the list"
sections.text: What it does: checks whether each element on the left side appears in the vector on the right side. Returns TRUE or FALSE for each element. %in% is optional: it is just one of filter() 's comparison signs (alongside == , > , < , etc.). You use it only when you want to match against a list of values rather than a single value - e.g. a code list. To match pnr against the cohort, use semi_join (see above). Analogy: Imagine a guest list for a party. icd3 %in% c("G30", "F00", "F03") is like standing at the entrance and checking: "is this diagnosis code on the list?" You will see %in% in almost every filter() call in the project. Sending a local list into a lazy query - two ways. The register is not in R yet. filter(c_diag %in% my_codes) usually works anyway - dbplyr and arrow use the local vector when no column is called my_codes - but if a column has that name, the column wins and you quietly get the wrong rows. !! forces the vector's contents into the query: filter(c_diag %in% !!my_codes) . Explicit, guards against that name clash, and what this guide uses throughout. semi_join() sends the list over as a temporary table: semi_join(tibble(c_diag = my_codes), by = "c_diag", copy = TRUE) . Needs no !! , and holds up better for very long lists, where !! writes the whole vector into the SQL as one enormous IN (...) . For pnr against the whole cohort, prefer the semi_join() form - it is the same idea, and cohort lists are long: semi_join(tibble(pnr = cohort_pnrs), by = "pnr", copy = TRUE) .
sections.code: icd3 g30 f00 f03 these three codes everything atc my_atc all atc local see below

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: distinct(col1, col2)
sections.text: What it does: removes duplicates - keeps only unique combinations. Analogy: A person may have received the diagnosis F00 ten times. You only need to know whether they ever had it. distinct(pnr, icd3) reduces it to one row per person per code. distinct(pnr) gives you just the list of unique person IDs.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: slice(n)
sections.text: What it does: keeps only the nth row, within each group if the data are grouped with group_by() . Use slice() on data that are already in R. On a lazy table (before collect() ) what happens depends on how the table was opened: A DuckDB table through dbplyr stops with " slice() is not supported on database backends". An arrow table ( open_dataset() ) stops too. A duckplyr table can run it without an error, by pulling the table into R first. On a whole register that is the RAM problem in Phase 5. Before collect() on a DuckDB or duckplyr table, use slice_min() or slice_max() with with_ties = FALSE instead (see below). On an arrow table even a grouped slice_max() stops ("Slicing grouped data not supported in Arrow"), so filter first, collect() , and slice in R. slice_max(column, n = 1) and slice_sample(n = 1) do a similar job without a separate arrange() step: slice_max(date_contact, n = 1) keeps the row with the latest date per group; slice_sample(n = 200) picks a random sample of rows instead (used for a practice cohort, not for choosing a real one). slice_max() and slice_min() keep ties by default, so a person with two contacts on the same latest date gets two rows. Add with_ties = FALSE to get exactly one row per group: When dates tie, the row that is kept is arbitrary. If the result must be reproducible, break the tie on a second column after collect() , for example arrange(desc(date_contact), recnum) %>% slice(1) within group_by(pnr) .
sections.code: group_by pnr group per person arrange desc year newest first slice keeps record slice_max date_contact with_ties one row also dates tie

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: group_by(col1, col2)
sections.text: What it does: divides data into groups so subsequent operations happen separately within each group. Analogy: Imagine you have a stack of patient records and sort them into piles by ID number. group_by(pnr) does exactly that - but only in memory. All subsequent steps ( arrange , slice , summarise ) now happen one pile at a time.
sections.code: group_by pnr group per person arrange date_contact oldest first slice earliest contact after collect see ungroup remove grouping afterwards

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: ungroup()
sections.text: What it does: removes the grouping. Important: always call ungroup() after you are done with group_by() . If you forget it, data remains grouped, and later operations can behave unexpectedly.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: arrange(column) / arrange(desc(column))
sections.text: What it does: sorts rows ascending (default) or descending ( desc() ). Typically used with group_by() %>% slice(1) to find the first or newest record per person.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: summarise(new_col = function(col), .groups = "drop")
sections.text: What it does: reduces each group to one summary row. .groups = "drop" removes the grouping automatically afterwards.
sections.code: group_by pnr group per person summarise first_e66 min date_contact na.rm earliest e66

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: count(col1, col2)
sections.text: What it does: shorthand for group_by(col1, col2) %>% summarise(n = n()) : how many rows share each combination of values. Analogy: You want to know how many contacts fall in each calendar year. count(year) gives you that table directly, without writing group_by() and summarise() yourself.
sections.code: all_dx already collected into year safe here see below mutate contact_year date_contact count one row per number contacts arrange

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: n_distinct(column)
sections.text: What it does: counts how many different values a column has - not how many rows. Analogy: count(pnr) tells you how many rows each pnr has (useful for finding duplicates); n_distinct(pnr) tells you how many different people there are in total, in one number. Often used inside summarise() alongside other counts, or on its own: n_distinct(cohort$pnr) .

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: ntile(x, n)
sections.text: What it does: divides rows into n equal groups (quantiles). Not used for income quintiles in register-based studies following SEPLINE guidelines. SEPLINE recommends comparing against population-specific cut-points (Q20/Q40/Q60/Q80) stratified by sex × 5-year age group × reference year - not ntile() on your cohort alone. See SEPLINE. row_number() numbers the rows 1, 2, 3... within each group (after group_by() ), instead of dividing them into buckets like ntile() does - useful for keeping, say, only the first 3 contacts per person: filter(row_number() <= 3) .

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: Join - assemble tables
sections.text: This is one of the things that takes the longest to understand, but is essential for all register work. A join puts two tables together based on a shared key - typically pnr . The three joins below ( inner_join , semi_join , left_join ) are the ones this guide actually uses, and are explained here because each has a DST- or DuckDB-specific catch worth knowing before you rely on it. right_join , full_join and anti_join are real too, just rarely needed here - see Joins - link two tables for the full comparison table across all five, multi-key joins, and how to validate a join after running it.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: inner_join(y, by = "key")
sections.text: What it does: keeps only rows that exist in BOTH tables. Analogy: It is like a VIP list at the entrance. You must be on BOTH lists to get in. Used when a match is meaningful - e.g. inner_join(cohort) keeps only hospital contacts for persons who are actually in the study.
sections.code: inner_join cohort select pnr surgery_date only contacts members

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: semi_join(y, by = "key")
sections.text: What it does: keeps the rows from the left table that have a match in y - but adds no columns from y . So it is a filter where the list of allowed values lives in another table. Analogy: You have all of LPR and a list of your cohort. semi_join keeps only the LPR rows whose pnr is on the cohort list - the same result as filter(pnr %in% ...) , but faster and more reliable on lazy (Arrow/DuckDB) tables. Where is the local list? The list itself is the tibble you pass as the second argument ( y ); by = "pnr" only says which column to match on - not where the list is. Because y is an ordinary table, you do not need !! . That is the difference from filter(pnr %in% !!cohort_pnrs) , where the vector sits directly in the condition and !! is what injects it. Use semi_join to filter a register down to the cohort. Add copy = TRUE . Your local tibble lives in R, and the register lives in DuckDB (from read_register() ) or Arrow (from open_dataset() ). dplyr will not join across two different sources on its own: copy = TRUE gives it permission to copy the small local table into the register's source so the join can run there. Without it, the join stops with an error. It does no harm when both tables are already in R, which is why every semi_join() example in this guide includes it.
sections.code: lpr_adm semi_join tibble pnr cohort_pnrs copy keep only cohort rows

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: left_join(y, by = "key")
sections.text: What it does: keeps all rows from the left table. Rows without a match in the right table get NA for the columns that came from the right. Analogy: It is like checking whether your patients have a particular finding, without discarding any of them. All patients are still there - those with the finding have a date, those without have NA . Used everywhere when adding flags and covariates to the cohort.
sections.code: full_cohort start all cohort members left_join hip_fracture pnr retained only those hip fracture get

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: bind_rows(df1, df2, ...)
sections.text: What it does: stacks data frames on top of each other (same columns, more rows). Analogy: Like taking three piles of paper and putting them in one pile. Used e.g. to combine LPR2 + psychiatric LPR2 + LPR3 into one combined diagnosis table.
sections.code: bind_rows lpr2_results lpr2_psyk_results lpr3_results combine all three source tables

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: Reshaping
sections.text: pivot_wider() and pivot_longer() (below) are explained briefly here as functions; for when to reshape at all, and the group_by() + slice() alternative that avoids it for most cohort work, see Long ↔ wide format.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: pivot_wider(names_from = col, values_from = col)
sections.text: What it does: transforms a long format (one row per visit) to a wide format (one row per person with one column per time point). Analogy: Imagine a patient with five weigh-in visits - all in the same column with five rows. pivot_wider() transforms it into one single row with five columns: weight_3mo , weight_6mo , weight_12mo , etc.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: pivot_longer(cols, names_to, values_to)
sections.text: What it does: the reverse of pivot_wider() - takes several columns and stacks them into two: one naming which column each value came from, one holding the value itself.
sections.code: pivot_longer cols starts_with weight_ names_to timepoint values_to weight

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: !! (bang-bang, two exclamation marks)
sections.text: What it does: injects a local R variable into a DuckDB/dplyr query. Analogy: Imagine asking an assistant to find all rows with a code from a list. If you say "find all with a code from the list my_atc ", the assistant first looks for a column in the database with that name, and only uses your list if there is none. You can say: "find all with a code from this list" and hold the list up. !! is the equivalent of holding the list up. You will see !! in front of local R variables (typically code and year lists) inside filter() calls.
sections.code: filter atc my_atc says column

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: !!column_name := value (inside mutate)
sections.text: What it does: creates a column whose NAME is determined by an R variable - not written directly in the code. Normally you write a fixed column name to the left of = in mutate() : But in the NMI calculation (Nordic Multimorbidity Index) we loop over a list of chronic conditions ( "mi" , "stroke" , "diabetes" , ...) and want to create one column per condition. The column name is therefore stored in a variable: Two things differ from normal: !! : as in filter() : injects the R variable's contents instead of interpreting it as a column name := : used instead of = , because R requires it when the left side of an assignment is dynamic. It is not possible to write mutate(!!name = 1L) - only mutate(!!name := 1L) works. 1L is an integer (see as.integer() / 1L ) - flag columns are stored as integers to save memory.
sections.code: mutate always creates column called condition_name variable contains string injects content equivalent next iteration stroke

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: substr(string, start, end)
sections.text: What it does: extracts part of a text string based on character positions. Analogy: You have the ICD code "DG30" . DST has prepended a "D" - it does not belong in standard ICD-10. substr("DG30", 2, 4) says: "give me characters from position 2 to 4" and returns "G30" . Register codes carry no decimal point. F00.1 is stored as DF001 , so the subtype digit is just the fifth character. Prefer substr(x, 2, 5) when you extract. substr() returns whatever is there when the string is shorter than the window you ask for, so it never pads and never errors: "DG30" gives "G30" and "DF001" gives "F001" . The shorter window is the lossy one, because substr(x, 2, 4) always returns three characters and therefore turns "DF001" into "F00" , discarding the subtype. Use the three-character version when you deliberately want a three-character grouping, and keep the original column beside it either way, so you can still tell F00.1 from F00.0 later without going back to the register.
sections.code: substr c_diag digit code dg30 g30 di110 i110

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: paste0(x, y)
sections.text: What it does: concatenates text strings without spaces. Used for compact construction of ICD code lists.
sections.code: paste0 creates c10 c11 c12 c43

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: paste(x, y, sep = "_")
sections.text: What it does: concatenates text strings with a chosen separator.
sections.code: koen birth_year sep creates e.g. matching key

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: toupper(x) / tolower(x)
sections.text: What it does: converts text to upper or lower case respectively.
sections.code: toupper c_opr ensures procedure codes match regardless capitalisation

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: grepl(pattern, x)
sections.text: What it does: returns TRUE / FALSE for each element in x that matches a search pattern (regular expression). Analogy: It is like "Ctrl+F" on a text document, but applied to entire columns at once. grepl("^C34", icd4) finds all 4-digit codes starting with C34 . Used e.g. to match ICD codes against diagnosis patterns in indices such as NMI (Nordic Multimorbidity Index).
sections.code: grepl c34 icd4 c340 c341 c342 etc.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: str_detect(x, pattern) <small>- stringr</small>
sections.text: What it does: the same job as grepl() above, just from the stringr package instead of base R, with the arguments in the opposite order ( str_detect(x, pattern) vs. grepl(pattern, x) ). Returns the same TRUE / FALSE per element. Used throughout the guide's diagnosis- and ATC-matching code (e.g. NMI) - functionally interchangeable with grepl() , pick whichever reads better in context.
sections.code: str_detect c_diag de1 any diabetes code e10 e14 prefix

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: as.Date(x)
sections.text: What it does: converts text or datetime to a simple date object. DST stores some date-times as "2021-03-15 14:32:00" . as.Date() removes the time parts and gives a clean calendar date. Use it after collect() , when the data are in R - see DST pitfall 4 for why.
sections.code: as.date kont_starttidspunkt after collect

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: ymd(x) / dmy(x) (from lubridate)
sections.text: What it does: reads dates that are not in ISO form ( "2021-03-15" ). Without a format , as.Date() expects the year first, and it does not stop on a day-first date: as.Date("15/03/2021") silently gives 0015-03-20 . The lubridate parsers take the order from the name ( ymd = year-month-day, dmy = day-month-year, mdy = month-day-year).
sections.code: ymd year month day dmy as.date gives

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: year(date) (from lubridate)
sections.text: What it does: extracts the year from a date. Use it after collect() , on data that is in R. On a lazy table the database has to translate year() , and depending on your fastreg version and backend that can stop with an error. If you need years before collect() , count or filter on the date column itself, and take the year in R afterwards.
sections.code: year surgery_date

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: difftime(date1, date2, units = "days")
sections.text: What it does: calculates the difference between two dates.
sections.code: as.numeric difftime surgery_date foed_dag units days age surgery years

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: min(x, na.rm = TRUE) / max(x, na.rm = TRUE)
sections.text: What it does: finds the smallest/largest element in a vector and ignores NA .
sections.code: summarise first_date min date_contact na.rm earliest contact per person

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: pmin(x, y) / pmax(x, y)
sections.text: What it does: compares two vectors position by position and returns the smallest/largest for each element. Analogy: Imagine two lists of dates - date of death and study end date. pmin(death_date, study_end) selects for each person what came first. Dates across the guide The functions above are the building blocks. The concrete date tasks are shown where they belong in the workflow: Age at index ( /365.25 , leap years): Comparison cohort Baseline year for annual registers ( year(index_date) - 1 ): Socioeconomic variables SAS integer dates ( origin = "1960-01-01" ): Pitfalls on DST Follow-up time and event variable ( pmin() ): Joins Start/stop format (time-varying covariate): Time-varying variables
sections.code: pmin death_date as.date na.rm censoring either death study end alive

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: as.integer(x) / 1L
sections.text: What it does: converts to integer. The L suffix (e.g. 1L , 0L ) specifies that it is an integer rather than a decimal. Flag columns are stored as integers ( 1L / 0L ) to save memory.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: is.na(x)
sections.text: What it does: returns TRUE for NA values (missing values).
sections.code: filter is.na pnr remove rows without person date_hip_fracture hip fracture

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: set.seed(n)
sections.text: What it does: fixes the starting point for random number generation. Analogy: Imagine shuffling a deck of cards. Without set.seed() you will shuffle differently every time. With set.seed(42) you always shuffle in the same way - and can thus reproduce your results exactly. Always call it before matching loops to ensure reproducibility.
sections.code: set.seed fix random seed reproducibility sample pool_pnrs size always selects same pnr

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: sample(x, size)
sections.text: What it does: draws random elements from a vector. Used in matching logic to select random control persons from a pool.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: split(df, group_vector)
sections.text: What it does: splits a data frame into a list of sub-data-frames, one per unique group. Analogy: Imagine sorting patient records into piles by year and sex. split(pool, paste(koen, birth_year, sep = "_")) gives you one pile per combination, so the matching code can work quickly within one pile at a time.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: vector("list", n)
sections.text: What it does: creates an empty list with space for n elements. Pre-allocation is faster than letting R expand the list one element at a time in a loop.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: seq_len(n)
sections.text: What it does: generates the sequence 1, 2, ..., n. Safer than 1:n in loops, because it handles the case n = 0 correctly.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: unlist(list, use.names = FALSE)
sections.text: What it does: flattens a list of vectors into one long vector.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: Diagnostics and debugging
sections.text: The functions below help you find out what went wrong . For the actual list of known error messages and what fixes them - "code stopped" or "code gave nothing back" - see Troubleshooting; for "the code ran fine but the answer is wrong," see DST pitfalls.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: class(x)
sections.text: What it does: tells you what type of object x is. Always check class() first if you get a strange error.
sections.code: class my_object tbl_df data.frame memory duckplyr_df duckplyr frame newer fastreg looks like tibble but may still lazy tbl_duckdb_connection duckdb query yet fetched arrow_dplyr_query arrow filesystemdataset dataset straight open_dataset

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: nrow(df)
sections.text: What it does: returns the number of rows. Used to print cohort sizes and verify that exclusions have worked. glimpse(df) (from dplyr ) gives a quick look at every column at once - name, type, and the first few values - transposed so it fits on screen even with many columns. A faster first check than head() when you just landed a new extract and want to see what you got.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: cat("text\n")
sections.text: What it does: prints text to the console without quotation marks. \n is a newline. Used for progress messages: cat("Extracting NMI score...\n") .

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: stop("message")
sections.text: What it does: stops the code with an error message. Used to give an understandable error if a required file is missing.

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: stopifnot(condition)
sections.text: What it does: a sanity check . If the condition is TRUE , nothing happens and the code continues. If it is FALSE , the code stops with an error. Use it for assumptions that MUST hold, e.g. "one row per person": What do you do if it stops? Then the assumption does not hold - e.g. there is more than one row per person. Find the duplicates and fix the cause: Duplicates often come from a join that multiplied rows, or from duplicate person-year rows in the source data.
sections.code: stopifnot n_distinct pnr errors there are duplicates count filter see which recur distinct keep_all keep one row per person correct

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: gc()
sections.text: What it does: runs R's garbage collection, which frees the memory of objects you have removed. R's help ( ?gc ) says this "may prompt R to return memory to the operating system", so the memory use you see does not always drop. Use it after you are done with large registers - you share RAM with everyone else on the DST server.
sections.code: large_register remove object free its memory

sections.title: Functions: overview
sections.heading: Package overview
sections.text: See Overview of registers for confirmed column names on all registers these packages work against. sections.title: Good coding practice
sections.text: Use this page when you start writing your own scripts rather than running the guide's examples one at a time: how to split a project into scripts, name things, check your data early, and keep your memory use down on the shared DST server. Read it before the project grows, because habits are cheaper to set up than to retrofit. Come back to Mind your RAM if your session slows down or is closed. Your results must be reproducible : a reviewer, a colleague or you in six months should get the same numbers by running your scripts again. In short: one script per step, run each script top to bottom (never across), give objects meaningful names, and comment the why rather than the what .

sections.title: Good coding practice
sections.heading: 1. Structure your scripts logically
sections.text: One script per step. Put each step of the analysis in its own .R file, named with a number that tells you the order to run them in: The script numbers tell anyone who sees the folder the order to run them in. Use subfolders as the project grows - e.g. R/ , output/ , datasets/ . A predictable order within each script. Whatever the script does, the same frame recurs: a header, load packages, import data - then the actual work - and finally save the result. Only the middle part changes from script to script: The same steps - header, packages, paths, data, save - recur in every script; only the actual work changes. The options() call belongs here, once, next to the library() calls: it is what lets read_register("bef") find a register by name, and it is the step people most often discover by getting an error. See Point fastreg at your registers. The header at the top tells you in five seconds what the script does, who wrote it and what it needs. More on good section headings and comments in section 5. Avoid jumping back and forth between cleaning, modelling and plotting. A script should read and run from top to bottom. If your code jumps around, it becomes impossible to follow - even for yourself. Larger projects? For a pipeline of several scripts, the targets package orchestrates the whole workflow and reruns only the steps whose inputs changed - reproducible, and fast to re-run.

sections.title: Good coding practice
sections.heading: 2. Run scripts top to bottom - never across
sections.text: A script should run from line 1 to the end without interruption and give the same result every time. Avoid running two lines from one file, jumping to another and back. Never run code manually across scripts. If your result depends on you having run line 14 in script 02 before line 7 in script 03, it is not reproducible. Instead, do a saveRDS() at the end of script 02 and a readRDS() at the start of script 03. When you think you are done: restart R ( Session → Restart R ) and run the whole script from line 1 again. Does it run clean? Then it is reproducible.

sections.heading: 3. Use meaningful object names
sections.text: The name should describe what the object contains . In six months you will not remember what a and b were. participant_data and bmi_model explain themselves.

sections.title: Good coding practice
sections.heading: 4. Use snake_case consistently
sections.text: Consistent naming makes code far easier to read. Pick snake_case (lowercase with underscores) and stick to it: What matters is not which style, but that you are consistent.

sections.title: Good coding practice
sections.heading: 5. Headings and comments make the code readable
sections.text: Headings and comments are what make a script navigable - for a reviewer, a colleague or yourself in six months. Three things to get into the habit of: A short description at the top of each script: what it does, what it needs as input, and what it produces (the header from section 1). Section headings that run out to the right margin: write the heading, then fill the rest of the line with dashes, as in the example in section 1. That one line does two jobs: it breaks the file up visually, and it makes the heading a section your editor can navigate to (see below). A comment on each substantial line of code: but explain why , not what . Comment the "why", not the "what". The code already shows what happens. A good comment explains why - the decision behind it. Explain choices, assumptions and sources - not the obvious. It takes five minutes to write a good comment now and an hour to understand the code again in three months.
sections.code: bad comment just repeats code calculate bmi bmi weight height better explains decision used adjustment variable primary models

sections.title: Good coding practice
sections.heading: Find your way around a long script
sections.text: Your editor keeps an outline of the file you are editing: an automatically generated table of contents. You do not write it. The editor builds it from your code, listing every function you define plus every comment line you have marked as a section heading. A 600-line extraction script stops needing to be scrolled. Where to find it. In RStudio the outline is a panel on the right-hand side of the editor. The same list also sits in the dropdown at the bottom left of the editor pane, the one that normally reads (Top Level) : it is clickable, and a lot of people have looked past it for years. Each entry in the outline is a comment line ending in dashes, and the small triangles in the left margin of the editor fold a section away. The dropdown at the bottom left shows the section the cursor is currently in. What Windows / Linux macOS Toggle the outline panel Ctrl+Shift+O Shift+Cmd+O Open the jump-to dropdown Shift+Alt+J Cmd+Shift+Option+J Insert a new section Ctrl+Shift+R Shift+Cmd+R What turns a comment into a heading. A comment line that ends with four or more - , = or # characters. All three work and they are interchangeable; dashes are simply the most common. Whatever comes before that trailing run becomes the label in the panel: That trailing run is the entire mechanism. A comment without it never appears in the outline. A space before the run is not required, it is just easier to read. That has a consequence worth knowing, and it is the subject of the warning below. What you get out of it, in order of usefulness: Jumping: click an entry and the cursor goes there. This is the main point. Folding: a triangle appears in the left margin of each section, so you can collapse everything except the part you are working on and see the shape of the whole script on one screen. Orientation: the panel is a map. A colleague opening your script for the first time sees what is in it before reading a single line, which is exactly how register code is usually read. Getting the most out of it: Name a section after what the step does, not what it touches: # Restrict to study period ---- beats # Dates ---- . Number them (1., 2., 2.1) so the outline reads as a sequence, and so a colleague can write "what happens in section 4?" in an email. Run the dashes out to the right margin rather than stopping at four. It costs nothing, the heading then doubles as the visual break in the file, and Ctrl+Shift+R writes it for you. Keep a contents list in the script header mirroring the section numbers. The outline only works inside an editor; a contents list also works in a diff, in a code review and on paper. Check that it works. Press Ctrl+Shift+O in a file you have just marked up. If a heading is missing from the panel, its marker is missing or too short (three dashes instead of four). If the panel is instead full of entries called (Untitled) , the file has rule lines in it - #----- on a line of its own, usually boxing a heading in. Since no space is required before the marker, each rule line counts as a heading with no text in front of the dashes. Delete them and put the dashes on the heading line instead. You will meet this in scripts you inherit from colleagues. The outline is also a check on the script itself. For a simple script it should read as the four steps from section 1: header, packages, data, save. If it does not, the script does not follow the structure.

sections.heading: 6. Avoid hard-coded "magic numbers"

sections.text: If you copy the same code more than a few times - e.g. a Table 1 for each exposure group - write a function. Functions reduce errors: fix something once, and it is fixed everywhere.

sections.title: Good coding practice
sections.heading: How to write your own function
sections.text: A function has three parts: a name , some arguments (the input in the parentheses), and a body (the code between { } ). Whatever the last line produces is what the function returns. A concrete example - a function that computes age at a given date: You can read more about writing functions - arguments, default values and when they pay off - in Writing functions in The Epidemiologist R Handbook .

sections.title: Good coding practice
sections.heading: Share functions across scripts with a separate file
sections.text: A function only helps within the script it is defined in. As soon as a second script needs it, you copy it over - and now you have two versions that drift apart. You fix a bug in one of them, months pass, and you can no longer tell which analysis was run with which version. The fix is one shared file that both scripts read. Three steps: 1. Put the definitions in their own file , e.g. 00_functions.R . The 00_ prefix places it first, before the numbered scripts (see section 2). 2. Delete the definitions from the scripts and read the file instead, right after the library() calls: 3. Verify it before you trust it. Restart R completely first ( Session → Restart R , or Ctrl + Shift + F10 ) so you know an old copy is not still sitting in memory: Move the constants too. get_prior_hip_fracture_pnrs() uses hip_fracture_icd3 . If you move the function but leave the constant behind in the old script, the function does not fail when you source it - it fails later , at a random point deep inside a run, with object 'hip_fracture_icd3' not found . Anything a function refers to but does not take as an argument has to move with it. source() runs the whole file, top to bottom. Everything at the top level is executed, not just the function() {} blocks. So the file must contain definitions only : no read_register() , no saveRDS() , no cat() , no test calls. Otherwise you re-run the data loading every single time you source it, and a ten-second step becomes ten minutes. The path is relative to your working directory. source("00_functions.R") looks in the folder R is currently standing in. Open your work through the .Rproj file and that folder is fixed to the project folder, so the short path always works - see Phase 3 - Log in to DST. If getwd() shows something else, you opened R without the project.

sections.title: Good coding practice
sections.heading: 9. Fail early - check your data before the analysis
sections.text: It is cheaper to catch an error straight away than to discover it in a finished result. Insert explicit checks of your assumptions: If the check fails, the script stops immediately - instead of carrying a hidden error forward into your models.

sections.title: Good coding practice
sections.heading: 10. One object = one purpose
sections.text: Avoid overwriting the same object again and again. It makes debugging hard, because data means something different depending on how far you have got: Now you can inspect each intermediate step ( raw_data , clean_data , analysis_data ) separately - invaluable when something looks wrong.

sections.title: Good coding practice
sections.heading: 11. Mind your RAM in the shared environment
sections.text: On Forskermaskinen (the shared environment) all users share the same RAM. R loads data directly into RAM, so a single large extraction can slow the server for everyone. That is why DST automatically kills processes (RStudio sessions, jobs, etc.) when memory is close to full - and if your session is killed, you lose all unsaved work. DST does not state in its RAM guide (PDF, Danish) at what level this happens, so do not plan around a fixed limit. Save often, and write to disk along the way. Save your code continuously, and write intermediate results to disk with saveRDS() (cf. sections 2 and 10), so you do not lose hours of work if your process is killed. Concrete habits that keep RAM use down: Load only what you need. Select columns and rows before data lands in RAM - see Read only what you need ( open_dataset() + filter / select , read_sas(col_select=, n_max=) ). Clean up as you go. Delete large objects once you no longer need them: Close unused sessions , and start a fresh session when you begin a new task ( Session → Restart R ) - this also clears out old objects. Keep an eye on usage. Two views, and you want both. The Task Manager shortcut on the server's desktop → the Users tab → your project ident → Memory tells you what the machine is doing. To see what your R session is holding, see below. Still a large table after collect() ? Consider data.table Loading less comes first. Filter rows and select columns while the register is still lazy, so DuckDB does the heavy work and only the result reaches R's memory. Most slow or memory-hungry scripts are fixed there, not by switching package. Sometimes the table is still large after collect() : every prescription for a whole population, say, with many rows per person. If grouped calculations or joins on such a table are slow in dplyr , the data.table package is worth a look, for two reasons: It is fast on large tables in memory. Grouping, sorting and joining are what it is built for. It can change a table in place. Adding a column with := changes the existing table, where mutate() hands you a modified copy. On a table of several GB that saves both time and RAM. The syntax is table[rows, what to do, by = group] : You do not have to choose one package for the whole project. A data.table is still a data frame, so filter() , left_join() and the rest keep working on it. Rewrite only the step that is slow, and leave the rest of the script as it is. data.table is on DST, so library(data.table) is all you need. It is also the package heaven is built on (see heaven in the package overview). An introduction is in Data Table in The Epidemiologist R Handbook .

sections.title: Good coding practice
sections.heading: Seeing your memory use from inside R
sections.text: The Task Manager tells you the machine is running out of memory. It does not tell you which object is the problem. R can, and you do not need any extra packages for it. How much is this session using right now? Read the (Mb) columns. used is what your session holds at this moment, max used the high-water mark since the session started. The Vcells row is the one that matters for data: it counts the memory holding your actual values. Calling gc() also asks R to hand back memory it no longer needs, so it is useful after an rm() . Which object is eating it? That prints something like lpr_raw 4.2 Gb next to cohort 1.3 Mb , and the culprit is usually obvious immediately. Then rm(lpr_raw); gc() . A single object, before you decide to keep it: RStudio shows it too. The Environment pane lists every object with its size, and the dropdown at the top of that pane has a Memory Usage... report with the session total. It is the same numbers as above, without typing anything - handy while you work, though the code is what you want when you need to compare two approaches. object.size() measures the object, not the query. A lazy parquet connection from open_dataset() or read_register() is a few KB no matter how large the register behind it is - that is the whole point of lazy loading (see Phase 4). The size only becomes real after collect() . So a small object.size() on a lazy object is good news, not a measurement error. If the shared environment cannot handle your analyses, you can look into a hosted server or high performance computing. What is actually installed on the shared machine is listed in DST's hardware and software overview--) (PDF, Danish). DST's official advice, with code examples in R, Python and STATA, is collected in DST guide: Reducing RAM use in the shared environment (PDF, Danish).

sections.title: Healthcare costs
sections.text: Use this page if your study needs healthcare costs per person. The registers hold no single cost variable: costs are assembled from several sources, each priced in its own way. This page says where the costs are, and how to read the DRG registers at Statistics Denmark (DST), which put a price on hospital contacts. Check your own delivery. The registers and years below were checked against DST's register overview in November 2026. The Danish Health Data Authority (Sundhedsdatastyrelsen, SDS) changes the tariffs and the grouping logic every year, so column names and years can change. Compare with colnames() in your own data.

sections.title: Healthcare costs
sections.heading: Where costs come from
sections.text: Somatic hospital contacts: priced by DRG (Diagnosis Related Groups). SDS places each hospital contact in a DRG group and sets a tariff for each group every year, the average operating cost of a patient in that group (SDS DRG rates). In the LPR2 period, inpatients were grouped by DRG and outpatients by DAGS (Dansk Ambulant Grupperings System) (SDS, DRG-grouped LPR). Today all somatic patients are settled with DRG tariffs (Takstvejledning 2024, section 3.1). Which registers DST holds is in DRG data at DST. Psychiatric hospital contacts: are not settled by DRG. Inpatients are settled with a bed-day rate and outpatient visits with a visit rate. SDS calculated indicative DRG and DAGS tariffs for psychiatry up to tariff system 2018 (Takstvejledning 2024, section 3.2), and DST holds them in DRGPSYK_HEL and DRGPSYK_AMB . Whether the current DRG registers hold psychiatric activity is unclear, see Psychiatry in the LPR3 DRG registers. Keep somatic and psychiatric costs apart. Primary sector (general practice, specialists etc.): fees in sysi / sssy (Overview of registers). Prescription medication: patient co-payment and reimbursement in LMDB. Medication given in hospital: Hospital medication (SMR), but read What a DRG price covers before you add it to DRG prices.

sections.title: Healthcare costs
sections.heading: DRG data at DST
sections.text: DST holds the DRG-grouped data in a separate set of registers for each period, so a study period that crosses 2018 needs more than one set (DST's register overview): Register Content Years Status DRGSOMA_HEL , DRGSOMA_AMB LPR2, inpatients and outpatients 2002-2017 Closed 15 January 2024 DRGSOMA_KONTAKT , DRGSOMA_SGHFORLOB , DRGSOMA_PROCEDURE Contacts, hospital courses and procedures 2018 Closed 15 January 2024 DRGPSYK_HEL , DRGPSYK_AMB Indicative psychiatric tariffs 2004-2018 Closed 15 January 2024 DRG_KONTAKTER , DRG_SGHFORLOB LPR3, contacts and hospital courses Tariff years 2021-2025 Updated yearly DRG_DIAGNOSE , DRG_PROCEDURE and three more LPR3, diagnoses, procedures and internal codes Tariff years 2022-2025 Updated yearly The columns of DRG_KONTAKTER and DRG_SGHFORLOB are listed on Overview of registers. The LPR2 registers, and stays that crossed into LPR3 in 2019 In DRGSOMA_HEL and DRGSOMA_AMB , V_PRIS is given in 1,000 kr. ("Angivet i 1.000 kr."), and for inpatients V_AAR is the year of discharge from the last contact of the course, so costs follow the discharge year (SDS, DRG-grouped LPR). A stay that crossed the change to LPR3 in 2019 is priced on its LPR3 course. Its LPR2 course gets the group 90UA07 "Flyttet til DRG LPR3" (moved to DRG LPR3) (SDS, DRG-grouped LPR3 data, tariff system 2019, section 3.4.3.3).

sections.title: Healthcare costs
sections.heading: The year of an LPR3 DRG file is the tariff year
sections.text: In DRG_KONTAKTER and DRG_SGHFORLOB the year in the file name is the tariff year ("Takståret"), not the year the activity took place. Each yearly file holds that year and the two years before it, given by AKTIVITETSAAR (DST, register note for DRG_KONTAKTER%20takster%20%E2%80%93%20DRG%20kontakter.html)). The first release grouped tariff system 2021 with activity years 2019 to 2021 and tariff system 2022 with 2020 to 2022 (DST, register history for DRG_KONTAKTER, 14 May 2024). AKTIVITETSAAR is the year the last contact of the hospital course ended (SDS, DRG-grouped LPR3 data, tariff system 2025, section 3). Do not stack the yearly files. Most activity is in three files, priced each time with a different tariff system. Prices compare within one tariff system. Tariffs hold for one calendar year, and SDS groups several activity years in each file so that the years "kan sammenlignes i samme takstsystem" (can be compared in the same tariff system) (SDS, tariff system 2025, section 6.3). Prices are in the tariff year's price level. A tariff system gives its tariffs in that year's price and wage level, for example "2024 pris- og lønniveau" in Takstvejledning 2024 (section 3.1). Bring all years to one price year before you sum or compare across years. There are two consistent ways to choose rows. The first is one tariff system: take one file and its three activity years. The prices compare across those years, but you get three years at most. The second is each year's own tariffs: take each activity year from the file with the same tariff year ( AKTIVITETSAAR equal to the year in the file name). There are no files for tariff years 2019 and 2020, so take those two activity years from the 2021 file. The second way follows from how DST builds the files; it is not a DST recommendation.

sections.title: Healthcare costs
sections.heading: Contact or hospital course: price one level
sections.text: Both registers carry a price. In DRG_KONTAKTER , PRIS_DRG is the tariff of the contact's DRG group. In DRG_SGHFORLOB , PRIS_DRG_DRGSGHF is the tariff of the hospital course's DRG group. TOTALPRIS_DRG and TOTALPRIS_DRGSGHF add the long-stay price at each level (SDS, tariff system 2025, Tabel 25). Summing contact and course prices counts the same activity twice. Use the hospital course unless you have a reason not to. Somatic hospital treatment is settled "pr. DRG-sygehusforløb" (per DRG hospital course) (Takstsystem 2026, section 3.1.1), so TOTALPRIS_DRGSGHF is the price that was settled. A contact price comes from grouping that contact on its own. It helps when you need to place costs at a date within a long course, but the sum of the contact prices need not equal the course price.

sections.title: Healthcare costs
sections.heading: What a DRG price covers
sections.text: A tariff reflects the calculated direct costs of treating the patient and of rehabilitation. It does not include, for example, civil-servant pensions, interest or depreciation (Takstvejledning 2024, section 3.1). Medication can go wrong in both directions: Ordinary hospital medicine is in the DRG price. Medicine treatment is itself grouped and priced in DRG, for example in the groups 34PR01 to 34PR10 "Medicin-behandling" (Takstsystem 2026, Bilag B3.2). Adding costs from the Hospital Medication Register on top of DRG prices can count it twice. Expensive medicine is not. Medicine dispensed for more than 1,000 kr. per day is a special service (særydelse, SYD02), settled separately at cost (Takstsystem 2026, Bilagstabel 7), so the DRG price leaves it out. DST's variable lists for DRG_KONTAKTER and DRG_SGHFORLOB have no column for special services.

sections.title: Healthcare costs
sections.heading: Psychiatry in the LPR3 DRG registers
sections.text: SDS writes that the DRG-grouped LPR3 data hold "Kun somatisk aktivitet" (somatic activity only) (SDS, tariff system 2025, section 3.4.1.2). DST's register history for DRGPSYK_HEL says the register was closed because the psychiatric tariffs are now included with the somatic ones "i det nye DRG" (in the new DRG), in DRG_KONTAKTER and DRG_SGHFORLOB (DST, register history for DRGPSYK_HEL, 15 January 2024). The two statements do not agree. Tabulate SPECIALE in your own delivery before you assume that psychiatric contacts are present or absent.

sections.title: Healthcare costs
sections.heading: See also
sections.text: Overview of registers: the columns of DRG_KONTAKTER and DRG_SGHFORLOB . The Plana-Ripoll group's code on OSF: the idea of assembling costs from these sources comes from there. Its variable names are from a 2022 delivery and should not be assumed current.

sections.title: Hospital medication (SMR)
sections.text: Use this page if your study needs medication given in hospital, which is not in the prescription register LMDB (see Medication (ATC)). Cancer drugs and biologics given at a hospital are typical examples. SMR is not a DST register. It is held by the Danish Health Data Authority (Sundhedsdatastyrelsen, SDS), its data quality has not yet been evaluated, and some clinical specialties are missing (Rosenkrantz et al. 2024). This page says what to check before you rely on it.

sections.title: Hospital medication (SMR)
sections.heading: What SMR holds
sections.text: The Hospital Medication Register (Sygehusmedicinregisteret, SMR) holds medication given or dispensed at public hospitals and hospital outpatient clinics, reported by the five regions. The regions started reporting on 15 May 2018, so there is nothing before that date (data declaration, June 2026, section 1.2). Private hospitals, hospices and specialist hospitals run as independent institutions are not reported (data declaration, June 2026). You apply for SMR through the Forskerservice of SDS, which says that data are as a rule made available on research machines at SDS or at DST (Forskerservice). Ask Forskerservice how SMR will reach your project before you plan the linkage to your DST registers. SDS also warns that replacement civil registration (CPR) numbers are not unique across regions, so read V_CPR together with the region (data declaration, section 4.1.16). The column names below are the ones in SDS's data declaration. Check them against the columns in your own delivery with colnames() .

sections.title: Hospital medication (SMR)
sections.heading: Completeness differs by region and drug
sections.text: At the end of 2022 SDS wrote that heavy medicines (cancer drugs and biologics) were missing for Region Nordjylland and Region Syddanmark. Dispensed medicine was missing for Region Hovedstaden, Region Sjælland, Region Nordjylland and Region Syddanmark, and only partly reported by Region Midtjylland. A cost could be calculated for only about 60% of the reported administrations (SDS, gevinstrealisering i forbindelse med SMR2-projektet, 9 March 2023). The June 2026 declaration describes cancer drugs region by region: Midtjylland reports them from early 2019 for oncology departments, from September 2019 for haematology outpatients, from mid-2021 for haematology inpatients and from early 2023 for children and young people. Nordjylland does not give parenteral cancer drugs in the medication module, so they are not reported. Reporting from the haematology department starts in August 2025. Syddanmark does not handle cancer drugs in the medication module. An electronic treatment scheme was in use in some departments in September 2025, and SDS calls the data incomplete. Hovedstaden and Sjælland do not report cytostatics dispensed for home treatment. A zero count for a cancer drug or a biologic in a region is therefore not evidence of no use. The same section lists other gaps, such as intensive care and anaesthesia, eye departments and some outpatient clinics. Read the entries for the departments and drugs in your study.

sections.title: Hospital medication (SMR)
sections.heading: Breaks when a region moves to reporting guide 2.0
sections.text: Each region moves from reporting guide 1.x to reporting guide 2.0 (called "SMR2" in the declaration) on its own date. Rows from before and after the move are not the same kind of rows. Guide 2.0 dates, mixtures and infusion times by region Region Guide 2.0 from Mixtures Infusion time in D_ADM before 2.0 Nordjylland April 2025 One row per administration from March 2022, no dose for the components Take-down time, from April 2022 (end date not given) Midtjylland October 2025 A main row plus one row per component from February 2021, no component dose Start time, but the row is reported at take-down, from June 2019 Syddanmark September 2025 Not registered in the medication module Take-down time until autumn 2023, start time after Hovedstaden, Sjælland No date in the declaration Not split into components Start time chosen by the user What changes in your data at the move (data declaration, sections 2.4 and 4.1): Rows that disappear. Guide 2.0 does not allow dose 0 (an administration that was planned but not given), future administrations or the patient's own medicine. Nordjylland, Midtjylland and Syddanmark reported dose 0 before the move, Midtjylland reported dispensed medicine as administrations dated in the future from February 2021, and Nordjylland reported own medicine from May 2018. Earlier periods therefore contain rows that later periods do not. Dropping rows with V_ADM_DOSIS 0 in every period removes the first of these differences, but not the other two. A new administration key. Under 2.0 K_ADM_ID is a new synthetic key. SDS writes that it "Er ikke kompatibel, med nøglen i version 1.x." Do not use it to link rows reported before and after a region's move. Deleted rows. A row that was reported and later deleted in the hospital system stays in SMR with C_SLETTET = 1 . Rows that are not deleted have C_SLETTET = 0 . If your delivery has the column, remove the deleted rows. Dose units. Before 2.0 each region used its own unit list. In Hovedstaden and Sjælland the unit can be a rate or a concentration, such as mg/kg, mg/ml or microgram/kg/min, instead of an amount. Check the units in V_ADM_DOSIS_ENHED before you sum doses. Infusions. The table above shows which time D_ADM holds for a continuous infusion. An infusion reported at take-down can fall in a later month than it started.

sections.title: Hospital medication (SMR)
sections.heading: ATC codes change over time
sections.text: C_ATC is the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) code that was valid when the drug was given (data declaration, section 4.1.22), and WHO revises the ATC system every year. A drug can therefore have one code early in the register and another later. The monoclonal antibodies are an example: they were under L01XC and are now under L01F in WHO's ATC index. A filter on the old code alone loses the later rows, and the drop looks like a break in the register. Look up whether the drugs in your study changed code during your study period, and filter on both the old and the new code.

A region where a drug is absent, or where the count jumps at a move to guide 2.0, tells you where the register cannot answer your question. The sketch below uses the declaration's column names in lower case and the monoclonal antibodies as the example, under both their old and their new ATC code. smr is your opened SMR table, opened in the same way as lmdb in Extract the dispensings: read_register() with your SMR table's name, then rename_with(tolower) . sections.title: Immigrants and descendants
sections.text: Use this page if your study needs to describe or adjust for immigrant status or country of origin. The registers do not hold ethnicity. They hold what the Civil Registration System (CPR) records about birthplace and citizenship, for the person and for the parents, and Statistics Denmark (DST) derives groups from that. This page says how DST defines the groups and what to check before you use them. SEPLINE, the national guideline behind the socioeconomic variables, says the same: country of origin and immigration status are an attempt to approximate ethnic minority status, not ethnicity itself (Hjorth et al. 2025, section on ethnicity).

sections.title: Immigrants and descendants
sections.heading: Where the variables are
sections.text: Information Register Variables From Person of Danish origin, immigrant or descendant BEF ie_type 1985 Country of origin BEF opr_land 1985 Date, direction and country of each migration VNDS haend_dato , indud_kode , indud_land 1973 First and latest immigration BEF foerste_indvandring , seneste_indvandring 2004 Months of residence in Denmark BEF opholdmd_dk 1985 Ground of residence, for example refugee OPHG kategori , grundlag , forklar 1997 BEF is the population register and VNDS the migration register. DST closed VNDS in February 2026 and split it into VNDS_ind , VNDS_ud and VNDS_hist ; see the register reference for which one you have. Sources: Hjorth et al. 2025, Table 13, and DST's variable list for BEF. SEPLINE gives 2004 for all three BEF migration columns, but DST's variable list has opholdmd_dk from 1985. Column lists for BEF and VNDS are in the register reference.

sections.title: Immigrants and descendants
sections.heading: Immigrant, descendant or Danish origin (ie_type)
sections.text: DST's definitions, from its documentation of IE_TYPE: Code Group DST's definition (our translation) 1 Persons of Danish origin At least one parent is both a Danish citizen and born in Denmark, wherever the person was born. 2 Immigrants Born abroad, and no parent is both a Danish citizen and born in Denmark. 3 Descendants Born in Denmark, and no parent is both a Danish citizen and born in Denmark. 9 Not stated (uoplyst) The codes and labels are in DST's classification Herkomst, v1:1980, valid from 1 January 1980 and still valid. DST's own page for IE_TYPE says that the variable has no value set, so run count(ie_type) on your own delivery to see which codes it holds, including the one for unknown. When no parent is known, DST uses the person's own information: if there is no information on either parent and the person was born abroad, the person is also counted as an immigrant (our translation). A person with no known parent who is a foreign citizen is a descendant, and a person with no known parent who was born in Denmark is of Danish origin.

sections.title: Immigrants and descendants
sections.heading: Country of origin (opr_land)
sections.text: opr_land is a country code, and it is not the country of birth. DST defines it from birth country and citizenship country by these rules (DST, OPR_LAND): A person of Danish origin always has Denmark. If no parent is known, the origin is taken from the person's own information. For an immigrant it is the country of birth, for a descendant the country of citizenship. If only one parent is known, it is that parent's country of birth, or the parent's country of citizenship if the parent was born in Denmark. If both parents are known, it is the mother's country of birth, or her country of citizenship if she was born in Denmark. So a descendant's country of origin follows the parents, not the place where the descendant was born. DST's definition does not tell you whether one of the parents was born in Denmark. SEPLINE suggests a separate group for people of Danish origin with one parent born in Denmark and one parent born abroad (Table 14 in Hjorth et al. 2025). The parents are found through mor_id and far_id in BEF. A parent's opr_land does not give that parent's birthplace: by the rules above, a parent born abroad to a Danish-born Danish citizen is of Danish origin and has Denmark. Some codes are not current countries. DST lists former states such as the Soviet Union, which appear when a person is still recorded in CPR with that country, and areas such as Palestine (5157), Gaza (5223), the West Bank (5393) and East Jerusalem (5437). A number of codes were retired and folded into others, for example East Germany (5184) into Germany (5180) on 3 October 1990. Group through DST's classification below rather than by hand, and check with anti_join() that every code in your data gets a group.

sections.title: Immigrants and descendants
sections.heading: Western and non-Western, and other country groupings
sections.text: DST publishes country codes in the classification Lande i personstatistik, v1:2021, valid from 1 January 2021. It has three groupings. Grouping Groups Vestlige/Ikke-vestlige lande (Western and non-Western countries) Denmark, Western countries, non-Western countries, unknown EU/EØS-lande (EU/EEA and countries outside the EU/EEA) EU/EEA, outside the EU/EEA World regions (the default hierarchy) Europe, Africa, America, Asia, Oceania, stateless and unknown, with subgroups such as EU-27 without the United Kingdom DST's classification lists the Western countries and gives no definition. They are the EU countries, the United Kingdom, Andorra, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Monaco, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland, the Vatican, Canada, the USA, Australia and New Zealand. Denmark, the Faroe Islands and Greenland form a group of their own. The United Kingdom is Western and not in the EU/EEA group, so the two groupings are not the same. In the EU/EEA grouping, Denmark, the Faroe Islands and Greenland sit inside the EU/EEA group, so set people of Danish origin apart with ie_type first if you compare EU/EEA with the rest. DST has used the Western and non-Western grouping since 2002. In 2019 DST concluded that it is still usable for statistics (our translation) and kept it. One reason is that it is written into current legislation. DST describes the aim as groups that differ as much as possible from each other and are fairly uniform within, not groups by culture, and notes that Japan is non-Western. At the same time DST added the EU/EEA grouping, and 93.4 percent of Western immigrants and descendants fall in the EU/EEA group (Elmeskov, DST, 11 July 2019). SEPLINE gives Western and non-Western as one possible split, lists world regions and EU/EEA against the rest as the alternatives from DST, and recommends the most detailed reporting the data allow. If you build your own regional grouping, define it in the methods.

sections.title: Immigrants and descendants
sections.heading: Migration type and arrival
sections.text: Which register holds the migration events, and how to use them to decide residence on an index date, are covered in Phase 10 and in the VNDS section of the register reference. For the reason for migration, the registers say little. The ground of residence in OPHG is registered from 1997 and can be used to identify refugees. Before 1997 there is a register at DST with mainly imputed values, which SEPLINE does not recommend for small study populations. Some studies approximate refugee status by country of origin and arrival in 1986 to 1992 (Hjorth et al. 2025, section on ethnicity). Length of stay can be calculated from the migration events or taken from opholdmd_dk in BEF from 1985.

sections.title: Immigrants and descendants
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Status can change. A descendant whose Danish-born parents both keep a foreign citizenship stays a descendant. If one of them becomes a Danish citizen, DST classifies the child as of Danish origin, and the country of origin changes with it. Decide the date at which you fix the status, and report it. Before 2008, one status per year. SEPLINE states that before 2008 ie_type and opr_land are only available for people who lived in Denmark the whole calendar year. DST's page for IE_TYPE describes the population as people with permanent residence in Denmark on 1 January of the year (our translation). Newly registered residents and people without a Danish CPR number, such as asylum seekers, are missing. After 2008 the information is quarterly. SEPLINE suggests using a nearby year if the index year is missing (Hjorth et al. 2025). Event tables from the second quarter of 2019. In DST's event tables, such as births, deaths and migrations, ie_type and opr_land are formed on the event date and not at the end of the quarter. No history before arrival. Births, diagnoses and education abroad are not in the Danish registers. For education, see how missing education is handled. A sensitivity analysis restricted to people born in Denmark reduces the problem for your outcome, but it also removes the immigrants, who may be the group your question is about. Not a measure of ethnicity. The definitions depend on citizenship and birthplace, and they say nothing about how a person identifies. SEPLINE adds that these variables proxy many other circumstances and are often mediators of socioeconomic differences, not confounders. Emigration. People leave and return. Use the migration events to censor at emigration, see Attach date of death and emigration.

sections.title: Immigrants and descendants
sections.heading: Count the groups in your cohort
sections.text: Check by eye on your own data before you build on it. The sketch reads the most recent BEF snapshot up to the year before index, the same baseline year as the socioeconomic recipes, so the status is fixed before follow-up starts. It keeps unknown as its own category, as on the socioeconomic variables page, and keeps people with no BEF row in that period apart from DST's own unknown. To split into Western and non-Western, join opr_land to DST's country classification above. Do not type the list of countries by hand.

sections.title: Register-based research at Statistics Denmark
sections.text: This guide is for researchers who start a register-based study on the Statistics Denmark (DST) research servers and do the data work themselves in R. It is written with clinicians and PhD students in mind. You do not need experience with registers, and the R you need to begin with is in phase 2. It assumes that your project already has access to DST and that your registers have been delivered. It does not cover how to apply for data, and it does not teach statistical methods: the analysis pages show which R tools fit a register study and point to courses and books for the theory. The guide is organised as 14 numbered phases, from planning a study to getting the results out through DST's output control. If you are new, start at phase 1 - Plan your study and take the phases in order; the links at the bottom of each page lead to the next one. If you already know R and only need the DST side, start at phase 3 - Log in to DST. The look-up pages further down are for use as you go. To find something, use the search box in the top bar for exact words, or Search by meaning when you do not know what the guide calls it or want to search in Danish.

sections.text: What each phase covers. The sidebar groups the phases into five stages. sections.text: Use this page every time you have pulled data into R and before you build anything on it: it collects the commands for checking what an extract actually contains. You need an extract to look at, so do Phase 6 - First extraction first. When you are done you know the size, column types, values, missing values and date ranges of your extract, and whether each register you use reaches the end of your follow-up. $ - access one column in a table data$koen means: "the column koen in the table data ". Replace data with your own dataset name and koen with your own column name. You will see $ everywhere in R code. Want to practise the commands in RStudio? All examples on the page use bef_data - a BEF extract with columns such as koen , alder and foed_dag . You can generate it with two lines, provided you have run the preparation block in Phase 6:

sections.title: Inspect and understand your data
sections.heading: The shape: size, columns and types
sections.text: Those four work on data that is already in R. On a lazy object - one you have opened but not yet collect() ed, called bef in the examples below - checking the column names is fiddlier than it looks, and both of the obvious ways can mislead you: names() on a lazy DuckDB connection made with to_duckdb() returns the connection's parts ( src , lazy_query ), not the table's columns. colnames() works on the DuckDB objects read_register() gives you, but on a lazy Arrow query that has been through rename_with() it can return NULL without any error, so columns that exist look missing. (Seen with arrow 23.0.1; other arrow versions may behave differently.) The reliable version fetches the structure with zero rows: arrow::schema(bef) also works on an Arrow connection and gives you the types as well - see arrow::schema() . Example with simple data What type is each column? class(bef_data) tells you whether you have real data ( "data.frame" / "tbl_df" ) or still just an unsent query. You can see four different kinds of return value: "data.frame" / "tbl_df" without "prudent_duckplyr_df" - data is in R. You can use all functions. "prudent_duckplyr_df" (followed by "duckplyr_df" "tbl_df" "tbl" "data.frame" ) - a lazy DuckDB table from read_parquet_duckdb() , or from read_register() in fastreg 0.14.3 or newer. It says "data.frame" , but nothing is fetched yet. Missing collect() . "FileSystemDataset" (from open_dataset() ) or "tbl_duckdb_connection" (from to_duckdb() , or from read_register() in fastreg 0.14.2 or older) - a lazy Arrow/DuckDB connection. Missing collect() . "arrow_dplyr_query" - an Arrow query with one or more piped steps (e.g. filter() or select() ), but not yet executed. Missing collect() . class() can help you debug Does the object look like data but behave strangely, or does your code fail with a mysterious message? Run class(your_object) - if it is not "data.frame" , or it still includes "prudent_duckplyr_df" , you are probably missing a collect() . The full table of what class() can return - and why - is in Phase 5 - Extracting data step by step. What does a row actually look like?

sections.title: Inspect and understand your data
sections.heading: The values: what is actually in each column
sections.text: Two things must be in place before the commands in the rest of this section work 1. Give your extraction a name. If you just write open_dataset(...) or read_register(...) without storing it in an object, R only prints a quick preview and throws the result away - there is nothing to inspect afterwards. Assign it a name with <- (see Phase 2 - What is an object?) so you can reuse it. 2. Pull the data into R with collect() first. Every command that uses $ (e.g. table(bef$koen) , unique() , summary() , min()/max()/median() , hist() , colSums(is.na()) ) needs real data in R - $ cannot extract a column from a lazy Arrow/DuckDB connection. Check with class(bef) : if it does not say "data.frame" / "tbl_df" , or it still says "prudent_duckplyr_df" , you are missing a collect() . You do not rewrite read_register() / open_dataset() to pull the data in - keep working with the object you already made. Reuse the name and store the result, usually under the same name, so bef is overwritten and is now real data. On a real register, always reduce it with filter() / select() first: (If you want to keep the lazy connection, give the fetched data a new name instead: bef_2015 <- bef %>% filter(year == 2015) %>% collect() .) glimpse() , head() and dplyr verbs ( count() , filter() , select() ) do work fine on the lazy connection, though (for column names, use the zero-row trick above). So peek lazily, filter() / select() it down, and collect() a small slice before you dig into the values. As noted at the top of the page, $ is R's way of saying "this column in this table": data$koen is the column koen in the table data . table() hides NA by default. Without useNA = "ifany" , table() only counts the "real" values and drops missing values entirely - so the distribution looks complete even when part of the column is NA . Always add useNA = "ifany" (show the NA row only if NAs exist) or useNA = "always" (always show the NA row) when inspecting a column, so you spot missing values instead of overlooking them. Example with simple data
