sections.title: Inspect and understand your data
sections.heading: Summarise data
sections.text: What is NA? NA ( Not Available ) is R's term for a missing or unknown value. A cell can have NA because the information was not recorded, not reported, or does not exist for that person. Most calculation functions return NA if there is one NA in the data - unless you write na.rm = TRUE ("remove NAs"). is.na(x) returns TRUE for NA values and FALSE for everything else. When is NA a problem? It depends on which column is missing: NA in a key variable (index date, pnr, outcome) is serious - these persons cannot be correctly included in the analysis, and you must decide whether to exclude them. NA in a covariate (e.g. income) can often be handled - e.g. with a separate "unknown" category or imputation. NA from a join means the person was not found in the right-hand dataset. What that means depends on the register. In an event register (prescriptions, hospital contacts) no row usually means no event, so NA is effectively a "no". In a status register (education, income, employment) no row means the information is unknown for that person, so NA is genuinely missing and must not be recoded to "none". Check what a missing row means for each register in your own delivery's documentation (DST's variable descriptions). Always check colSums(is.na(data)) immediately after an extraction or a join, so you detect unexpected gaps before they propagate silently through the analysis. For continuous variables:

sections.title: Inspect and understand your data
sections.heading: Check missing values
sections.text: colSums(is.na(bef_data)) returns one line with a counter per column: Here foed_dag is missing for 3 - everything else is complete. A column with 0 has no NAs at all. colSums(is.na()) counts only true NA . In register data, "missing" is often stored as an empty or blank string (whitespace) or a sentinel code - not as NA . A column can therefore show 0 NAs and still be full of empty values: e.g. a fixed-width key field filled with blanks (a 13-character field that looks empty but is 13 spaces, not NA ). So also check for blank values - e.g. sum(trimws(bef_data$pnr) == "", na.rm = TRUE) - and look at nchar() / unique() on a slice. This matters most for join keys : a blank-but-not- NA key causes silent join errors (rows that look filled but don't match).

sections.title: Inspect and understand your data
sections.heading: Check that every register reaches the end of your follow-up
sections.text: A register in your delivery does not necessarily run as far as DST says the register does. It may have been converted a year ago, ordered for fewer years, or be a register that has closed for good ( dodsaars stops in 2001, see pitfall 1). Nothing errors when your follow-up runs past the end of the data: people simply look as if nothing happened to them, which quietly skews censoring, outcomes and matching. So for every register you use, check its first and last year or date against your study period before you build anything on it: For event registers, use the date column rather than year : year is the folder the row was filed under, not when the event happened. The first and last date show only the two ends. One wrong date far in the future is enough to make a register look complete, so count the rows per year as well: a register that stops early has a last year with far fewer rows than the years before it. The year is taken in R, after collect() , because the DuckDB backend that newer fastreg versions use cannot translate year() and stops with an error on a large register. It also helps to know when the parquet copy was made. If the folder has not changed in a long time, newer years are probably missing: If a register stops before your follow-up ends, either end follow-up at the register's last date, or ask your data manager whether a newer delivery or the raw SAS files cover the missing years. Coverage is one of several things a delivery can get wrong. The rest are on Check your delivery. sections.title: Link your extracts
sections.text: Use this page to turn your cohort and your separate extracts into the one analysis-ready dataset that every analysis page starts from. Your extracts from Phase 6, Extract from LPR and Phase 11 are stored as separate RDS files. Once each extract is down to one row per person (Long ↔ wide format), you join them onto the cohort, check the joins, and calculate follow-up time and the event variable. When you are done you have analysis.rds . Paths and variable names in the examples are generic - replace them with your own. First get each extract down to one row per person. left_join() only behaves predictably when the table you join on has one row per key ( pnr , or pnr + index_date ). Many register extracts have multiple rows per person (long format). Reduce them to one row per person with group_by() + slice() or pivot_wider() - explained in Long ↔ wide format. This page assumes your extracts are already in that shape.

sections.title: Link your extracts
sections.heading: Joins - link two tables
sections.text: In register-based research you almost always work with data from two or more tables that need to be linked. All joins in dplyr take two tables and one key column they share (e.g. pnr ). When you join your finished person-level extracts onto the cohort , the key is usually pnr . Inside a register it is other keys: joining contact and diagnosis in LPR, for instance, happens on recnum or dw_ek_kontakt , not pnr (see the overview of LPR join keys). A value that is measured relative to the index date (socioeconomic position, a comorbidity score) is joined on pnr + index_date , so it still lands on the right row when the same person is in the cohort with more than one index date. The ER diagram below shows both - extracts joined onto the cohort: The key is marked PK (primary key) in the cohort and FK (foreign key) in each extract. The symbol --o is standard ER notation ("crow's foot"): = exactly one, o = zero or one. So the line reads: each person in the cohort matches zero or one row in the extract. This describes the shape you must ensure before the join - not something left_join() checks or fixes. If an extract has several rows per pnr , left_join() happily proceeds and duplicates the cohort rows (row explosion). That is why the callout above tells you to get each extract down to one row per person first , and why check 1 in Validate your join afterwards (did the row count grow?).

sections.title: Link your extracts
sections.heading: Join with multiple keys
sections.text: Multiple keys only become relevant when at least one of the tables has several rows per person - otherwise pnr alone is enough. With multiple keys all the listed columns must agree before two rows count as a match ( pnr and year , not pnr or year ). The typical case is panel data: registers with one row per person per year . BEF, AKM and so on have a pnr row for every calendar year. Join two of them on pnr alone and each of the person's rows is paired with all of the person's rows in the other table: with 5 years in BEF and 5 in AKM you get every combination, 5 × 5 = 25 rows instead of 5. Add the year as an extra key and those 25 are filtered down to the 5 where the year also matches - 2018 against 2018: If instead you join two extracts that each have one row per person (e.g. finished person-level extracts onto the cohort), pnr alone is enough - there is no extra dimension to keep track of. Do not assume "one row per person per year" - check it. A BEF delivery can contain duplicate (pnr, year) rows (the delivery this guide was written from did), and adding the year as a key does not save you from those: a person with two 2018 rows still doubles. Count first, and reduce to one row per person per year if you find any. left_join() will not warn you. It just returns more rows than you started with, which is why check 1 in Validate your join is to compare nrow() before and after.

sections.heading: Validate your join
sections.text: Joins rarely fail with an error message - but they can produce silently wrong results. Always check these three things after a left_join() : anti_join() as diagnostics anti_join(cohort, outcome, by = "pnr") returns the cohort members that are not found in the outcome table. Use it for "who in my cohort has no death date record?" (all alive - expected) or "who is missing from register X?" (unexpected - investigate).

sections.title: Link your extracts
sections.heading: Stack tables vertically - bind_rows()
sections.text: bind_rows() and left_join() solve two fundamentally different problems : bind_rows() left_join() What it does Stacks tables vertically - adds rows Combines tables horizontally - adds columns Requires That the columns have the same names That the tables share one common key column Result More rows, same number of columns Same number of rows, more columns Matches on key? No - all rows from both tables Yes - match on pnr or other key Typical use LPR2 + LPR3 → one combined register Link outcome or covariate to cohort table bind_rows() is not a join. It does not look at pnr and does not match. It simply places table 2's rows below table 1's rows - like pasting two Excel sheets together vertically. Columns missing in one table (e.g. a column that only exists in LPR3) are automatically filled with NA for rows from the other table. Counting diagnoses across this combined all_dx ? Expect a jump around 2019-2020 that isn't a real change in disease occurrence - see why. When do you use which? bind_rows() - when you have two versions of the same register (LPR2 + LPR3, exposed + comparators) and want to merge them into one. left_join() - when you want to attach a new variable (outcome, date of death, age) to your cohort table.

sections.heading: Attach date of death and emigration
sections.text: Death and emigration end follow-up, so the follow-up calculation below needs both dates on the cohort. read_register() requires fastreg set up with the path to your registers - see Parquet and fastreg if you did not convert them from SAS yourself. Date of death (DOD) Emigration date (VNDS) Emigration censors just like death - the person leaves the study on the day they emigrate. VNDS contains one row per migration event. Take the first exit after the index date , not simply the first ever: a person may have left and come back, and an exit before index censors nothing. Whether the person was resident at index at all is decided in Phase 10. The date of death is one date per person, so pnr alone is the right key. The emigration date depends on the index date, so it is keyed on pnr and index_date : a person who was drawn as a comparison person on two different dates then gets the right exit for each of them.

sections.title: Link your extracts
sections.heading: Derived variables: create new columns
sections.text: Once the extracts are joined, you almost always need to compute new variables from the columns you now have. That is mutate() : it adds a column calculated from existing ones. Two habits worth keeping: Compute a variable once and reuse it, so age at index is the same number in the matching and in Table 1. if_else() for yes/no, case_when() for several categories - and use the same type in every branch ( 1L / 0L , or text in all of them). Both are in the Function guide. The censoring date and the event indicator are derived variables too, but they need dates from several extracts at once, so they come next.

sections.title: Link your extracts
sections.heading: Calculate follow-up time and event variable
sections.text: Before you can analyse, each cohort member needs a censoring date (when follow-up ends) and an event variable (did they experience the outcome?). The censoring date is the earliest of: event date, date of death, emigration date, the date a comparison person becomes exposed themselves (crossover) and end of study period. death_date and emigration_date were joined on above; the outcome date is joined on first here. pmin() compares vectors position by position and returns the smallest value per person - it is the vectorised version of min() . na.rm = TRUE ensures that a missing death date (= alive) does not make the censoring date NA . Crossover. A comparison person who later becomes exposed stops being a comparison person on that day, so follow-up is censored at crossover_date (made in Phase 10, NA for the exposed and for comparison persons who never become exposed). Without that line, time after their own exposure is counted as unexposed time. If your cohort has no crossover_date column (no comparison group, or one that can never become exposed), leave the line out. The alternative to censoring is to let the person switch group at crossover and contribute exposed time from then on. That needs a dataset with several rows per person, see Time-varying exposure. Zero or negative follow-up. The outcome and emigration dates above are taken only after index, so they cannot give time_days <= 0 . A death date on or before the index date can, and so can an index date after study_end . Such a person was never at risk, and zero or negative time breaks the analysis ( log(0) in Poisson, meaningless Cox time), so the filter() above drops them. Count how many, and look at a death on or before index: it points to a problem in the cohort or the death register. The filter() does not catch prevalent cases. A person who had the outcome before index has no event after index in the extract, so they stay in the cohort as at risk, with no warning. Remove prevalent cases in Phase 10, and check by counting the people in the cohort with an outcome code on or before index in LPR. Competing risks? If a competing event (typically death) must be handled separately (see Time-to-event), then instead of a binary outcome (0/1) build a status with three values - what happened first :

sections.heading: Assemble the final analysis dataset
sections.text: By now your cohort is built in Phase 10: a table with pnr and index_date (and exposed / case if you have a comparison group - renamed to exposure in the final select() ) - one row per person , unless your comparison group was matched with replacement , in which case the same pnr can carry several rows, one per index_date it was matched on. The recipe below works for both: everything measured relative to the index date is joined on pnr + index_date , see comparison cohort's callout on it. Your outcomes, covariates and censoring variables are extracted as separate RDS files (Phase 9, Phase 11). This last step joins them onto the cohort with left_join() , calculates follow-up time, and keeps only the columns the analysis needs. Cohort construction - including the matching - belongs to Phase 10. Here we assume the cohort already exists; this page only assembles the analysis dataset around it. Design choices (comparator, immortal time, matching ratio) are decided back in Phase 1. End with select() - keep only the columns the analysis requires. sections.title: Laboratory results
sections.text: Use this page when a laboratory value is part of your study: an exposure, a covariate at baseline or an outcome (for example HbA1c or creatinine). You need your cohort from Phase 10 and the list of analysis codes you want. You end with an .rds file of results for your cohort, one row per result, filtered to the cohort before collect() . The column dictionary is Laboratoriedatabasens Forskertabel.

sections.title: Laboratory results
sections.heading: What the laboratory table is: LAB_F, not DST, not LPR
sections.text: LAB_F (Laboratoriedatabasens Forskertabel) is delivered by Sundhedsdatastyrelsen (SDS) through Forskerservice. In the clinical epidemiology literature it is usually called RLRR (Register of Laboratory Results for Research). It is not on DST's register list. It is not LPR. LPR is hospital contacts. This table is one row per laboratory result. It is very large, so semi_join() and filter() have to run before collect() .

sections.title: Laboratory results
sections.heading: One delivery, several table names
sections.text: lab_dm_forsker , lab_forsker and laboratorieproevesvar are cuts of the same delivery, not separate registers. Using more than one double-counts. Column names are not the same in every cut. The dictionary section names the columns this extract uses on lab_dm_forsker : patient_cpr , analysiscode , samplingdate , value , unit . The Version 4 dictionary has more columns than that. A delivery may not include every column in the dictionary, so do not treat a full dictionary listing as the column list of the file you were sent. lab_dm_forsker : person column patient_cpr , result column value . lab_forsker : a narrower cut of the same delivery (fewer columns). laboratorieproevesvar : a narrow cut seen in at least one project delivery. The person column is cprnummer and the result column is samplevalue , not patient_cpr and value . The guide's schema describes this cut as four columns and names those two. It does not name the other two; check them with colnames() on your own file.

sections.title: Laboratory results
sections.heading: The October 2025 delivery: table names may change
sections.text: Sundhedsdatastyrelsen updated the laboratory delivery on 3 October 2025 (announcement →): "Det nye LAB erstatter den tidligere version af LAB" (the new LAB replaces the earlier version of LAB). The announcement names four tables, laboratorieproevesvar , Dimlaboratoriekoder , DimNPU and Proevesvar_optaelling , but never mentions lab_dm_forsker by name, and does not say what happens to projects already using it. The official data dictionary the guide is built from (PDF) is Version 4, dated 1 December 2023, nearly two years before that announcement, and it documents lab_dm_forsker only. Whether lab_dm_forsker is being retired, and what laboratorieproevesvar 's columns are after the October 2025 change, we do not know. Check the order sheet ("bestillingsark") on Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's site, or your own delivery, before relying on either name.

sections.title: Laboratory results
sections.heading: Extract lab results for your cohort
sections.text: You choose the analysis codes. Laboratory tests are coded in NPU (Nomenclature for Properties and Units), a terminology maintained by IFCC and IUPAC and used for laboratory results in Denmark, Norway and Sweden (NPU leaflet, IUPAC 2019). Look up the codes for your tests at npu-terminology.org, and write the list and its source into your code. read_register() requires fastreg set up with the path to your registers, see Parquet and fastreg if you did not convert them from SAS yourself. The register name below is the lab_dm_forsker cut. If your file is laboratorieproevesvar , rename cprnummer to pnr and keep samplevalue instead of value . The table stays one row per result. Collapse to one row per person only when your definition needs that, the same way as in Long and wide format.

sections.title: Laboratory results
sections.heading: Synthetic data, on your own computer
sections.text: fiktive can build a lab_dm_forsker table for local practice. It is not on DST. This synthetic table has not been run against a DST delivery, so do not treat it as a check that the pipeline works on the server. Install once with remotes::install_github("sara-schwartz/fiktive") , as in Phase 6. To use real IFCC/NPU terms, set options(fiktive.labterm_fetch_ifcc = TRUE) before generating. That option downloads and caches a public IFCC code list. FIKTIVE_LABTERM (or options(fiktive.labterm) ) is the other route: a LabTerm or IFCC file you already have, not a download. Without one of those, fiktive does not invent NPU codes. Do not take column names from fiktive 's labka generator. That is a different database (LABKA, see Coverage).

sections.title: Laboratory results
sections.heading: Which results reach the table
sections.text: NPU is not its own column. It sits inside analysiscode , together with DNK codes: codes for local Danish use, kept in the same NPU database but marked "DNK" instead of "NPU" (NPU database). Only those coded results reach the table, about 95 per cent. A laboratory's own local codes never arrive. There is nothing to filter them in with. Patients who declined consent are absent from the table. That absence is not a coded value, so there is no code to filter on.

sections.title: Laboratory results
sections.heading: Coverage: from 2008, complete per laboratory by 2010-2016
sections.text: Coverage starts in 2008, not the 1990s. Complete coverage arrives per laboratory between 2010 and 2016. The start year, the table of periods per region and laboratory, the 95 per cent and the consent rule above are all in Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's documentation of the research table. See also Laboratoriedatabasen →. For years before 2008, projects used the separate regional database LABKA (Arendt et al. 2020; Grann et al. 2011). Neither paper gives literal column names, so the guide gives none.

sections.title: Laboratory results
sections.heading: Results are text: convert value with care
sections.text: value is text, not a number. Alongside numeric results the reference section lists POSITIV , NEGATIV , IKKE PÅVIST , INGEN VÆKST and the blood-type codes. as.numeric() turns every one of them into NA . R prints only "NAs introduced by coercion", which is easy to miss in a long script, and on a DuckDB table before collect() there is no warning at all. Either way, exactly the samples where something was found are dropped. The same would happen to any result written with a sign, such as <5 . On laboratorieproevesvar the same column is called samplevalue . Before you convert, list the values that are not plain numbers, and decide what each should become: Do not compare a numeric result across laboratories, or across time, without unit . The same analysiscode can mean a different scale when the equipment or the sample material differs, including inside one laboratory over time. Keep unit in the extract.

sections.title: Learning resources
sections.text: Use this page to find material that teaches what this guide assumes or only touches on: R itself, epidemiological methods and statistics. If you only pick one, start with the DDEA introductory course if you are completely new to R, or The Epidemiologist R Handbook if you know a bit of R and want to go straight to health science applications.

sections.title: Learning resources
sections.heading: Getting started - learn R
sections.text: Resource What it is DDEA introductory course A 3-day workshop on reproducible data analysis with R, RStudio, Quarto and Git, run several times by the Danish Diabetes and Endocrine Academy (DDEA). The material is free to use (CC BY 4.0). Best starting point if you are completely new. R for Data Science Free e-book by Hadley Wickham, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel and Garrett Grolemund (2nd edition) - the standard reference for modern R with the tidyverse. Concept-based, read from start to finish. Cookbook for R Task-based reference: "how do I do X?" with direct code examples. Strongest for its ggplot2 graphics recipes (legends, faceting, colours). Note: parts of the base-R and data-handling sections predate the tidyverse, so the syntax can differ from the rest of this guide. Quick-R Compact reference for R syntax and statistics, good for quick lookups mid-script. The address now redirects to DataCamp, which hosts the pages.

sections.title: Learning resources
sections.heading: Health science and epidemiology
sections.text: Resource What it is The Epidemiologist R Handbook Practical reference written for epidemiologists and health researchers - covers data cleaning, analyses and visualisation with health science examples. Most relevant chapters for register work: dates, joins, data cleaning, regression and survival analysis. Most pages in this guide link to the matching chapter. Zheer's R Coding Café A bi-weekly open coding café, each session starting with a short presentation, for people working at Steno Diabetes Center Aarhus and several Aarhus University departments. CRAN Task View: Epidemiology Package list for epidemiology - incidence rates, matching, cohort analysis. Good starting point when looking for the right package. CRAN Task View: Survival Analysis Package list for survival analysis - Cox regression, Kaplan–Meier and competing risks. Podcasts: Resource What it is SERious Epi Podcast from the Society for Epidemiologic Research on epidemiological methods: study design, confounding, selection bias, measurement error. Casual Inference Podcast on causal inference and statistics, in an informal conversational format.

sections.title: Learning resources
sections.heading: Methods and statistics
sections.text: Resource What it is Learning Statistics with R Free e-book by Danielle Navarro - covers statistical theory and R implementation side by side, from basic probability to regression and ANOVA. Written for a non-mathematical audience. Relevant if you want to understand the statistics you are running, not just copy the code. Causal Inference: What If (Hernán & Robins) Free PDF - the standard reference on causal inference, confounding and DAGs. Epidemiological methods, not R. Analysis of mechanisms (mediation analysis course) A 3-day course on modern mediation analysis for PhD students and postdocs in diabetes and endocrinology, sponsored by the DDEA. Use it when you need to decompose an effect into direct and indirect (mediated) paths. General method, not register-specific.

sections.title: Log in to DST
sections.text: Use this page the first time you log in to the research server at Statistics Denmark (DST), and come back to it for the log-off routine. It takes you from the browser login to an RStudio project in your own folder. It assumes you already have access: a personal ident, a project number, and the FortiToken app that gives you the one-time code. When you are done you can run R code on the server and you know the rules that apply while you do. DST's own connection guides (PDF, in Danish, with screenshots) for Windows, Mac and Linux are listed on DST's page about the research machines. The steps below follow them.

sections.title: Log in to DST
sections.heading: Step 1 - Install Windows App (Mac only)
sections.text: On a Mac, open the App Store, search for "Windows App" (from Microsoft) and install it. On Windows you install nothing: the login page downloads an .rdp file, and you open it.

sections.title: Log in to DST
sections.heading: Step 2 - Log in
sections.text: 1. Go to remote.dst.dk in your browser. 2. Enter your ident (4 letters) as username and your code for remote.dst.dk as password. 3. Enter the 6-digit token code shown in the FortiToken Mobile app on your phone. 4. Click the server you want to connect to. You see only the buttons you have access to. For R, choose Python/R . If you choose FSE Windows instead, you land on a selection desktop and click through to Python/R from there. 5. Log in to the server with your project ident, which is your ident followed by the project number: dstfse\abcd123456 (or abcd123456@dstfse.local ), and the password for that project user. Do not tick "remember my credentials": DST's guide warns that it gives problems when you change password.

sections.title: Log in to DST
sections.heading: If you cannot log in
sections.text: DST's page about the research machines has separate guides (PDF, in Danish) for changing your password, resetting a forgotten one, installing and setting up FortiToken, and connecting from abroad. If none of them covers your problem, contact DST's service desk; the email, phone number and opening hours are in the footer of the connection guides.

sections.heading: Step 3 - Find or create your own folder
sections.text: Open File Explorer and navigate to the workspaces folder under your project. Create a folder with your name or ident if it does not already exist: Recommended structure within your folder:

sections.heading: Step 4 - Mac keyboard: switch to Unicode mode at every connection
sections.text: On a Mac, special characters such as , $ , \ , @ , { and } do not come out right in the remote session by default. Switch the keyboard to Unicode mode with Ctrl + Cmd + U inside the remote window (or in the menu bar: Connections, then Keyboard Mode). Character Mac shortcut in Unicode mode Pipe \ Option + i [ Option + 8 ] Option + 9 { Option + Shift + 8 } Option + Shift + 9 \ Option + Shift + 7 In RStudio on the server, code is run with Ctrl+Enter (not Cmd+Enter).

sections.title: Log in to DST
sections.heading: Create your R project
sections.text: An R project collects all your scripts, output files and settings in one folder. Give each study its own project. A project is first of all a folder: you still save your own files in it (in R/ , datasets/ , output/ ). What it adds is the .Rproj file. When you open the project, RStudio sets the working directory to the folder where .Rproj lives. So getwd() points to your project folder, and you can use relative paths ( datasets/cohort.rds ) instead of writing the full path or setwd("E:/...") at the top of every script. Each project also keeps its own settings and history, so studies do not get mixed up. 1. Open RStudio 2. File → New Project → New Directory → New Project 3. Give the project a name and choose a location under your workspace folder 4. Click Create Project Run getwd() now and you get the path to your project, e.g. E:/workdata/[projectnumber]/workspaces/[your-name]/[your-project-name] Two settings to change once, under Tools → Global Options : Do not save the workspace: under General, set "Save workspace to .RData on exit" to Never. Otherwise RStudio asks "Save workspace image?" every time you close it; the answer is always No. Optional, for a faster start: under Packages, uncheck "Enable packages pane". You use library() and install.packages() in the code anyway. Reinstall duckplyr at the start of every session DST has duckplyr pre-installed, but in an old version that is missing functionality, so several patterns in this guide will not work with it. Install the current version from CRAN, and repeat after every log-out or server reset: the reset puts the old pre-installed version back. duckplyr is the package behind read_parquet_duckdb() and, from fastreg 0.14.3, behind read_register() .

sections.title: Log in to DST
sections.heading: The rules you sign up to, in short
sections.text: You certify to these before you get access, and breaking them carries sanctions (page in Danish). The four that catch people out in ordinary daily work: No images of the screen: the ban covers photos and screenshots alike, so you cannot snap a console output to paste into a message to a colleague. Nothing leaves except through repatriation: not by email, not on paper, not by retyping it. See Phase 14 - Export and repatriation. Never put real data in a written question: when you describe a dataset or a problem to a colleague, a data manager or DST, use made-up examples. A pasted error message with a real pnr in it is a rule breach. Work somewhere private: your institution or your home workplace. Not a train, a bus, a café or a library. Log out of the server when you leave the screen, also for a short while; a screensaver is not enough. You may show your screen only to people who are approved for the data you are working with. The full text is short and worth reading once: Rules for working with microdata (page in Danish).

sections.title: Log in to DST
sections.heading: Log off correctly when you are done
sections.text: Closing the remote window with the cross only disconnects you. DST's connection guide says so directly: the programs you had open stay open on the server until the next time you log on. A session left like that keeps holding the server's RAM (see Mind the RAM). Log off in this order: 1. Log off the Python/R desktop (where RStudio runs): use the Logoff icon on the desktop, or Sign out in the Start menu. 2. Log off the FSE Windows desktop in the same way, if you came in through it. Skip this step if you went straight to the Python/R desktop. 3. Log out of remote.dst.dk in your browser with the Logout button at the top of the page.

sections.title: Long ↔ wide format
sections.text: Use this page when an extract has many rows per person and you need it down to one row per person before you join it onto the cohort (Link your extracts). The registers you extract from are almost always in long format with many rows per person. This page explains the difference and shows the two ways you reshape an extract: group_by() + slice() and pivot_wider() / pivot_longer() . Paths and variable names in the examples are generic - replace them with your own.

sections.title: Long ↔ wide format
sections.heading: Wide vs. long format
sections.text: Imagine three persons with weight measurements at two time points. Wide format - one row per person, one column per time point: pnr weight_baseline weight_6mo 001 120 95 002 105 88 003 98 80 Long format - one row per observation, one column for time point and one for value: pnr timepoint weight 001 baseline 120 001 6mo 95 002 baseline 105 002 6mo 88 003 baseline 98 003 6mo 80 Both formats contain the same information - they are just arranged differently.

sections.title: Long ↔ wide format
sections.heading: Which formats are where?
sections.text: Register Format Why BEF Long One row per person per snapshot (quarterly); check which dates your delivery has LPR (lpr_adm + lpr_diag) Long One row per diagnosis per contact - one admission can have 10 diagnoses LMDB Long One row per dispensed prescription - the same person can have hundreds DOD Wide One row per deceased person - already one-per-person Your analysis dataset Wide One row per person - one column per covariate Registers are usually in long format. Your analysis dataset should typically be in wide format.

sections.title: Long ↔ wide format
sections.heading: Two ways to get one row per person
sections.text: The key choice is what you want out of the long register: You want… Use Result One representative value per person (newest snapshot, first event, earliest date) group_by() + slice() One row per person, same columns Several time points side by side as separate columns pivot_wider() One row per person, one new column per time point In register-based research group_by() + slice() is usually the one you need: you want "the newest" or "the first" value per person. You use pivot_wider() when you explicitly want to compare several time points.

sections.title: Long ↔ wide format
sections.heading: group_by() + slice() - one representative row
sections.text: The pattern is always the same: group by pnr , sort so the desired row is on top, take the first row per group. For baseline covariates you usually want the snapshot that applied at the index date, not the newest one: join on the index date and keep only snapshots on or before it before you take the first row. Always remember ungroup() . group_by() puts a "grouped_df" tag on your data.frame, which all subsequent operations inherit. That means: mutate() calculates per group, not across the entire dataset n() counts rows per group, not in total summarize() gives one result per group These errors are hard to detect because the code runs without error messages and produces seemingly reasonable numbers. ungroup() removes the tag and makes the data.frame normal again. Rule of thumb: always end a group_by() chain with ungroup() .

sections.title: Long ↔ wide format
sections.heading: Long → wide with pivot_wider()
sections.text: You CANNOT pivot_wider() an entire LPR table. LPR potentially has hundreds of unique ICD codes per person - pivot_wider() would give you one column per code, i.e. thousands of columns and a dataset that is impossible to work with. Instead use the pattern from Extract from LPR: extract the first date for one specific diagnosis group (with group_by() + slice() above), save as extract_hip_fracture.rds , and join it as one column with left_join() . Practical example: employment status from AKM - long to wide AKM (the Labour Classification Module) stores one row per person per year - long format. If you want to compare employment status at baseline and follow-up side by side, you can pivot: In practice you would typically not pivot AKM - you filter to one specific year with filter(year == index_year) and use group_by() + slice() above. Pivot is relevant when you explicitly want two time points side by side in the analysis.

sections.title: Medication (ATC)
sections.text: Use this page to extract dispensed prescriptions for your cohort and turn them into a variable: a first dispensing date, a user/non-user flag, or the raw material for exposure time. You need your cohort from Phase 10, and you end with an .rds file of dispensings, one row per fill, that the later steps on this page reduce to one row per person. Prescriptions are in LMDB (Lægemiddeldatabasen). In the literature the same data are described as the Danish National Prescription Registry, the part of the Register of Medicinal Product Statistics that holds prescriptions filled by individuals at community pharmacies (Pottegård et al. 2017). LMDB has one row per dispensed prescription, so one person can have hundreds of rows. The two columns you almost always use are: atc : the drug's ATC code (Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical classification), for example "A10BA02" for metformin. eksd : the dispensing date, the day the prescription was collected at the pharmacy. Use it as the prescription date, in the same way as date_contact in LPR (the National Patient Register). The full column list is in Overview of registers.

sections.title: Medication (ATC)
sections.heading: What LMDB covers, and what it does not
sections.text: LMDB starts in 1995, and the data are considered complete and valid from that year (Pottegård et al. 2017). There is no medication history before 1995, so a lookback window that reaches further back is empty for everyone, and "no prescriptions" will look like "not a user". LMDB only holds prescriptions dispensed at community pharmacies. The following are therefore missing (Pottegård et al. 2017): drugs given during hospital admission; drugs supplied directly by hospitals or treatment centres (for example chemotherapy, immunosuppressants and methadone for substance use); drugs for certain institutionalised people (typically because of psychiatric illness); over-the-counter medicine. For a drug that can be bought both with and without a prescription, LMDB only shows the prescribed part. For in-hospital medication there is a newer Hospital Medication Register (Sygehusmedicinregisteret) with data from May 2018. Its data quality has not yet been evaluated, and some clinical specialties are missing (Rosenkrantz et al. 2024). It is held by the Danish Health Data Authority. What to know before using it is in Hospital medication (SMR). Until 1996, a child's prescriptions were recorded under the mother, not the child. Prescriptions for children were issued in the mother's name until 1996, and in the child's own name after that (Pottegård et al. 2017). If your cohort includes children with drug exposure in those years, filtering LMDB by the child's own pnr misses those prescriptions without any error: they are in the register, but under another person's pnr . The source gives no exact date in 1996, so the cautious choice is to treat a child's dispensings as reliable from 1997.

sections.title: Medication (ATC)
sections.heading: Exposure, outcome or covariate: one extract, different date filters
sections.text: Medication can be an exposure, a covariate or an outcome. As for diagnoses (Extract from LPR), you make one extract of the dispensings, and the role is decided by where eksd falls relative to index_date : Role When What you do Page Exposure The date exposure starts First eksd = the person's index date Phase 10 Covariate (medication at baseline) eksd < index_date (e.g. 6-12 months before) Ever/never or a count in a window before index Comorbidity Outcome (new treatment) eksd > index_date First eksd after index Outcomes Time-varying (on/off treatment) Changes during follow-up Start/stop format Time-varying If the first dispensing defines the index date, require a period before it with no dispensing of the drug (a washout). Otherwise people who have been on the drug for years enter as new users. LMDB starts in 1995, so nobody has a washout that reaches further back than that.

sections.title: Medication (ATC)
sections.heading: Extract the dispensings for your cohort
sections.text: ATC codes have no D-prefix (unlike ICD codes in LPR, see Understand LPR), so you match directly on the start of the code. read_register() requires fastreg set up with the path to your registers, see Parquet and fastreg if you did not convert them from SAS yourself. substr(atc, 1, 5) == "A10BJ" matches the whole ATC group (all GLP-1 analogues; GLP-1 is glucagon-like peptide-1). For several groups at once, use a regular expression as in LPR: grepl("^A10BJ ^A10BA", atc) . Code matching (regex, %in% with a code list, !! ) is explained in Extract from LPR and Functions: overview. Reducing to one row per person is explained in Long ↔ wide format. Here it is slice(1) for the first dispensing, but it could also be ever/never or a count in a window (see the role table above).

sections.title: Medication (ATC)
sections.heading: Define users: at least N dispensings within a window
sections.text: One dispensing is weak evidence of treatment, because some people fill a prescription once and stop. A common definition is therefore at least two dispensings within a window, with the onset date being the date the definition is first met. Sort with arrange() before lag() . lag() works on row order, not on dates. If the rows are not sorted by person and date, gap_days is computed against an arbitrary earlier row, and the result is wrong without any error. The two numbers are your choices, not standards, so write them into your methods. One dispensing can be enough for a drug taken once; for a chronic treatment two or more is the usual requirement. The same definition is how medication enters a comorbidity definition: for conditions treated largely outside hospital, LMDB catches people LPR never sees. Whether to define a condition from diagnoses, prescriptions or both is discussed on Comorbidity. Many ATC conditions at once: regmorbidity::mb_extract_medication_batch() The recipe above is the one to keep for one drug, or a few. It opens LMDB with read_register() , filters, collects, and calls flag_users() . Use this fold-out only when you need many ATC conditions, each with its own "N dispensings within a window" rule. Doing that with the recipe above scans LMDB once per condition. mb_extract_medication_batch() in regmorbidity puts every condition that shares the same (min_prescriptions, window_days) into one query, and only the onset rows come back to R. In the bundled code list, pain is 4 dispensings within 365 days. The other ATC conditions are 2 within 365 days, so those are one query and pain is a second. Onset is the dispensing that meets the rule. The package is on GitHub only and in development; it computes no score and is not a comorbidity index. On 26 September 2026 the 15 ATC conditions then in the bundled list (14 on the 2-within-365 rule, plus pain) matched mb_flag_users() on the real LMDB at DST. Conditions have been added to the list since. The DST check covers those 15, not automatically a condition added later. Do not use mb_extract_diagnosis_batch() from this page. It has not been run on DST. code_col has to be atc . The shorter columns ( atc1 to atc4 ) do not hold the full code the list is matched against. The result is one .rds per condition in outdir . Resume skips a rule-batch only when every condition in that batch already has a file. If one file in the batch is missing, the whole batch runs again and overwrites the files that were already there.

sections.title: Medication (ATC)
sections.heading: Which ATC column?
sections.text: LMDB does not hold the ATC code once. It holds it five times, at five levels, in five separate columns. DST's variable list for LMDB labels them ATC-kode detaljeret and ATC-niveau 1 to ATC-niveau 4 . They are cumulative: each level repeats the levels above it and adds its own characters. Column ATC level Characters Example What it is atc1 1 1 C anatomical main group atc2 2 3 C09 therapeutic subgroup atc3 3 4 C09A pharmacological subgroup atc4 4 5 C09AA chemical subgroup atc 5 7 C09AA05 chemical substance The column names and their levels come from DST's variable list. The character counts are not stated there; they follow from the WHO standard, where level 2 is by definition the three-character code (WHO Collaborating Centre for Drug Statistics Methodology). A pattern longer than the column can never match, and R will not tell you. atc2 holds three characters. grepl("N02A", atc2) compares a four-character pattern against three-character values, so it matches nothing: zero rows, no error, no warning. The same goes for filter(atc2 %in% c("A10A", "A10B")) . An empty result looks like a finding rather than a bug, and it is easy to write up as "no exposed patients" when the truth is that the filter could not fire. So filter on atc , not on the level columns. It is seven characters, it contains every level as a prefix, and substr(atc, 1, 3) gives you exactly what atc2 holds. There is no case where a level column lets you filter something atc cannot: Use ^ to anchor the pattern at the start of the code. It costs nothing and it is the right habit from LPR, where a code genuinely can turn up mid-string.

sections.title: Medication (ATC)
sections.heading: Which way should you write the filter?
sections.text: There are two ways to keep the codes you want, and the length of your codes decides which one to use. ATC codes are not all the same length: N02 is three characters, A10BA is five. Your code list Use Why All codes have the same length substr() + %in% Faster, and easy to read Codes have different lengths grepl() with ^ Handles any length All codes the same length. Cut atc down to that length, then check whether the result is on your list: substr(atc, 1, 3) means "the first three characters of atc ". Change the 3 to match your codes: use 1, 5 for five-character codes such as A10BA . Codes of different lengths. One substr() cannot serve N02 and A10BA at the same time, because they need different cut lengths. Use grepl() instead, which matches whatever you give it: In doubt? Use grepl() . It works for every code length, so it is never wrong. substr() + %in% was about twice as fast on a twenty-million-row test, which is worth having when you fetch many drug groups at once, but a correct slow filter beats a fast broken one. Does it save memory to filter on atc2 first? (No) It is a reasonable thing to wonder, since atc2 is the short column, but the filter runs before anything is loaded: nothing reaches your memory until collect() , and what lands there is the rows that survived, which are the same rows either way. substr(atc, 1, 3) gives you exactly what atc2 contains, so the two are the same query. There is a practical catch as well. Comorbidity definitions often need more than three characters ( A10BA rather than A10 ), and atc2 cannot narrow that far. You would filter on atc2 , then bring in atc afterwards to get down to the codes you actually wanted: two steps for a result one step gives you. And if a code longer than three characters is compared against atc2 on its own, it matches nothing and returns no rows without an error, so it is worth doing in one step on atc .

sections.title: Medication (ATC)
sections.heading: What the level columns are for: grouping
sections.text: When you want a descriptive breakdown by therapeutic subgroup, atc2 is a ready-made grouping column and saves you a substr() : Check this on your own extract before you trust it Two minutes, and it settles both whether the columns exist and how they are coded: Expect C / C09 / C09A / C09AA / C09AA05 across a row: each column repeating the one before it. If instead you see isolated fragments ( 09 in atc2 ), every ^ -anchored pattern in this section is wrong for your delivery and you should filter on atc only. Note that names(lmdb) may not answer this. On a dbplyr table (what read_register() from CRAN fastreg 0.14.1 returns) it gives the object's own parts ( src , lazy_query ), not the table's columns, so it looks as though the columns are missing. colnames() works on the DuckDB object read_register() returns; if you opened LMDB with open_dataset() instead, use names(collect(head(lmdb, 0))) - see Phase 7, Inspect your data. atc3 and atc4 are not filled in for every product. Not all preparations are classified to that depth, so do not assume the columns are complete. Count the blanks in your own extract before you build anything on them.

sections.title: Medication (ATC)
sections.heading: Tell products apart when they share an ATC code: vnr and indo
sections.text: ATC classifies by active substance, not by product or indication. Two brands with the same substance therefore get the same ATC code and cannot be told apart on atc alone. Ozempic (semaglutide, type 2 diabetes) and Wegovy (semaglutide, weight loss) both have A10BJ06 : filter on ATC only, and you mix diabetes treatment with weight-loss treatment. Two columns separate them: vnr (varenummer): the unique key to the actual product (package). It is the only reliable way to isolate one specific product. name / packtext hold the product text if you want to recognise it by eye. indo (indication code): a coded indication, not free text. The approved indications come with the package files the Danish Medicines Agency (Lægemiddelstyrelsen) sends out every 14 days (Sundhedsdatastyrelsen, note on the antibiotic statistics, PDF, Danish). The code is recorded only when the prescriber picks an indication from the drop-down menu in the electronic prescription. If the doctor types the indication as free text instead, it is not transferred to the register and indo is left blank. So it can in principle separate the same substance across indications, but it is often empty. Use vnr as the primary product key and indo as a supporting signal, not a clean filter. Keep the two names in the last line apart: vnr on its own is the register's column holding the varenummer, the product's ID, just as pnr is the person's ID. ozempic_vnr is your own R vector of the varenumbers you looked up for Ozempic; you choose the name yourself (same pattern as the code list in Extracting data step by step). %in% keeps the rows where vnr is found in your list, and !! sends your local list into the lazy query (explained in Extract from LPR and Functions: overview). Which vnr belongs to which product depends on package and strength (one product has several varenumbers). Look them up in the medicine taxonomy for your exact study period rather than assuming, and document the list in your code. For indo , Harbi & Pottegård 2024 found a recorded indication code on 82% of prescriptions (about 88% corrected) and almost 100% correct when present. Their data are from 2019 and 2020; the authors expect more missing codes before 1 October 2017, when electronic prescribing became mandatory. Missingness varies by drug class (about 8% missing for systemic anti-infectives versus 28% for blood-related agents). 5.6-36% of codes are nonspecific (e.g. "for the heart" for beta-blockers); whether a nonspecific code is usable depends on your question. The code texts are in DST's format library on the research machine ( indo_tekster , see DST's notes on LMDB). A validly recorded code does not mean the prescriber chose the correct indication: drop-down menus make wrong choices easy, so the code is not necessarily the clinical truth.

sections.title: Medication (ATC)
sections.heading: From dispensings to exposure time: DDD, PDC and MPR
sections.text: A dispensing is not the same as intake. eksd tells you the prescription was collected at the pharmacy, not that the patient took the drug, or for how long. For an exposure that lasts over time you need exposure windows built from the amount dispensed, not just a count of dispensings. That covers treatment episodes, grace periods (the gap allowed between two prescriptions before a person counts as having stopped) and adherence measures such as PDC (proportion of days covered: the share of follow-up time covered by medicine) and MPR (medication possession ratio: the amount dispensed divided by the length of the period). The LMDB columns for the amount are apk (number of packages), packsize (units per package) and strnum (the numeric strength; the unit is in strunit ). volume is the number of defined daily doses (DDD) per package (Pottegård et al. 2017, table of variables). The DDD is the WHO's "assumed average maintenance dose per day for a drug used for its main indication in adults", a unit of measurement and not necessarily the dose your patients were prescribed (WHO Collaborating Centre for Drug Statistics Methodology). So apk volume gives DDDs dispensed, which is a crude duration only if your patients take one DDD a day. DST's variable list has voltypecode and voltypetxt next to volume but no labels for them; look at the values in your own extract before you rely on volume . The dosage field doso is essentially empty (recorded for about 0.06% of prescriptions in the validation by Harbi & Pottegård), so dose must be derived from the package columns. Ready-made tools are in heaven : medicinMacro() estimates prescription lengths and average doses from LMDB, and hypertensionMedication() defines hypertension from the use of at least two classes of antihypertensive drugs. Exposure defined by future dispensings gives immortal time bias. If you require a person to fill a prescription (or two) after index to count as exposed, then by construction they survived until that date, and the time between index and the fill makes the exposure look protective (immortal time bias). Start follow-up for the exposed at the first dispensing, or treat medication as a time-varying exposure.

sections.title: Missing data
sections.text: Use this page when your analysis-ready dataset (Phase 12) has missing values in covariates, exposure or outcome, before you fit the analysis model. It shows how to see where values are missing and how to run the two common approaches: complete-case analysis and multiple imputation with mice . When you are done you have either a complete-case dataset or a pooled estimate from imputed data. Register data almost always have missing values. Some are structural (a variable was not collected in all years) - that is not random, so think about why a value is missing before you handle it. Paths and variable names in the examples are generic - replace them with your own. naniar and mice must be installed in your R environment on DST. How far this page goes It shows how to run the methods, not when they are substantively defensible. Choosing between complete-case and imputation, and judging whether the missing mechanism allows either, is a methods question - read the theory elsewhere: Flexible Imputation of Missing Data : free online book by the mice author, Stef van Buuren. Sterne et al. (2009), BMJ: "Multiple imputation for missing data in epidemiological and clinical research: potential and pitfalls".

sections.title: Missing data
sections.heading: Approach 2: multiple imputation (mice)
sections.text: mice stands for Multivariate Imputation by Chained Equations and is the most widely used R package for multiple imputation (mice on CRAN). The idea is to fill in the missing values several times , fit your model on each completed dataset, and combine the results, so the uncertainty from the imputation itself is counted.

sections.title: Missing data
sections.heading: How does it find the values?
sections.text: For each variable with missing values, mice builds a regression model that predicts the variable from the other variables. A missing value is not filled in with a single "best guess", but with a random draw from the predicted distribution. That is why the 20 datasets differ. "Chained equations" describes how mice handles several variables with gaps at once: it takes them one at a time, imputes the first from the others, moves on to the next and now uses the just-filled first variable as well, and so on. It runs several rounds through (the chain) until the variables are imputed consistently from one another. Imputation affects both the estimate and the confidence interval . The estimate is the average across the 20 datasets. The confidence interval is built on Rubin's rules , the standard method for combining results from several imputed datasets (Rubin 1987): it adds the spread between the datasets on top of the model's own uncertainty. The more the imputed values disagree from dataset to dataset, the larger that contribution, and the wider the confidence interval. That is exactly the point: if there is little in the observed data to impute from, the uncertainty should reflect it.

sections.title: Missing data
sections.heading: When can you use it?
sections.text: Imputation makes most sense when a non-trivial share of the data is missing and complete-case would either be biased or waste too many rows. If complete-case is already unbiased (see the regression case below), the main gain from imputation is power, not correctness. mice rests on the MAR assumption ( missing at random ). MAR does not mean the gaps are pure chance. It means that the reason a value is missing lies in something you have measured, not in the missing value itself. Analogy: suppose older patients more often skip a question. As long as you have age recorded, this is no problem - within each age group, those missing the answer resemble those who answered, and mice can fill in from the observed ones. The gap is due to age (which you have), not the missing answer itself. The assumption cannot be tested in the data, only judged on substantive grounds. Missing covariates: the classic use. Here, include the outcome in the imputation model. It sounds backwards, but it is necessary: leave the outcome out and you pull the covariate-outcome association artificially toward null. Including the outcome adds no extra assumption, it simply respects the association you will later estimate. If the analysis is a Cox model, the "outcome" in the imputation model is the event indicator plus the Nelson-Aalen estimate of the cumulative hazard, not the raw follow-up time (White & Royston 2009, doi:10.1002/sim.3618). mice::nelsonaalen() computes it: Missing exposure: here it is more uncertain. In principle exposure can be imputed like any other variable, but it is more fragile, and whether it is defensible at all depends heavily on the situation and on how well the exposure can be predicted from the other data. Seek specific guidance before doing it. Missing outcome: here imputation gains least. If you impute only the outcome from the same variables already in the analysis model, you typically end up with the same result as complete-case. A real gain requires extra auxiliary variables that predict the outcome. An alternative is inverse probability weighting (IPCW), see IP weighting. The MAR assumption is what matters, not the percentage. mice only corrects bias if missingness is MAR : that the reason a value is missing lies in the observed data. If a variable is missing precisely because of the value that is missing (for example, the sickest patients never get it measured), the data are MNAR ( missing not at random ), and then mice can introduce its own bias and give false precision. This is why imputation is not automatically better than just accepting some missing: Under MCAR ( missing completely at random ) complete-case is already unbiased, just less efficient. In a regression model, complete-case is in fact unbiased when missingness does not depend on the outcome given the covariates, even when it is not MCAR. (Analysing only the observed means conditioning on being observed. For odds ratios, complete-case is also unbiased when missingness depends on the outcome alone, not on the covariates - only the intercept is biased.) mice is only as good as the imputation model you give it. Pick the wrong variables to predict the missing values, and the filled-in values, and hence your result, will be wrong too. mice invents no information; it only exploits the associations that are already in the data.

sections.title: Missing data
sections.heading: How much missing is okay?
sections.text: There is no real percentage threshold (5% / 10% / 40% are rules of thumb with no foundation). What matters is the mechanism and how well the missing values can be predicted from the rest. In practice: report how much is missing per variable (STROBE), treat results with very high missingness on a key variable as hypothesis-generating (a guide for randomised trials gives "more than 40%" as an example, Jakobsen et al. 2017, doi:10.1186/s12874-017-0442-1), and run complete-case and mice side by side as a sensitivity analysis. If they point the same way, you stand on firmer ground. The analysis models themselves are in Phase 13 - Analysis; fit them inside with(imp, ...) and pool as above. Further information Further depth in The Epidemiologist R Handbook : Missing data

sections.title: NMI - Nordic Multimorbidity Index
sections.text: Use this page when you want to adjust for, or describe, mortality risk at baseline with one score. NMI (Nordic Multimorbidity Index) is a weighted score built from hospital diagnoses and filled prescriptions. It combines 50 mortality predictors, 29 diagnosis-based and 21 prescription-based, into a single continuous score. You need your cohort from Phase 10 ( pnr and index_date ), and you end with extract_nmi.rds : one score per person and index date. Article: Kristensen et al. Clinical Epidemiology 2022 - doi:10.2147/CLEP.S353398 Important: NMI was developed to predict mortality; use it with care as a measure of comorbidity burden. NMI was developed and validated to predict 5-year mortality (Kristensen et al. 2022, \~425,000 Danish residents aged ≥40). The authors call it a multimorbidity measure and write that it "can be used as a confounder summary score" (Discussion), on the premise that 5-year mortality is a general marker of health and multimorbidity. This guide still does not use it as a measure of disease burden, because its predictors were selected and weighted for how much they added to the mortality model, not to cover disease burden. As a result: Several common chronic diseases are not included in the model (e.g. hypertension and type 1 diabetes). Some items are mortality proxies, not diseases in their own right (e.g. laxatives, iron). Some weights are negative (e.g. statins -3, angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs) -2), which only makes sense in a mortality model, not in a measure of disease burden. If your goal is comorbidity burden, define comorbidity directly instead. See Comorbidity for how to define comorbidity from diagnoses and prescriptions. Use NMI when your goal is mortality risk, and if you use it as a confounder summary score, say in your methods that it is a mortality-based score.

sections.title: NMI - Nordic Multimorbidity Index
sections.heading: What NMI gives you
sections.text: A continuous mortality-risk score per person. It was developed and validated in Danish data to predict 5-year mortality, where it discriminated better than the Charlson and Elixhauser indices; the authors say it should still be validated in other Nordic countries (Kristensen et al. 2022, abstract). Use it as: A covariate: summarising mortality-associated illness in a Cox or logistic model. A summary variable: for mortality risk in Table 1.

sections.title: NMI - Nordic Multimorbidity Index
sections.heading: Leave out predictors that are your exposure or outcome
sections.text: Your own exposure or outcome should not be one of the score's predictors. The article advises avoiding items closely related to the exposure under study. In a dementia study, for example, drop the dementia predictors ( dx_F00_G319 and rx_N06D ), since dementia would otherwise be part of the score you adjust for. Say in your methods which predictors you dropped.

sections.title: NMI - Nordic Multimorbidity Index
sections.heading: R implementation
sections.text: There is no official R package; the University of Southern Denmark (SDU) publishes a Stata implementation. The R version below runs in two steps: extract, then compute. These code examples are based on Pernille Errebo Tonnesen's translation of the SDU Stata code to R. How far this has been checked, and how far it has not. Checked (30 August 2026): every one of the 50 indicators and all 50 weights below were compared against SDU's own online_nmi.do , character by character. All 29 diagnosis patterns and 21 ATC patterns match, the weights match (including the two negative ones, C09C/C09D at -2 and C10AA at -3), and both assessment windows match: 5 years before index for diagnoses, 6 months for drugs. Not checked: we have not run the two implementations on the same people and compared the resulting scores. Matching code is not the same as matching output. Differences can still arise upstream of the patterns - in which diagnosis sources you feed in, how dates are handled, and how the tables are joined. So this is a faithful transcription, not a validated implementation. If the score carries weight in your analysis rather than serving as a covariate among many, compare a sample against the Stata version before you publish.

sections.title: NMI - Nordic Multimorbidity Index
sections.heading: 1. Extract diagnoses and prescriptions
sections.text: What NMI needs, and over which period: Diagnoses: a 5-year lookback before index, from LPR2 somatic and psychiatric (up to March 2019) and LPR3 (from March 2019). A somatic-only pull (e.g. lpr_adm alone) misses the psychiatric predictors (F00-03, F10, F17). The article used primary and secondary diagnoses, and the example below does the same (types A and B). If you add more types, report it. Prescriptions (ATC): a 6-month lookback before index, from LMDB. Only that window, not the whole register. Diagnoses - You can use the two approaches from Extract from LPR: either extract all diagnoses and ATC codes for the whole cohort (not recommended - time-, RAM- and space-heavy, especially for a large cohort), or filter to only the codes NMI needs before collect() , so the saved .rds files stay small. You can also use the get_lpr_diagnoses() pattern from Extract from LPR as in the example here: See the code: extract NMI diagnoses (LPR2 + LPR3) Prescriptions: extract LMDB for the cohort, keeping only NMI's ATC classes and, unlike the diagnosis extraction above, already windowed to each person's 6 months before index_date . read_register() requires fastreg set up with the path to your registers, see Parquet and fastreg if you did not convert them from SAS yourself. Why prescriptions are windowed at extraction and diagnoses are not The deciding factor is rows per person in the raw extract, not "prescriptions vs. diagnoses" as such. A handful of common drug classes (painkillers, antidepressants) can mean hundreds of fills per person across LMDB's full history, refilled roughly monthly for years. Hospital diagnoses are comparatively rare events per person, even for NMI's more serious conditions. That density difference is what turns the compute step's join in step 2 below from harmless (diagnoses) into one that has pulled tens of GB into RAM and crashed the R session in practice (prescriptions) - it is not something inherent to either register. If your own diagnosis extraction turns out to be unusually large (a broad ICD code list, a hospital-heavy cohort), the same fix applies there too: window at extraction instead of after collect() , the same way as below. See the code: extract NMI prescriptions (LMDB), windowed You started from full_cohort.rds (Phase 10: pnr + index_date ) and now have nmi_diagnoses.rds and nmi_lmdb.rds . Save them. Because the extraction is filtered to only NMI's codes, the files are small, so you rarely need to clean up. If memory is tight anyway, free it with rm() + gc() (see Phase 5) rather than restarting the whole R session.

sections.title: NMI - Nordic Multimorbidity Index
sections.heading: 3. Look at and describe the score
sections.text: The score is one number per ( pnr , index_date ) in extract_nmi.rds . It is joined to your analysis dataset in Phase 12; inspect it there. NMI is right-skewed (many low, a few high), so median [IQR] often describes it better than the mean, though mean CI is fine for comparing groups. See the code: describe the NMI score For a formatted Table 1 across groups, gtsummary::tbl_summary(by = exposure) does this automatically - see Descriptive tables. Consider whether the 5-year lookback should be an inclusion criterion. NMI's diagnosis window needs at least 5 years of register data before the index date. If you make full lookback an inclusion criterion (only people with at least 5 years of prior residency/coverage in Denmark), apply it when you build your cohort, not here, and apply the same requirement to any comparison cohort, so both groups have the same depth of data before index. Decide it in Phase 1 and apply it in Phase 10. Example: make the 5-year lookback an inclusion criterion (conceptual) The idea is to require that each person has resided in Denmark (and is therefore covered by the registers) for at least 5 years before their index date. You check this against residence/migration data (VNDS/BEF) and apply it as a filter before you match a comparison cohort: Apply the same requirement to the comparison cohort's assigned index dates, so the two groups are comparable.

sections.title: OSDC - Open Source Diabetes Classifier
sections.text: Use this page when diabetes is part of your study: as an exposure, an inclusion or exclusion criterion, or a covariate, and especially when you need to tell type 1 from type 2 diabetes, which diagnosis codes in LPR (the National Patient Register) alone do not do reliably. OSDC is an open source algorithm, published as the R package osdc , that classifies diabetes from diagnoses, prescriptions, podiatrist services and HbA1c results. You need access to five registers (listed below). You end with one row per person with diabetes, their type and the date they enter the diabetes population. Article: doi:10.2147/CLEP.S407019 Documentation and code: steno-aarhus.github.io/osdc The package README says that minor changes have been made to the algorithm since the validated version in the article, and that more are expected; the changes are listed in the repository.

sections.title: OSDC - Open Source Diabetes Classifier
sections.heading: What OSDC gives you
sections.text: classify_diabetes() returns one row per person classified as having diabetes, with five columns. People without diabetes are not in the output: "no diabetes" means "not in the table". Column Contents pnr Personal identifier raw_inclusion_date The date of the person's second inclusion event (inclusion requires two) stable_inclusion_date The same date, but NA if it falls before 1 January 1998 has_t1d TRUE / FALSE : type 1 diabetes has_t2d TRUE / FALSE , defined as !has_t1d , so the two are complements The inclusion events are HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol or more, a hospital diagnosis of diabetes, a diabetes-specific podiatrist service and a purchase of glucose-lowering drugs. The dates are inclusion dates, the date a person enters the diabetes population, not a date of disease onset, and there is no age at onset. Choosing between the two dates is a study decision. Before 1998 the register data may not be good enough to tell new (incident) cases from existing (prevalent) ones, so stable_inclusion_date is blank for inclusions before then. The 1998 default is one year after pregnancy data in LPR became usable for dropping purchases related to gestational diabetes. Filter on stable_inclusion_date and every case included before 1998 leaves your cohort without an error. Use raw_inclusion_date and you keep them, at the cost of dates the package's authors flag as uncertain. Decide which, and say which in your methods section. The cutoff is an argument, stable_inclusion_start_date , if your LPR and LMDB data start later than 1997.

sections.title: OSDC - Open Source Diabetes Classifier
sections.heading: Run osdc on your project
sections.text: osdc is on CRAN. Install it, then load it: install.packages() installs dependencies that are missing, but it does not update ones that are already installed; R's own help advises running update.packages() first. The pre-installed packages on DST may be old, so if library("osdc") stops with a version error, update the package it names. classify_diabetes() takes one argument per register ( lpr , hsr , lab_forsker , bef , lmdb ). Each must be a DuckDB table covering all the years you have, for example a connection to your parquet files. LPR must first be combined into one table, and so must the two health insurance registers, with join_registers() . The getting-started guide, steno-aarhus.github.io/osdc/articles/osdc.html, walks through this step by step. Is osdc available on your project? It is confirmed on DARTER (project 708421). It is likely available on other projects too, but this has not been verified. Check with "osdc" %in% rownames(available.packages()) on your own server (the package is not pre-installed, so available.packages() shows whether it can be installed). If it is missing, you can ask DST to install it.
sections.code: install.packages osdc

sections.title: OSDC - Open Source Diabetes Classifier
sections.heading: The registers osdc needs
sections.text: classify_diabetes() uses BEF, LPR, LMDB, the health insurance registers ( sysi / sssy ) and laboratory results, and needs all five: it has one argument for each (osdc design vignette). Missing one of the five? Two different reasons, two different fixes: sysi / sssy : these are ordinary DST registers. If they are missing, your project has not requested them; ask for them to be added. Laboratory results: these are not a DST register. They come from the Danish Health Data Authority (Sundhedsdatastyrelsen) through a separate Forskerservice application, so they never appear in DST's own overview. See Laboratory results for the table names and how the data are reached. Which glucose-lowering drugs count as inclusion events? Not every purchase of a glucose-lowering drug (ATC A10 ) counts: All GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 is glucagon-like peptide-1) are dropped, because this drug class is used extensively for weight loss in people without diabetes. Dapagliflozin and empagliflozin, two SGLT-2 inhibitors (sodium-glucose co-transporter 2), are dropped when bought on their own, because Danish guidelines recommend them for heart and kidney failure in people without diabetes. Combination drugs with a GLP-1 receptor agonist or an SGLT-2 inhibitor together with another glucose-lowering drug do count. Purchases during pregnancy are dropped, and so is metformin bought by women under 40 or with a polycystic ovary syndrome indication code. The exact logic is in the algorithm vignette and the code on GitHub.

sections.title: OSDC - Open Source Diabetes Classifier
sections.heading: The type is decided with data from after your index date
sections.text: Run on all years, the type classification uses information from after your index date. Type 1 versus type 2 is decided from the person's whole record: the share of diagnoses that are type 1, and insulin purchase patterns. A person's type can therefore depend on events that had not happened on your index date. If you use the type as a baseline variable, you classify people with information from the future (look-ahead misclassification). This applies to a pre-computed population too, since it is run on all years. To avoid it, run classify_diabetes() yourself on register data filtered to before your index date, so the classification only sees pre-index information. If you change the algorithm itself, for example to count GLP-1 receptor agonists, the published validation no longer applies.

sections.title: OSDC - Open Source Diabetes Classifier
sections.heading: On DARTER: a pre-computed population
sections.text: DARTER (project 708421): where the pre-computed files are, and the old population On DARTER the OSDC classification is already computed, so you do not need to run the algorithm yourself unless the look-ahead problem above matters for your study. The path and the name osdc (and read_register("osdc") ) are DARTER-specific; on other projects the file is named differently and lives elsewhere. The 2024 population was generated, on the latest data, after the package was updated and released on CRAN. It is valid for inclusions until the end of 2024 and replaces the previous population file: use one or the other, never both. The previous files are kept for reproducibility. Parquet: E:/workdata/708421/cleaned-data/parquet-external/osdc/2024 , which read_register("osdc") finds on DARTER .csv , .rds or .dta : E:/workdata/708421/cleaned-data/diabetes_register_pop/2024 The previous population (up to 2022), for reproducibility only. It has a different output format; the column names below apply only to the old file.

sections.text: Diabetes status is one variable among the others you extract in Phase 11. When you have them all, join them onto the cohort in Phase 12, Assemble and prepare the dataset.

sections.title: Outcomes
sections.text: Use this page to extract the dates a time-to-event analysis needs: the date of the first outcome event after index, and the dates of death and emigration that end follow-up. It builds on Extract from LPR, which explains the diagnosis extraction and defines the helper used below. You finish with one small .rds file per date ( pnr plus one date column), ready to be linked onto the cohort in Phase 12. Why you need death and emigration dates as well as the outcome In a time-to-event study you follow each person from the index date until the outcome occurs, or until the outcome can no longer be observed. A person who dies or emigrates disappears from the Danish registers, and you cannot know whether they later developed the outcome. So you censor them on the death or emigration date. Follow-up then ends at the earliest of outcome, death, emigration and end of study. If a competing event (for example death) precludes your outcome rather than just ending follow-up, it is a competing risk. That is handled in the analysis, see Competing risks.

sections.title: Outcomes
sections.heading: Extract the first outcome event after index
sections.text: The outcome is typically the first hospital diagnosis after index, taken from LPR (Landspatientregisteret, the Danish National Patient Register). read_register() requires fastreg set up with the path to your registers, see Parquet and fastreg if you did not convert them from SAS yourself. group_by(pnr) , arrange() and slice(1) keep only the first event per person, which is what most outcome definitions need. The pattern is explained in Long ↔ wide format. The join inside get_lpr_diagnoses() assembles one extract: it puts LPR's contact and diagnosis tables together so that pnr , date and diagnosis sit in one table. Linking the finished extract onto your cohort is a separate step that comes later, in Link your extracts, once all your extractions are done.
