sections.title: Outcomes
sections.heading: Death and emigration dates for censoring
sections.text: Extract the date of death from DOD (the register of deaths, column doddato ) and emigrations from VNDS (the migration register, rows with indud_kode == "U" ), each as its own table filtered to the cohort. The worked code for both, including keeping only the first emigration after index, is in Link your extracts; the column names are in Overview of registers. Follow-up time is then calculated from the outcome, death and emigration dates in Calculate follow-up time and event variable.

sections.title: Outcomes
sections.heading: Misclassification: a diagnosis code is a proxy
sections.text: A register diagnosis is a proxy for the real condition, with its own validity (sensitivity and positive predictive value, PPV). How wrong it is shapes your result: Non-differential misclassification: errors unrelated to exposure (the same code validity in both groups) usually bias the effect toward the null, so a real effect looks weaker than it is. Differential misclassification: the outcome is captured more completely in one group (for example, exposed people are in contact with the health system more often and so get diagnosed more). This can bias the estimate in either direction. What you can do about it: use validated code definitions where they exist, look up the PPV of your codes, and run a sensitivity analysis with a stricter or looser definition. For the validity of LPR diagnoses, start with the review by Schmidt et al. 2015, Clinical Epidemiology (the Danish National Patient Registry). Background on measurement bias: Hernán & Robins, What If , chapter 9.

sections.title: Outcomes
sections.heading: Where does your codelist come from?
sections.text: Applying a codelist (regex, %in% ) is the easy part. Deciding which codes make up your condition is the hard part. Use a published, ideally validated list where one exists, and document and share your own so others can reproduce it. ICD-10: for example mltc-codelists, ICD-10 codelists for many chronic conditions, with the accompanying methods paper (Prigge et al. 2025, Communications Medicine ). ATC (Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical codes, for medication): define drug groups from the WHO ATC/DDD index and published drug-class definitions. See Medication (ATC).

sections.title: Algorithms & special packages
sections.text: Look things up here when you need a tool for a task: a published algorithm for a covariate (diabetes type, mortality risk, socioeconomic position), a package for data management, or an analysis package, and whether it is available on DST. It is a reference page, not a step in the phases; come back to it from whichever phase you are in. The guide does not teach the statistical methods: for that you need a statistician, a course, or the packages' own documentation.

sections.title: Algorithms & special packages
sections.heading: 1. Validated algorithms
sections.text: Published, peer-reviewed methods you can use directly to construct covariates. SEPLINE is a guideline rather than a package: worked, not yet validated code for it is on Socioeconomic variables. Algorithm What it does Use it to Article Open Source Diabetes Classifier (OSDC) Finds people with diabetes and classifies them as T1D or T2D Define a diabetes population, type and inclusion date doi:10.2147/CLEP.S407019 Nordic Multimorbidity Index (NMI) Weighted mortality-risk score (50 predictors) Predict 5-year mortality; use with care as comorbidity burden doi:10.2147/CLEP.S353398 SEPLINE - Socioeconomic Position in Epidemiological Research National guideline for socioeconomic variables Education, income, employment as covariates doi:10.2147/CLEP.S520772 Charlson for comorbidity burden (not NMI): both heaven::charlsonIndex() and EpiForsk (see below) calculate Charlson comorbidity score from LPR diagnoses - both are on DST.

sections.title: Algorithms & special packages
sections.heading: heaven - Danish register data toolkit
sections.text: (pre-installed on DST; not on CRAN - github.com/tagteam/heaven) Functions built specifically for Danish register data by Thomas Gerds (University of Copenhagen, Biostatistics): Lexis-splitting for time-varying covariates, drug exposure windows from LMDB, risk-set matching, Charlson score, average income, hypertension from prescriptions, and built-in lookup tables for education and ATC codes. What heaven can do - and when to use it Lexis-splitting: split follow-up time across multiple time axes when a covariate changes over time (age, calendar period, time since exposure). Drug exposure from LMDB: calculate exposure periods from prescription data (e.g. "was the person on metformin at index date?"). Charlson comorbidity score from LPR diagnoses: Risk-set matching: match cases to controls at index date ( incidenceMatch() ; exposureMatch() when exposure defines the case): Average income over the years before a date: what Socioeconomic variables does by hand: Hypertension from prescriptions: hypertensionMedication(data, vars, index.date, medication.definition = hypertensionATC) . Defines hypertension from the use of at least two classes of antihypertensive drugs, either at a given index date or across the whole period. The arguments are not self-explanatory, so run help(hypertensionMedication) before using it. Find records by partial code match: findCondition(data, vars, keep, conditions, exclusions, match = "contain") . The packaged version of "keep the rows whose code starts with one of these", the pattern used throughout Extract from LPR. Run help(findCondition) for the argument order. Municipality to region: kommuneRegion(kommune) converts a numeric 3-digit municipality code to one of the five regions. Valid from 2007. Input must be numeric, not character. Built-in lookup tables: two of them replace hand-written code lists: heaven is confirmed available on DST - use library(heaven) directly. It is not on CRAN, so outside DST it must be fetched from GitHub. Function documentation lives in the package itself ( help(name) ); the maintainers also keep a worked walkthrough at examples/user-heaven.org. heaven returns data.table tables, and dplyr still works on them This guide uses dplyr (part of the tidyverse) for handling tables. heaven is written with data.table , which is another package that does the same job in a different style. That means the tables heaven hands back are data.table tables rather than the ones you are used to. You do not need to learn data.table to use heaven . A data.table is still an ordinary table, so filter() , mutate() , select() and left_join() all work on it exactly as before. The only thing you will notice is that it looks a little different when you print it in the console: it numbers the rows and shows the column types differently. If you want to be completely sure you are back on familiar ground, convert the result once with as_tibble() and carry on:

Most important functions and when to use them flatten_date_intervals() : overlapping contacts A person can have two overlapping admissions in LPR (e.g. a transfer). See below for what it requires. charlson_score() needs every diagnosis in each person's lookback window, not a code list: it matches the codes to Charlson categories itself. sections.text: (CRAN; confirmed on DST - github.com/ekstroem/dataReporter) Automatically generates an HTML/PDF report of all columns in a dataset: distribution, missing values, outliers and type checks. sections.heading: fiktive - synthetic Danish register data
sections.text: (GitHub only - local use only - github.com/sara-schwartz/fiktive) Fictitious register tables for practising and testing code locally without DST access. Not used on the server. Install with remotes::install_github("sara-schwartz/fiktive") . What it generates is the "Available registers" table in the package README, not the whole registers-guide schema. That table currently covers population ( bef , quarterly), labour classification ( akm ), cancer, deaths and cause of death ( dod , dodsaars , dodsaasg , dodsaarsager ), family income ( faik ), laboratory results ( lab_dm_forsker , labka ), prescriptions ( lmdb ), LPR2 somatic contacts and their child tables, LPR3 contacts, diagnoses, and procedures, psychiatric LPR ( t_psyk_ ), live births ( mfr ), primary-care settlements ( sysi , sssy ), education ( udda ), and migrations ( vnds , vnds_hist , vnds_ind , vnds_ud ), plus the bundled cohort tables dch and dchng . A child table has to be in the same generate_registers() call as its parent. See Phase 6, First extraction.

sections.title: Algorithms & special packages
sections.heading: fastreg - SAS → parquet (and reading registers back)
sections.text: (CRAN; install.packages("fastreg") - dp-next.github.io/fastreg) The recommended tool for converting SAS registers to parquet. It converts ( convert() , partitioned by year, with a use_template() targets pipeline for the whole workspace) and reads back ( read_register("bef") returns a lazy DuckDB connection, reading all yearly subfolders as one dataset). Set options(fastreg.project_rawdata_dir=, fastreg.project_workdata_dir=) once, then refer to registers by name. See Parquet and fastreg - SAS → parquet. read_register() only finds registers in fastreg's own format ( /year=YYYY/part-XXX.parquet ). For any other parquet the package has list_parquet_datasets() , read_parquet_dataset() and read_parquet_file() - see When read_register() cannot find the register.

Published in R Journal 2021. Example: Table 1 Output control: counts below DST's threshold (fewer than 5) must not be exported, and a suppressed cell must not be recoverable from totals or other cells. The rules, and what to do about a small number, are in Export and repatriation. Z.gtsummary.addons::round_5_gtsummary() shows counts of 0-4 as "<5" and rounds the rest to the nearest 5 - not on DST, import via data manager. It rounds every count in the table, N included, so its "<5" does not sit next to an exact total. Exact numbers for the same people elsewhere (a flowchart, the text, another table) can still give it back - see A hidden number must not be possible to work out.

sections.title: Parquet and fastreg
sections.text: Use this page when you set up the reading of registers for a project. Most people need only the first section, Point fastreg at your registers: one options() call at the top of each script, which every read_register() example in this guide assumes. The later sections are for the person who converts SAS files to parquet (once per register, usually one person for the whole project), for registers that read_register() cannot find by name, and for heavy whole-population joins that must stay inside DuckDB. Which file types you meet on the server, and what opens each one, is Phase 4 - File types and loading; the extraction pattern itself is Phase 5.

sections.title: Parquet and fastreg
sections.heading: What is parquet, and why use it?
sections.text: Parquet is a file format built for exactly the kind of work this guide does: a large table, read many times, usually filtered down to a few columns and a cohort's worth of rows. A SAS file ( .sas7bdat ) or an .rds file has to be read in whole before you can use any of it; parquet lets you open a connection and read only what you actually ask for. That is why a filtered, cohort-sized extract from a register with tens of millions of rows can come back in seconds, without ever loading the whole register into RAM, and why almost every register on DST is worth converting to parquet once. The lazy pattern itself is explained in Phase 5 - Extracting data step by step.

sections.title: Parquet and fastreg
sections.heading: Point fastreg at your registers
sections.text: If someone else already converted the registers, you do not convert anything. You tell fastreg where they are, once per script , and then read them by name. Ask whoever set the project up for the exact paths: After that, read_register("bef") works by name, with no conversion and no path in each call. Set it once, at the top of the script, next to the library() calls. Every read_register() example in this guide assumes it has been set, and none of them repeat it: two lines of someone else's project paths in every code block would be noise, and it would suggest the call belongs next to each read rather than once at the top. Two things that otherwise cost you time: Write E:/ with the colon : the DST server is Windows, also when you log in from a Mac. fastreg's own guide shows E without the colon, but only because the example writes to a temporary folder with fs::path_temp() . The folder does not have to be the innermost one : you can set the path to a folder that holds several subfolders of parquet registers. read_register() searches further down for the register name.
sections.code: point fastreg converted registers done once per script options fastreg.project_workdata_dir workdata projectnumber parquet folder fastreg.project_rawdata_dir rawdata

sections.title: Parquet and fastreg
sections.heading: Convert SAS files to Parquet
sections.text: Most projects on DST receive registers as SAS files ( .sas7bdat ). Before you can use them with open_dataset() and lazy evaluation, they must be converted to Parquet once . After that you use them exactly like any other register. If your project's registers are already converted, skip this section. Why Parquet is worth it (SAS vs Parquet) SAS (.sas7bdat) Parquet Read time Slow: the whole file is read Much faster: only the columns you ask for are read Disk space Large Smaller (compressed) Requires package haven arrow Lazy evaluation No - all into RAM Yes - filter BEFORE collect

sections.title: Parquet and fastreg
sections.heading: Recommended: convert with fastreg
sections.text: The recommended tool is the fastreg package (dp-next, on CRAN). It converts SAS registers to Parquet (partitioned by year) and lets you read them back by name . Use fastreg's own guide for the conversion code. The exact commands are documented - and kept up to date by the maintainers - in fastreg's Getting started vignette. We link to the relevant section below instead of reproducing code that could drift out of date. You install it once with install.packages("fastreg") and point it at your raw-data and output folders as shown there. #### Convert a single file If you only need to convert one SAS file, use fastreg's convert() function - it writes a single register to Parquet. See the Getting started vignette for the exact call. #### Convert many files at once To convert a whole workspace , the fastreg team recommends its targets pipeline : use_template() copies a ready-to-run pipeline that converts all your registers in parallel - reproducibly, and re-runnable when a register is updated. See Converting multiple registers in parallel. If fastreg is not available on your project: convert manually with haven + arrow If you cannot install fastreg, you can convert a single register yourself. This is essentially what fastreg does under the hood: This writes one flat file with no year= subfolders, so read_register() cannot see it (see below). Open it with open_dataset(parq_path) as in step 4, or with fastreg's read_parquet_dataset(parq_path) . Read only what you need. Even before converting you can save RAM by limiting what is read in: read_sas() ( haven ) takes col_select = c(pnr, alder, civst) (pick columns), n_max = 10000 (first rows only - good for testing) and skip = . heaven::importSAS() (pre-installed on DST) is even more efficient for large files and can filter on values - e.g. keep = c("pnr","atc") , where = "..." (filter rows) or obs = 1000 . You can also convert to Parquet (or .dta ) in StatTransfer , available on every server in the shared environment.
sections.code: haven read sas file arrow write parquet dplyr rename_with sas_file rawdata projectnumber my_register.sas7bdat parq_path workdata parquet folder my_register read into read_sas reads entire ram call but you can use any standardise column tolower write dir.create recursive showwarnings write_parquet file.path my_register.parquet verify open lazily like other register open_dataset glimpse

sections.title: Parquet and fastreg
sections.heading: When read_register() cannot find the register
sections.text: This is the direct consequence of how the parquet was laid out, which is why it sits on the same page as the conversion. read_register() can only read registers that sit in fastreg's own format: That year= level is what produces the year column you filter on later. It is a partition marker, not a DST variable and not a date - see Phase 4 - reading a register split by year. Both halves count: the year= subfolder and the part- filename. This is not a bug but a deliberate choice. The function is built for data converted with fastreg's convert() , and is not meant to guess every way parquet files might otherwise be named. If the register is laid out differently - say as one flat folder of parquet files, or with filenames without part- - read_register() cannot see it, no matter how correctly you set the path. In that case you use one of fastreg's two other reading functions: Function You write Used for read_register("name") the register name registers converted with fastreg read_parquet_dataset("path/to/folder") the full path to the folder a folder of parquet files read_parquet_file("path/to/file.parquet") the full path to the file a single parquet file All three hand you a lazy DuckDB table , so the rest of your code is exactly the same whichever one you use. What kind of DuckDB table depends on the fastreg version: up to 0.14.2 (which includes the CRAN release, 0.14.1) it is a tbl_duckdb_connection made through arrow; from 0.14.3 (installed from GitHub) it is a duckplyr data frame whose class() starts with "prudent_duckplyr_df" . Check yours with packageVersion("fastreg") . read_parquet_dataset() does not use your options() path. Only read_register() looks names up under the folders you set. The two read_parquet_ () functions need the full path , including any subfolders below the folder you set. So if you set the path to a parent folder, you still have to write the whole way down: "E:/workdata/[projectnumber]/[your-parquet-folder]/lmdb" .

sections.title: Parquet and fastreg
sections.heading: Several registers on one DuckDB connection
sections.text: read_register() is the right tool for most extractions in this guide: a cohort-sized filter, a few columns, collect() . Some steps are different. They work on the whole Danish population and join two large registers before anything can be reduced, for example the income cutpoints in Socioeconomic variables. For those, open the registers yourself as views on one plain DuckDB connection : Edit the paths to your own project. If a register sits in one flat folder with no year subfolders, use '.../faik/ .parquet' and leave out hive_partitioning . Why this, and not read_register() , for these steps: Nothing is computed in R behind your back. From fastreg 0.14.3, read_register() hands you a duckplyr table. duckplyr uses the same DuckDB engine, but when it cannot translate a step it falls back to computing that step in R's memory instead, with no warning. fastreg opens registers as "thrifty", so for a large table that fallback stops with a materialization error rather than running in the database; for a smaller one the data quietly ends up in RAM. A tbl() on a plain DBI connection uses dbplyr , which only ever sends SQL to DuckDB, and show_query() shows you exactly what it sent. Both registers on one connection. A join runs inside the database only when both sides live on the same connection. Two tables opened separately either fail with an error asking for copy = TRUE , or have to be collected into R first, which is exactly what a whole-population step cannot afford. Exact quantiles. DuckDB computes quantile() exactly, interpolating the same way as R's default. Arrow datasets queried directly give approximate quantiles (up to about 1% off in testing, with a warning), which is not good enough for cutpoints. It can spill to disk. With memory_limit and temp_directory set, DuckDB writes intermediate results to disk instead of running out of RAM. This pattern has been run on DST for the income cutpoints in Socioeconomic variables and for extractions from LMDB.

sections.title: Plan your study
sections.text: Use this page before you write any code, ideally before you apply for data. It takes you through what to settle on paper: a precise research question, which registers cover your exposure, outcome and covariates, which covariates to adjust for (chosen with a causal diagram), and who your comparison group is. When you are done you have a one-page overview of the study and the start of an analysis plan. Nothing here needs R or access to Statistics Denmark (DST).

sections.title: Plan your study
sections.heading: What type of study are you doing?
sections.text: Almost all register-based research is observational: you observe what has already happened, without intervening. Registers record the past, so you cannot randomise anyone. The two classic analytical designs are case-control and cohort; Phase 10 shows how to build a matched cohort study. Case-control or cohort: what is the difference? The two designs differ in which end you start from: Cohort Case-control Starting point Exposure Outcome Direction Follows forward: exposed → outcome Looks back: case → prior exposure Best when Exposure is rare; multiple outcomes Outcome is rare; single outcome Effect measure Incidence, relative risk (RR), hazard ratio Odds ratio (OR) In registers Define exposed group + comparator cohort, follow forward Find all cases, select controls, look back at exposure A cohort study follows people forward in time from the index date and measures how many develop the outcome, which is why you can compute incidence and risk. It is well suited when you have several outcomes (see the all_dx approach in Extract from LPR). A case-control study starts from those who already have the outcome and matches them with controls without it. That is efficient for rare outcomes, but cannot compute absolute risk. With register data you can do both, because the entire population's history is available. Phase 10 shows a matched cohort study step by step, and Case-control the other design.

sections.title: Plan your study
sections.heading: Key concepts
sections.text: These five terms are used throughout the guide. Cohort: A group of people followed over time because they share a particular characteristic at a particular point in time. Example: all patients who underwent bariatric surgery in the period 2010--2024. Index date: The start date of follow-up, the point from which you begin counting. For operated patients this is typically the date of surgery. For matched comparators the same date as the matched operated patient is assigned. Exposure: The factor whose effect you are investigating, e.g. a surgery, a medication, or a diagnosis. Outcome: What you are measuring, e.g. onset of a disease, a hospitalisation, or death. Covariates: Variables you include to account for confounding, that is, factors that affect both exposure and outcome. Examples: age, sex, comorbidity, socioeconomic status.

sections.title: Plan your study
sections.heading: 1. What do I want to investigate?
sections.text: Formulate your research question precisely before looking at any data. The six questions below are the ones every later page assumes you have answered. Example study (illustration only). The examples on this page, and in many code examples across the guide, use one made-up study: does bariatric surgery change the risk of hip fracture? It is not a real project. The choices in it are there to show the method, not as recommendations for your study. Question Example Who is my population? Adults living in Denmark, 2010–2024 What is my exposure? Bariatric surgery What is my outcome? Hip fracture (ICD-10 S72) When does follow-up start? Date of surgery (index date) When does it end? Diagnosis, death, emigration, or end of study period Which confounders should be adjusted for? Age, sex, comorbidity, SES Make sure follow-up starts at the same moment eligibility and exposure are decided. When those drift apart you get immortal time bias.

sections.title: Plan your study
sections.heading: 2. Which registers cover what?
sections.text: These are the registers most cohort studies draw on, with the short names the guide uses for them. What do you need to find? Register Demographics (age, sex, residence) BEF - Population Register Hospital diagnoses and contacts LPR - National Patient Register (LPR2 + LPR3) Dispensed prescriptions LMDB - Prescription Register Date of death (for censoring) DOD - Death Register Emigration (for censoring) VNDS - Migration Register Education UDDA - Education Register Income FAIK - Family Income Register Employment AKM - Labour Classification Module Column names and join keys for each register are in Overview of registers. Which register answers which question is Phase 8 - Find your registers.

sections.title: Plan your study
sections.heading: 3. Choose your covariates using a DAG
sections.text: Adjusting for as many variables as possible is not the goal: adjusting for the wrong ones can introduce bias instead of removing it. A DAG (directed acyclic graph, a causal diagram) is a drawing of your assumptions about how exposure, outcome and other variables relate to each other. It makes your assumptions explicit and helps you choose the right set of covariates. Rules of thumb: Adjust for confounders: variables that affect both exposure and outcome (e.g. age, comorbidity). Do NOT adjust for mediators: variables that lie on the causal pathway between exposure and outcome (this removes part of the effect you want to measure). Do NOT adjust for colliders: common effects of two variables (this opens a spurious association). You do not have to work the rules out by hand. dagitty.net takes your drawing and returns the minimal adjustment set : the smallest group of variables that removes the confounding without opening a new bias through a collider. Example study (illustration only): a DAG for surgery and hip fracture, with a confounder, a mediator and a collider Does bariatric surgery affect the risk of hip fracture? !DAG of surgery → hip fracture with a confounder (age), a mediator (bone loss) and a collider (hospitalisation). Age is a confounder: it affects both the probability of surgery and of hip fracture. Adjust for it. Bone loss (lower bone density after surgery) is a mediator: it lies on the path surgery → bone loss → hip fracture. Do not adjust, because that removes part of the effect you want to measure. Hospitalisation is a collider: both surgery and hip fracture lead to hospitalisation. Do not adjust, because it opens a spurious association. You can paste the model straight into dagitty.net and have the minimal adjustment set computed: For this DAG the minimal adjustment set is {Age}: you only need to adjust for age. Where to learn to draw a DAG Causal Diagrams: Draw Your Assumptions Before Your Conclusions: free HarvardX course by Miguel Hernán. Hernán & Robins, Causal Inference: What If : the textbook (free PDF), also in Learning resources.
sections.code: dag age pos surgery exposure boneloss hipfracture outcome hospitalisation

sections.title: Plan your study
sections.heading: 4. Who do you compare with? The comparison cohort
sections.text: Many studies compare an exposed group with a comparison cohort (also called a comparator cohort). How you build it is a design decision to make on paper. At this stage you only need to settle four things: Who is an appropriate comparator? An active comparator (people with the same indication starting an alternative treatment, which reduces confounding by indication), or a matched sample of the background population. What decides the comparator's index date , since the exposure does not give them one. Which variables you match on, and at what ratio (e.g. age, sex and calendar year, 1:5). What happens if a comparator becomes exposed later. Each of these, plus eligibility at index, the shared exclusions and the immortal-time trap, is worked through in Phase 10 - Build your study population and Comparison cohort.

sections.title: Plan your study
sections.heading: 5. Write a one-page overview of the study
sections.text: Before opening R, answer these questions in writing: 1. Which variables do I need? (patient information - age, sex, diagnoses etc. - and for which years) 2. Which registers contain this information? (LPR, BEF, LMDB, ...) 3. In what order should data be assembled? (define population → extract outcome → extract covariates) Example study (illustration only): overview for the hip fracture study

sections.title: Plan your study
sections.heading: 6. Write an analysis plan
sections.text: An analysis plan is a document you write before looking at your data. It commits you to design, statistics and variables before results can colour your decisions. Skeleton: use the STROBE checklists (Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology). For studies on routinely collected data, RECORD extends STROBE, and RECORD-PE covers pharmacoepidemiology. Pre-registration: you can register the plan publicly before you start, for example on the Open Science Framework. Power and sample size. Even large registers have limited power (the ability to detect an effect that is really there) for rare outcomes or small subgroups. Already in the plan, consider the smallest effect you could meaningfully detect with your expected number of events. The pwr package does simple power and sample-size calculations; for survival and rate designs it is the number of events, more than the number of people, that drives your power.

sections.title: R: the bare essentials
sections.heading: RStudio for the first time
sections.text: RStudio is divided into four panels: !RStudio's four panels{fig-alt="RStudio interface with four panels"} Source: Wikipedia / RStudio, CC BY-SA 4.0 Top left - Script editor This is where you write and save your code. You can have multiple scripts open at once and switch between them using the tabs at the top of the panel. Remember to save changes regularly with Ctrl+S (Cmd+S on a Mac). Top right - Environment / History / Connections Environment: shows all objects you have created in the current R session - data frames, vectors, lists. Functions from packages (e.g. filter() from dplyr) are not shown here; only what you have created yourself. It also shows how much memory each object takes, which matters on a shared server - see Seeing your memory use from inside R. History: a log of all commands you have run in the console. Bottom left - Console Code is executed here and output and error messages are shown here. You can type commands directly in the console - but they are not saved. All work you want to keep must be in a script. Bottom right - Files / Plots / Packages / Help Files: a file browser for your folders and files on the server. Plots: graphs you create are shown here - even before they are saved. Packages: list of all installed packages. A tick next to a package means it is loaded with library() and ready to use. Help: help documentation, with description, arguments and examples for a function. Two ways in: type ?functionname in the console (e.g. ?filter ), or place the cursor inside a function name in your script and press F1 . If a panel disappears: go to View → Panes → Show All Panes in the menu bar at the top. You can also click the icon with four squares in the menu bar. Run code: place the cursor on a line and press Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Return on a Mac). On the DST server it is Ctrl+Enter also when you connect from a Mac, see Phase 3.

sections.title: R: the bare essentials
sections.heading: What is an object?
sections.text: x <- 5 creates an object . The arrow <- means "store what is on the right under the name on the left". From now on x stands for the value 5 - until you overwrite it yourself. The pattern is always the same: You name something so you can reuse it later without writing it out again. Almost everything in R is an object: a single number, an entire table, a model. When you fetch (part of) a register with collect() , for example, you typically store it in an object so you can keep working with it: The objects you create appear in the Environment panel in the top right of RStudio.

sections.title: R: the bare essentials
sections.heading: What is a function? A package? What does library() do?
sections.text: A function is a command that performs an action. filter(data, age > 50) is a function. sum(c(1, 2, 3)) is a function. You recognise functions by their parentheses. What is inside the parentheses? The parentheses are always there - but they are not always filled. It depends on whether the function needs input to know what to do: filter(age > 50) : requires the condition; otherwise it does not know what to filter on open_dataset("E:/workdata/...") : requires the path; otherwise it does not know what to open collect() : requires nothing; it already knows what to fetch, because the pipe has sent data forward to it Rule of thumb: in a pipe , empty parentheses usually mean the function acts on what has been passed forward via the pipe , without needing anything extra from you. Outside a pipe, empty parentheses just mean the function needs no input, e.g. getwd() , Sys.Date() or gc() . A package is a collection of functions written by others that you can load. R comes with base functions, but most of what this guide uses is in packages such as dplyr and arrow . library() loads a package so its functions are available in your session. You will see library(dplyr) at the top of almost every script.

sections.title: R: the bare essentials
sections.heading: Six functions and symbols you will meet throughout the guide
sections.text: You will see these in almost every extraction. You do not need to understand them in detail now, only recognise them. The symbol %>% (the pipe) is everywhere. It passes the result from one line forward as input to the next. df %>% filter(age > 50) means: "take df , and pass it to filter() ". This makes it possible to chain steps together and read code from top to bottom. Function What it does Example filter() Keep rows that meet a condition df %>% filter(age > 50) select() Choose which columns to keep df %>% select(pnr, age, sex) collect() Fetch parquet data into R's memory register %>% filter(...) %>% collect() mutate() Create a new column or modify an existing one df %>% mutate(age_cat = age > 65) left_join() Link two datasets - keep all rows from the left cohort %>% left_join(bef, by = "pnr") %>% The pipe - passes the result to the next function df %>% filter(age > 50) %>% select(pnr) The pipe %>% is explained in detail in Functions: overview, and collect() in Phase 5 - Extracting data step by step.

sections.title: Rates and rate ratios (Poisson)
sections.text: Use this page when you want an adjusted incidence rate ratio from your cohort: Poisson regression with person-time, when to choose it over Cox, its assumptions, and where to go when the rate changes with age or calendar time. You start from the analysis-ready dataset with event status and follow-up time (Phase 12), and you end with rate ratios ready for a results table. A rate is the number of events divided by the time people were at risk ( person-time ). An incidence rate ratio (IRR) compares the rate in two groups: if the rate is twice as high among the exposed, the IRR is 2. Rates fit register data well, because registers follow people over time and count events. In Descriptive tables you computed a crude rate per group. A Poisson regression gives an IRR that is adjusted for confounding (age, sex, other covariates), the same way logistic regression gives an adjusted odds ratio. Paths and variable names in the examples are generic - replace them with your own. survival , gtsummary and MASS must be installed in your R environment on DST.

sections.title: Rates and rate ratios (Poisson)
sections.heading: Poisson, Cox or logistic regression: which to choose
sections.text: Three models can be used on a "did the event happen?" outcome. The difference is whether time enters, and how : Logistic regression (Regression) only looks at yes/no and ignores time. Gives an odds ratio . Fits when everyone is followed equally long, or when time is irrelevant. Cox regression (Time-to-event) looks at the time until the first event per person and gives a hazard ratio . It models the rate without assuming a particular shape over time. Poisson regression (this page) looks at the number of events per person-time and gives a rate ratio (IRR) . It is strong when you want to work with rates across age groups or calendar periods , or when you have counted-up events and person-time rather than one time-to-event per person. Cox or Poisson? They often answer almost the same question, and HR and IRR agree closely when the Poisson model lets the baseline rate vary over follow-up (follow-up split into time bands, see below); with a single constant rate they can differ if the hazard changes over time. Choose Cox if you think in individual follow-up time and time-to-first-event. Choose Poisson if you think in rates per person-year split by age/calendar time (classic in register studies of e.g. cancer or mortality), or if your data are already counted up (events and person-years per group).

sections.title: Rates and rate ratios (Poisson)
sections.heading: Starting point
sections.text: You need two things per person, exactly as for the crude rate: the number of events ( outcome , here 0 or 1) and the person-time ( followup_years , follow-up time in years). Both are built in Phase 12.
sections.code: dplyr pipe gtsummary tbl_regression tidy output readrds path analysis.rds analysis ready dataset one row per person index matched replacement

sections.title: Rates and rate ratios (Poisson)
sections.heading: Poisson regression: rate ratio (IRR)
sections.text: The model is a glm with family = poisson . The new part, compared with logistic regression, is the offset : it tells the model how long each person was at risk , so it models the rate (events per time) and not just the number of events. family = poisson makes it a rate model. offset(log(followup_years)) is the person-time. It must be logged ( log() ), because the Poisson model works on the log scale. Without the offset you model the number of events, not the rate - and that is almost never what you want. Zero follow-up gives log(0) = -Inf , which is why the Phase 12 recipe drops people with no follow-up. exponentiate = TRUE shows rate ratios (IRR) instead of log-rate coefficients. An IRR reads exactly like an OR or HR: 1 = no difference , above 1 = higher rate, below 1 = lower. See Reading your result. Here outcome is 0/1 (one row per person), and the offset is the person's total follow-up time. That gives a valid IRR adjusted for the covariates you have at baseline (at study start/index) - not one that changes as people age. For that, see Rates that vary over time below.
sections.code: model glm outcome exposure age sex event count explained covariates offset log followup_years person time turns counts into rate needs see phase family poisson rate send table tbl_regression exponentiate ratios irr

sections.title: Rates and rate ratios (Poisson)
sections.heading: Assumptions
sections.text: The Poisson model rests on a few assumptions. If they fail, the confidence intervals in particular become misleading: Constant rate within each "band". The model assumes the rate is the same throughout the person-time a group contributes. If the rate changes strongly with e.g. age, you satisfy the assumption by splitting the person-time into age groups (see below), so the rate only has to be constant within each narrow band. Events are Poisson-distributed (mean = variance). If the variance is larger than the mean ( overdispersion ), the standard errors become too small and the confidence intervals artificially narrow. This is common in register data - see the fold-out below. Independent observations. One row (or one cluster of person-time) per person. If the same person appears several times (e.g. matched with replacement or recurrent events), use cluster-robust standard errors as in Regression. Log-linearity. Continuous variables are related to the log rate in a straight line. Check as for logistic regression, e.g. with splines. Check for overdispersion (and switch to negative binomial if needed) Overdispersion means the events vary more than a pure Poisson distribution allows. The consequence is confidence intervals that are too narrow. It matters for aggregated counts (events and person-years per group) and recurrent events ; with one 0/1 row per person, as above, there is nothing to check, and the model's own standard errors hold. A Poisson model with log(time) as offset solves the same estimating equations as a survival model with a constant rate (Holford 1980, doi:10.2307/2529982), and each person contributes independently to the likelihood. On aggregated data, check first, then two common fixes: Alternatively you can keep the Poisson model and use family = quasipoisson , which scales the standard errors up without changing the distribution. Both give wider, more honest confidence intervals than a pure Poisson when there is overdispersion.

sections.title: Rates and rate ratios (Poisson)
sections.heading: Rates that vary over time
sections.text: The model above assumes one rate throughout the person's follow-up. But in a register study the person ages along the way, and the calendar year changes - and the rate of e.g. cancer or death changes strongly with both. If you want the rate to vary with attained age or calendar period , the follow-up time must be split into intervals : one row per person per interval, so each row sits in one age band and one calendar year. You then count up events and person-time and fit the same Poisson model with age and period bands as covariates. The split rows from one person do not need cluster-robust standard errors: under the Poisson model the pieces "may therefore be treated as if they come from separate individuals" (Plummer & Carstensen 2011, doi:10.18637/jss.v038.i05). This is a standard move in register epidemiology, but it needs a bit more machinery than this page covers. Use survival::survSplit() or Epi::splitLexis() (Lexis objects), or the popEpi package, which is built for exactly rates, person-time and standardisation on register data. See Read more. SMR and SIR. If you want to compare your population's rate with a reference population (e.g. the rates for all of Denmark from Statistics Denmark), you use indirect standardisation : the standardized mortality/incidence ratio (SMR/SIR) is observed events divided by those you would expect from the reference rates. Epi and popEpi have ready-made functions. It is a descriptive standardisation, not an adjusted regression, so choose according to your question. Read more The Epidemiologist R Handbook , general background: Univariate and multivariable regression The Epi package: person-time, Lexis objects and rates on register data. The popEpi package: rates, SIR/SMR and standardisation, built for register data. Bendix Carstensen's course material (Statistical Practice in Epidemiology) - a thorough walkthrough of person-time, age/period splitting and Poisson rates.

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.text: Use this page to look up which register holds what, what its columns are called after rename_with(tolower) , and which of them most studies use. You need it when you plan your study and order data, and again when you write the extraction code. The registers are grouped by topic, with the most used first. To search every column in every register at once, use Find a variable; for quirks that give a silently wrong result, see Pitfalls. A starting point, not an authority. This page can be out of date or simply wrong, and your own delivery may differ from it. Verify against your files with colnames() (see Phase 7 - Inspect your data) before you rely on anything here. Found a mistake? Open an issue or use the feedback box on this page. Corrections are welcome. Where this comes from, and why it can still be wrong The tables on this page are generated from a schema built out of DST's published documentation: the variable list for each register and DST's order list, which names every variable in every DST register with its period. The health registers - LPR, LMDB, the death registers, the cancer register - are documented by Sundhedsdatastyrelsen on esundhed.dk instead, which is also the only source that publishes data types. Each register links to its own source, and every value set says underneath where its codes come from. Those sources change. Registers are extended, columns are added and retired, and a code can change meaning without changing its name. Names here are shown after rename_with(tolower) , and your own delivery may spell them differently or not contain them at all: what DST documents is the register, not what your project ordered. Key columns, the ones you use in the code, are marked in bold. Names apply after rename_with(tolower) . How to read the code examples: read_register() vs open_dataset() The code on this page opens registers with read_register("registername") (fastreg, by name - recommended). That requires fastreg set up with the path to your registers, see Parquet and fastreg if you did not convert them from SAS yourself. Without fastreg, use open_dataset("path/to/register/") instead and replace the path with your project's parquet folder. Everything else in the examples works the same either way.

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: Where to look things up
sections.text: This page shows the columns most studies use. When you need more than that, the question you are asking decides where to go: Your question Where to look What are all the columns in this register? The register's own variable list - follow the register name in the table below Does this register reach the end of my follow-up? Datasafari - shows the latest reference date and the next expected update Which registers exist at all, and which are closed? Oversigt over registre - over a thousand, with years covered. Luk means closed and never extended, as dodsaars and dodsaasg both are Can I even order this variable, and for which years? Bestillingsliste.xlsx - every variable in every DST register, with its period. The one to open while you are still planning What does code 330 mean? Klassifikationer - DISCED-15 for education, SOCIO for employment, DISCO for occupation Why does this variable jump in one particular year? Højkvalitetsdokumentation - breaks in the series and validity periods, for selected variables What does DST mean by "beskæftiget"? Hvad betyder - the words, not the columns. Look here when a variable measures something narrower than the everyday word suggests All of it hangs off Dokumentation af data →, DST's own hub, if you would rather start there. The health registers are documented separately by Sundhedsdatastyrelsen on esundhed.dk. And whichever you use: what DST holds is not what your project was delivered. Confirm against your own files with colnames() .

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: Overview - all registers
sections.text: The Often used column is the handful of columns most studies reach for, not the full list: follow the register link for every column DST documents, or the section below for the ones this guide explains. lab_dm_forsker is in the schema but not in this table, because it is reached through Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's Forskerservice rather than DST.

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: BEF - Population Register
sections.text: Status register - one snapshot per person per reference time point. Delivered quarterly since 2008 (March, June, September, December); before 2008 December only. Whether year == 2020 corresponds to a particular reference time point depends on the project convention - confirm in your project guide. A person is in a file only if they were alive and living in Denmark on that file's reference date, so someone who dies after that date is still in the file - use DOD to determine whether a person was alive on a specific date. BEF cannot on its own answer whether a person was resident in Denmark on a given date: between two snapshots people can both leave and come back. To decide residence on an index date, combine BEF with VNDS - see Phase 10 - the source population. BEF does not contain date of death. Use DOD ( doddato ) for censoring, not DODSAARS, which stops in 2001 (see below). DST's own documentation: statistikdokumentation/befolkningen →.

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: DOD - Death Register
sections.text: Døde i Danmark. One row per deceased person, covering 1970-2025 and still updated (DST register overview, last reference date 31 December 2025). This is the register you use to censor at death. It is a short one: DOD may not be in parquet on your project DOD is sometimes delivered only as a raw SAS file, in which case read_register("dod") will not find it and you read it with haven::read_sas() instead. Ask your data manager for the path. And check the span of your own delivery, which is the years your project ordered rather than everything DST holds:
sections.code: dod summarise min doddato max collect

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: DODSAARS - Cause of Death Register (ends 2001)
sections.text: Dødsårssagsregistret. One row per deceased person, with the cause of death. It carries a death date too, in d_dodsdto , which is why it is so often used for censoring - but its coverage stops on 31 December 2001 . Use it for causes of death up to 2001, and use DOD for the date. Censoring on dodsaars silently treats everyone who died after 2001 as alive. No error, no warning: they simply stay in your risk set to the end of follow-up, so survival looks better than it is and rates come out too low. The full version of this is pitfall 1 - four death registers. #### DODSAASG - the 2002-2022 link in the chain Coding of the underlying cause changed again in 2007, mid-register. Until then, trained coders at the National Board of Health interpreted each death certificate. From 2007, certificates are submitted electronically and it is the certifying doctor who assigns the ICD-10 code directly, with no central review of that classification afterwards. dodsaasg covers both halves of this change (2002-2022) with nothing in the data to tell them apart. See Helweg-Larsen 2011, The Danish Register of Causes of Death, Scand J Public Health 39(Suppl 7):26-29. #### DODSAARSAGER - the current register (2022-2024) Every register in the chain renames the same thing. The cause columns are c_dod1 to c_dod4 here, c_dod_1a to c_dod_1d in DODSAASG from 2002, and doedsaarsag_kode_1 and so on in DODSAARSAGER from 2022. The date column goes d_dodsdto , d_dodsdato , doedsdato - one letter between the first two. Code written for one part of the chain will not run against another, and a mistyped column name fails as a missing column rather than a wrong answer. Cause of death is split across three registers, by period. dodsaars runs to 2001, dodsaasg covers 2002-2022, and dodsaarsager covers 2022-2024. Both dodsaasg and dodsaarsager include 2022. A study spanning more than one of those windows needs all the registers that overlap its period, chained together. A single one gives you a silently incomplete picture: causes simply stop appearing after its last year. None of the three is the source for the date of death. For that, use DOD with the column doddato . The cause coding itself is documented by the Danish Health Data Authority: Dødsårsagsregisteret →. Do you ever need both DOD and DODSAARS? Only if your own DOD delivery does not reach back far enough for your study period. Then stack them, renaming so the date columns match, and note that the two registers overlap for 1970-2001 - so without the distinct() every early death is counted twice: On DARTER, see Register paths and datastores.
sections.code: deaths bind_rows dod select pnr death_date doddato dodsaars d_dodsdto mutate as.date distinct keep_all keeps dod row since comes first

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: VNDS - Migration Register
sections.text: One row per migration event per person. VNDS was closed in February 2026 and split into three registers ( VNDS_ind , VNDS_ud , VNDS_hist , described below). It is still documented here because it is the only migration register many projects have: a delivery made before the split will not contain the replacements. Check colnames() or your project's register list to see which you have. If you have both, use the new ones and do not mix them with VNDS , or you will count the same migration twice. For emigration dates used in censoring, combine VNDS_ud (2005+) and VNDS_hist (1973-2004) in place of the old VNDS . What the three replacement registers are, and why DST split them VNDS_ind : immigrations to Denmark from 2005 onwards. VNDS_ud : emigrations from Denmark from 2005 onwards. VNDS_hist : historical migrations 1973-2004, no longer updated. The split reduces duplicates that arose because immigration and emigration data came from different sources over the years. The earliest data is now frozen in the historical register. Source: DST notice, 19 February 2026. Use: filter(indud_kode == "U") → min(haend_dato) per pnr for first emigration date. Non-emigrants do not appear in VNDS with a "U" event and get emigration_date = NA . #### VNDS_hist - historical migrations (1973-2004) #### VNDS_ind - immigrations (2005 onwards) The two new registers drop indud_kode : which direction the event went is now carried by which register you are reading, so a combined series has to add the direction back itself. #### VNDS_ud - emigrations (2005 onwards)

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: 2. LPR2 - Somatic (up to March 2019)
sections.text: The register itself is owned by the Danish Health Data Authority, whose documentation covers what is reported and how it changed over time: Landspatientregisteret →. Join: lpr_adm LEFT JOIN lpr_diag ON recnum .

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: 3. LPR2 - Psychiatric (1995 -- March 2019)
sections.text: Psychiatric contacts before March 2019 are in separate registers from somatic LPR2. From March 2019, LPR3 covers both in one table. [] Before 1995: inpatients only, and ICD-8 The Danish Psychiatric Central Register is electronic from 1969, but covers only inpatients until 1995 (outpatient visits were added from 1995), and diagnoses before 1994 are coded in ICD-8 (numeric codes, e.g. 290-315, where 290 covers dementia) - not ICD-10 F-codes. These older data are normally not part of the standard extract and are requested separately, via Rigsarkivet or NCRR, Aarhus University. If your study covers that period, you have to map ICD-8 to your F-code groups yourself. If you forget to query the psychiatric registers for the period 1995--2019, you miss all dementia diagnoses (F00--F03) recorded at geriatric psychiatry outpatient clinics and memory clinics. Those patients will appear dementia-free and remain in the cohort as false negatives.

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: t_psyk_adm - Psychiatric contacts
sections.text: The key and person columns may be renamed in your delivery. DST's variable list gives both psychiatric tables RECNUM and PNR , the same names the somatic registers use. Several deliveries hand them over renamed: DARTER has k_recnum and v_cpr here, and v_recnum in the diagnosis table, so one key ends up with three names. That is data processing, not the register. Run colnames() first, and rename to recnum and pnr if yours differ:

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: 4. LPR3 (March 2019 and onwards)
sections.text: Before you join these two tables: lpr_a_kontakt / lpr_a_diagnose are not pure LPR3. They also hold LPR1, LPR2 and MiniPAS (records from private hospitals) rows, tagged by lprindberetningssystem , going back to around 2017. Filter both tables on lprindberetningssystem == "LPR3" first, or you will double-count contacts already in lpr_adm . See Understand LPR for why, and Extract from LPR for open problems with that filter. LPR3 covers both somatic and psychiatric contacts in one table. Join: lpr_a_kontakt LEFT JOIN lpr_a_diagnose ON dw_ek_kontakt . The "a" in lpr_a_diagnose does not mean A-type diagnoses. DST describes the LPR_A tables, which replaced the LPR_F tables in June 2025, as an "LPR analyse model" (Nyt om grunddata, 2nd quarter 2025). The table contains all types: A (main) and B (secondary), plus add-on codes (G, grundmorbus, is LPR2 only), so you still need to filter on diag_kode_type .

sections.heading: lpr_a_kontakt - Contacts

Look up the specialty code kont_ans_hovedspec in DST's specialty/department overview → (in Danish).

sections.title: Overview of registers
sections.heading: 5. LPR - SKS procedure codes
sections.text: SKS (Sundhedsvæsenets Klassifikations System - the Danish Health Classification System) is the Danish classification system for operations and procedures; the operation codes are based on the Nordic NOMESCO Classification of Surgical Procedures (NCSP). Bariatric surgery has e.g. codes KJDF10 (gastric bypass) and KJDF40 (sleeve gastrectomy). Look up codes in the SKS browser → (in Danish). SKS codes are split across two registers depending on period. For full coverage both must be queried and the results bound together. Neither procedure table holds pnr . It is fetched by joining to lpr_adm (LPR2) or lpr_a_kontakt (LPR3).

sections.heading: lpr_a_procregistrering - LPR3 SKS procedures (2019 and onwards)
sections.text: The LPR3 procedure table. It sits alongside lpr_a_kontakt and lpr_a_diagnose , and joins to contacts on dw_ek_kontakt exactly like the diagnosis table does. Column names confirmed against DST's variable list →. There is no pnr here , as in every LPR procedure table: it identifies procedures, not people. Join to lpr_a_kontakt to get one. A few rows have no contact to join to, and DST flags them for you in flag_proc_uden_kont . Count them before you drop them.

sections.text: Examination and treatment codes (ZZ codes) live in lpr_sksube (LPR2), separate from the operation codes in lpr_sksopr above. Join like the other SKS tables, via recnum . The register is shaped exactly like lpr_sksopr . Check that you actually have c_opr before planning around this register. DST documents it for every year 1999-2019, but at least one delivery contains only recnum , d_odto and year , which cannot tell one procedure from another. Run colnames() first.
