sections.title: Time-to-event
sections.heading: Kaplan-Meier curves
sections.text: survfit() computes the Kaplan-Meier estimate (the event-free proportion over time), and ggsurvplot() draws it nicely. With simulated numbers the curves look like this (here the exposed drop faster, i.e. they get the outcome more often): !Kaplan-Meier curves with simulated data. ggsurvplot() typically also adds a risk table below the figure.
sections.code: survminer ggsurvplot fit survfit surv time_days outcome exposure one curve per group pval show log rank test conf.int confidence bands around curves risk.table table below figure number risk over time xlab days since index axis labels ylab event free proportion

sections.title: Time-to-event
sections.heading: Before you export a Kaplan-Meier curve
sections.text: The curve and its risk table are output like any table. Each step in the curve is one or a few events, and each number at risk is a table cell, so check them against the small-cell rule (3 or 5, see Export). In the tail of the curve, where few people are left, this usually fails: one way out is to cut the x-axis ( xlim = in ggsurvplot() ) where the number at risk falls below your threshold. One minus the Kaplan-Meier curve also overestimates the risk when a competing event (typically death) can preclude your outcome: see Competing risks below.

sections.title: Time-to-event
sections.heading: Cox regression (hazard ratio)
sections.text: coxph() gives hazard ratios (HR) adjusted for covariates. tbl_regression(exponentiate = TRUE) shows them as HRs instead of log-hazards. A hazard ratio is a ratio of rates (hazards) over follow-up: 1 = no difference, above 1 = higher rate in the exposed, below 1 = lower. It is not a ratio of risks. See Reading your result. The difference with replacement. If the comparison cohort is matched with replacement (or there is crossover), the same person appears several times and the rows are not independent. Then you add one argument, cluster = pnr , to exactly the same model. It does not change the hazard ratio estimate; it replaces the standard errors with robust (sandwich) standard errors that allow for the repeated person, so the confidence intervals are no longer too narrow. Same idea as in Regression. Note the syntax: coxph() takes the cluster variable as an argument without a tilde ( cluster = pnr ), whereas sandwich::vcovCL() on the Regression page uses a formula with a tilde ( cluster = ~ pnr ). Same idea (cluster on person id), just two functions' different ways of receiving the variable. Stratified on the matched set. To compare each exposed person only with their own matched comparison persons, add strata(match_id) (the matched-set id from Comparison cohort): each matched set then gets its own baseline hazard. What is your time scale? The time axis (what the x-axis shows on e.g. a Kaplan-Meier curve) is a choice. By default it is time since index - how long each person has been followed since their own start date (that is time_days in the examples). But you can also follow people on: attained age : so the model compares people at the same age . That adjusts for age automatically and flexibly (a strong confounder for most outcomes), without you having to model the shape of age yourself. Common in register studies. calendar time : if the calendar period itself matters (e.g. treatment that has changed over the years). Time since index is simplest; age-as-time-scale is often stronger when risk is driven heavily by age. Technically you choose the time scale via what you put in as time in Surv() . With age as time scale, each person enters at their age at index ( delayed entry ), so Surv() needs both entry and exit age - Surv(age_at_exit, outcome) alone would count everyone as at risk from birth:

sections.title: Time-to-event
sections.heading: Check the assumption: proportional hazards
sections.text: The Cox model assumes proportional hazards (PH): that the hazard ratio is constant over follow-up. If it is not, a single hazard ratio does not describe an effect that changes over time. Check it with cox.zph() , which is based on the scaled Schoenfeld residuals (in short, whether the effect drifts over time). With register-sized data the test has the power to flag even a tiny departure, so a small p-value alone says little. Judge the plot: how much the curve slopes, and whether that changes what you would conclude. What to do if the assumption is violated If a variable violates the assumption, you can e.g. stratify on it ( + strata(variable) in the model, giving it its own baseline hazard) or model a time-dependent effect (let the effect change over follow-up). A third alternative is to drop the hazard ratio and use RMST ( restricted mean survival time ): the average event-free time within a fixed window (e.g. "months alive within 5 years"). You compare groups by the difference in RMST , measured in time units instead of a ratio, and it is valid even when PH is violated. In R: the survRM2 package.

sections.title: Time-to-event
sections.heading: Competing risks
sections.text: If another event can preclude your outcome (classically death, before the outcome can occur), it is a competing risk . One minus the Kaplan-Meier curve then overestimates the risk, because it treats those who died as if they were merely censored and could still get the outcome later. In register cohorts with older people or long follow-up this is common. Each person ends up in one of three places, and only the first thing that happens counts: (1) they never reach an event during follow-up ( censored ), (2) they get your outcome, or (3) they have the competing event (e.g. death). Someone who dies first can never reach the outcome, and the analysis must reflect that.

sections.title: Time-to-event
sections.heading: 1. Set up the data
sections.text: You need the same two variables as for an ordinary Cox model - but the status variable now takes three values instead of two (so we call it status instead of outcome ): time_days - the time from index to the first thing that happens (outcome, death or end of follow-up). status - what happened: censored, outcome or death. status must be a factor , and tidycmprsk requires "censored" to be the first level . The order of the levels is also where you tell R which level is your outcome and which is the competing risk: You build status_code (0/1/2) from the dates - what happened first : 0 = censored (e.g. end of follow-up, emigrated or otherwise lost), 1 = outcome, 2 = death. The construction lives in Calculate follow-up time and event variable (Phase 12). The number you give censoring does not matter - what matters is that the censored level is listed first in levels = (which is why it is 0 here).
sections.code: tidycmprsk cuminc crr mutate status factor status_code raw code one per person e.g. levels order sets meaning labels censored level must first outcome models death competing risk

sections.title: Time-to-event
sections.heading: 2. Describe the risk over time (CIF)
sections.text: Instead of Kaplan-Meier , use the cumulative incidence function (CIF, also called Aalen-Johansen). It allocates people correctly across the competing outcomes, so death no longer "steals" risk from the outcome. (This is about the curve ; the regression itself is still done with Cox, see step 3.)
sections.code: surv time status factor cumulative incidence each event type cuminc time_days exposure one curve per group also gives gray test difference

sections.title: Time-to-event
sections.heading: 3. Regression: pick the model to match your question
sections.text: There are two regression models, and they answer different questions: The rate of the outcome among those still alive and event-free: run an ordinary Cox model and censor the competing event. You do that by setting the event to status == "outcome" : both censored and dead people then become "no event". This is the cause-specific hazard, which is better suited to an etiological question (Lau, Cole & Gange 2009, doi:10.1093/aje/kwp107). The cumulative incidence (absolute risk) of the outcome: use Fine-Gray ( crr ), where the dead stay in the risk set. crr by default models the first event type after "censored" (here "outcome") and treats the rest ("death") as competing. This is the subdistribution hazard. Neither hazard ratio is a risk ratio. The subdistribution hazard ratio tells you the direction in which the exposure shifts the cumulative incidence (if the model fits), but not by how much; for the absolute risk, report the cumulative incidence (CIF) at fixed time points, for example at 1 and 5 years. Rule of thumb: which one do I pick? If you want to describe or predict risk (e.g. "what is the 5-year risk of the outcome?"), use the CIF and Fine-Gray. If you want to know whether the exposure changes the rate of the outcome in those still at risk, use the cause-specific Cox. Many studies report both.

sections.title: Time-to-event
sections.heading: Time-varying covariates (briefly)
sections.text: If a variable changes during follow-up (e.g. a blood test or BMI), it cannot be a single value per person. It must be in start/stop format (one row per interval), built with survival::tmerge() and analysed with coxph(Surv(tstart, tstop, outcome) ~ ...) . The reshaping itself is in Time-varying variables. Further information Further depth in The Epidemiologist R Handbook : Survival analysis

sections.title: Time-varying variables
sections.text: Almost everything else in this guide builds on one row per person with variables measured at index (baseline). Use this page when something changes during follow-up and you need to decide whether that matters. It helps you decide when the baseline setup is enough, shows how to build start/stop data for a time-varying covariate with survival::tmerge() , and tells you when the problem is beyond a reshaping. You need the analysis-ready dataset from Phase 12. This is a short orientation to a hard topic. Time-varying analysis ranges from a simple reshaping of the data (what we show here) to the causal methods for time-varying treatments ; for the latter, see for example What If, Part III. Paths and variable names in the examples are generic - replace them with your own. survival must be installed in your R environment on DST.

sections.title: Time-varying variables
sections.heading: What can vary?
sections.text: Three different things can vary over time, and they call for very different answers: Time-varying covariate / confounder: a background variable that changes (e.g. BMI, a blood test, a medication status, marital status). It cannot be a single value per person if it changes along the way. Time-varying exposure / treatment: the exposure itself starts, stops or switches during follow-up (a treatment the person goes on and off). A common register use is an exposure that starts after cohort entry: counting the person as exposed from entry creates immortal time bias, while letting exposure switch on at its start date in start/stop data avoids it. Exposures that go on and off are where it gets causally hard, see the feedback section below. Censoring is also time-varying: people leave follow-up at different times (emigration, death, loss to follow-up). This is already handled in your follow-up time and time-to-event setup, see Time-to-event.

sections.title: Time-varying variables
sections.heading: When is the baseline setup enough?
sections.text: Often. If your exposure is fixed at index (e.g. a diagnosis or a surgery on a given date) and you adjust for confounders measured at baseline , then the ordinary setup from Phase 10-12 - one row per person, covariates frozen at index, one follow-up interval - is the right one. You do not need time-varying analysis just because the data span time. Only consider it when a variable that matters for the analysis actually changes value after index. Rule of thumb: ask whether the extra complexity changes the answer. If a covariate drifts a little but is not a strong confounder, its baseline value is usually fine. If the exposure itself changes, or a strong confounder changes systematically with the exposure, read on.

sections.title: Time-varying variables
sections.heading: A time-varying covariate
sections.text: If you have a covariate that changes along the way (and that is not caught in feedback with the exposure, see the next section), the fix is mechanical: you build start/stop format (also called counting-process format). Instead of one row per person you get one row per person- interval , where the variable is constant within the interval. You build it with survival::tmerge() and analyse it with an ordinary Cox model. A person with two measurements becomes two rows, each with its own tstart / tstop interval and the value that applies within it: pnr tstart tstop measure outcome 001 0 180 5.2 0 001 180 365 6.8 1

sections.heading: Build start/stop data with tmerge()
sections.text: event(time, status) marks when the event occurs. tdc(day, value) lets measure change value on each measurement day.

sections.title: Time-varying variables
sections.heading: Analyse in a Cox model
sections.text: The time-to-event analysis itself (Kaplan-Meier, Cox, assumptions) is in Time-to-event. The detailed recipe for tmerge() and time-dependent effects is in the survival package vignette Counting process and timeline data sets (CRAN PDF).
sections.code: coxph surv tstart tstop outcome measure age time varying cox model

sections.title: Time-varying variables
sections.heading: Treatment-confounder feedback
sections.text: The start/stop Cox above is not always enough - and can even be wrong. The most important trap in time-varying analysis is treatment-confounder feedback : when a time-varying variable is both a confounder for the exposure and itself affected by past exposure. Classic example: a treatment (exposure) affects a biomarker, the biomarker affects whether the person gets more treatment, and the biomarker also affects the outcome. The variable is at once a confounder (normally handled by adjustment) and an intermediate variable / mediator on the path from past treatment to outcome (adjust for it and you block part of the effect you want to measure, introducing bias). In that situation you cannot simply put the variable into an ordinary Cox model, the way we did above. Adjusting and not adjusting both give a wrong answer. The solution is a whole different family of methods, g-methods : the g-formula (standardisation step by step over time) IP weighting / marginal structural models: the most accessible g-method. The guide introduces the weighting idea for a fixed exposure in IP weighting (IPTW and IPCW); marginal structural models extend it to a time-varying exposure g-estimation of structural models This falls outside this guide . If you suspect feedback, stop here, read up (for example What If, Part III), and involve a biostatistician before you analyse.

sections.heading: See also
sections.text: What If (Hernán & Robins), Part III - Causal inference for time-varying treatments (free PDF): the standard reference. Ch. 19 (time-varying treatments), ch. 20 (treatment-confounder feedback), ch. 21 (g-methods) and ch. 22 (target trial emulation). survival package vignette: Counting process and timeline data sets (CRAN PDF): the technical recipe for tmerge() and start/stop data. sections.title: Troubleshooting
sections.text: Use this page when something has already gone wrong: a red error message, a console that will not respond, or a result that came back empty. Start with the six steps, then look your message up in the two error tables, and if you are still stuck, the last section says where to ask without breaking DST's rules. If your code runs fine but you suspect the answer is wrong, use DST pitfalls instead: it collects the traps that produce a plausible-looking result without any error.

sections.title: Troubleshooting
sections.heading: Start here: six steps
sections.text: Before you go looking in the code, do this in order: 1. Read the error message: which line is mentioned? Which object name appears? 2. Run class(object) : is it data ( "data.frame" ) or still a connection ( "prudent_duckplyr_df" , which also says "data.frame" , or "tbl_duckdb_connection" or "arrow_dplyr_query" )? See Phase 5 - do you have data or just a connection? 3. Check the column names: is the column named exactly what you think? A single letter or difference in capitalisation is enough to fail. Use names(object) on data in R; on a lazy object use names(collect(head(object, 0))) , because names() and colnames() can mislead there (see Inspect your data). 4. Isolate the failing line: run it alone and see what happens. 5. Restart the R session (Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+F10) and run from the top. This clears stale objects left behind by earlier runs, which is a surprisingly common cause. It also throws away everything in memory, so read The console is stuck first if you have unsaved results. 6. Use ?functionname : type e.g. ?colSums in the console to open the help in the Help panel (bottom right) - what the function does, its arguments, and examples. Still stuck after that? Where to ask is at the bottom of this page.

sections.title: Troubleshooting
sections.heading: The console is stuck
sections.text: Before any of the above: if the console will not give you a > back, there is no error message to read. R is waiting, not failing.

sections.title: Troubleshooting
sections.heading: R shows + instead of >
sections.text: R could not finish reading your command and is waiting for the rest of it. Everything you type next is swallowed as a continuation, which is why the commands after it appear to do nothing at all. Press Esc to get out ( Ctrl+C if you are running R in a terminal rather than RStudio). The half-finished command is thrown away and the > comes back. What usually causes it: A missing ) or ] : put the cursor next to a bracket and the editor highlights its partner, or shows nothing if there is not one. An unclosed quote: "dementia instead of "dementia" . A trailing %>% with nothing after it: the pipe promises another step, so R waits for it.

sections.title: Troubleshooting
sections.heading: Something has been running too long
sections.text: Press Esc , or click the red stop sign that appears in the console toolbar while R is busy. That sends an interrupt and usually returns you to > . If nothing happens, R is inside compiled code that is not checking for interrupts. Large collect() calls on arrow or DuckDB do this. Then: 1. Session > Interrupt R. 2. If that does not work either, Session > Restart R (Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+F10). Restarting throws away everything in memory. On DST that can mean running an extraction again that took an hour the first time. Save anything expensive with saveRDS() before you start something long, so a restart costs you minutes instead of the morning. The same point, from the other direction, is in File formats: a full load of a large SAS file can cost you your unsaved work.

sections.title: Troubleshooting
sections.heading: Common R error messages
sections.text: Most R errors are small typos. Error message Usually means could not find function "..." Function name misspelled, or the package is not loaded ( library() ) object '...' not found The object/column does not exist (yet) or is misspelled (R is case-sensitive) unexpected symbol in "..." A typo just before: a missing comma, pipe ( %>% ) or quote unexpected '}' / unexpected ')' An unclosed or extra parenthesis/bracket Quick self-check of the code: A missing comma or pipe ( %>% )? Unclosed ( , or { ? Capitalisation ( PNR vs. pnr )? Are the data and packages loaded in this session? For a fuller walkthrough of debugging ( traceback() , browser() , print-debugging and reading error messages), see [Debugging from Zheer's R Coding Café, and the DDEA course's troubleshooting guide.

sections.title: Troubleshooting
sections.heading: Error messages specific to register work
sections.text: These are the ones you meet in a DST workflow rather than in R generally: Error message Typical cause Solution Error: Column 'pnr' not found The column is called PNR and rename_with(tolower) is missing. This happens with data not converted with fastreg, or converted with a fastreg older than 0.6.0: from 0.6.0 fastreg writes column names in lower case (NEWS) Add %>% rename_with(tolower) right after you open the data - see pitfall 3 Error: object 'my_list' not found my_list was never created in this session (not run, or misspelt) Run the line that creates it; check the name with ls() . !! does not fix this - see pitfall 8 for what !! is for Error: could not find function "read_register" library(fastreg) missing Add library(fastreg) at the top of the script non-numeric argument to binary operator Date column is character , not Date mutate(date = as.Date(date)) - see pitfall 4 rapi_execute / rapi_prepare error, or a date filter that returns 0 rows rapi only means that DuckDB could not run the query - the real cause is in the rest of the message. A common cause: a datetime column (e.g. kont_starttidspunkt ) is converted with as.Date() or compared with a date inside filter() before collect() Create the cut-off as a datetime before the pipe, cutoff <- as.POSIXct("2023-01-01", tz = "UTC") , then filter(kont_starttidspunkt >= cutoff) - see pitfall 4 Error in filter.default(...) , no applicable method for 'filter' , or object 'x' not found from a filter() call dplyr is not loaded, or another package has masked its filter() , so R runs stats::filter() (the "no applicable method" message also appears when the object is not a data frame or table) Add library(dplyr) as the last of your library() calls, or write dplyr::filter() Can't join ... due to incompatible types Join on columns of different type (e.g. numeric vs. character) on data in R (dplyr) or on a duckplyr table. Arrow gives its own Incompatible data types error. A DuckDB table opened through dbplyr gives no error at all, see No error, but zero rows Use mutate(pnr = as.character(pnr)) on both sides to match types object of type 'closure' is not subsettable The object you meant was never created (or is misspelt), so R found the built-in function of that name (e.g. data , df , c ) Create the object first / check its name. Unique object names (not data , df , c ) make this error easier to spot unsupported function in Arrow is not a mistake in your code - it is a gap in what the Arrow engine covers. Switch the connection to DuckDB with to_duckdb() , or collect() into R first and do the operation there. See Arrow vs. DuckDB.

sections.title: Troubleshooting
sections.heading: No error, but zero rows
sections.text: This is the failure mode that does not announce itself. A filter that cannot match returns an empty result, R reports success, and the empty table looks like a finding: "no patients were exposed". Two ways to produce it: A pattern longer than the column: atc2 in LMDB holds three characters, so grepl("N02A", atc2) compares four characters against three and matches nothing. See Medication (ATC). A type mismatch in a join or filter: a join on a character pnr and a numeric one fails in dplyr, duckplyr and arrow (see the table above). A DuckDB table opened through dbplyr ( to_duckdb() , read_register() in fastreg 0.14.2 or older, or a tbl() on a DBI connection) runs the join without an error: DuckDB turns the text into a number, so "0101" matches 101 . That can match too much as well as too little. And converting one side yourself can leave values that never meet: a code stored as a number loses its leading zero ( 0001 becomes 1 ), so it no longer matches the text "0001" , the same way a format table joined on the wrong type does (see Format tables). Make the key types match before every join. So treat an empty result as a bug until proven otherwise . Count the rows before and after the filter, and check that the values you filter on actually occur: If the second line shows three-character values and your pattern is longer, you have found it.
sections.code: dplyr count filter collect lmdb rows before atc2 what column really contains

sections.title: Troubleshooting
sections.heading: Where to ask
sections.text: Follow this order. AI is at the bottom because it is the easiest place to get a confident wrong answer. # Where When 1 Colleague or supervisor Ask first - they know your data and workflow 2 Google Search for the error message including Error: 3 Stack Overflow The world's largest collection of coding questions and answers 4 Zheer's R Coding Café r-coding-cafe.zheer.dk - register-data specific 5 Official package documentation Search the package name + "documentation" 6 AI (Claude, ChatGPT) Good for code problems, but easy to believe wrong answers - use only when you understand the answer Two ready-made references worth bookmarking: Common errors and Getting help, both in The Epidemiologist R Handbook. On DST there is an extra rule: no data in the question. DST's rules say that when you describe your dataset or a problem, you always use made-up examples. Not a value, not a row, not a pasted error message that happens to contain one. This applies to written questions to colleagues, to DST support and to any AI tool. When you need to show the problem, build a small fake dataset that reproduces it. (Showing your screen is a different rule: you may show it to people approved for the data you work with, see Log in to DST.) If you are new to R, do not make AI your first stop. It can write plausible-looking code that does not run, or that runs and gives a wrong result; use it next to your own understanding, not instead of it. How to ask a good help question (minimal reproducible example) A good help question is minimal (the smallest code that still shows the error), complete and reproducible . Bad: "My code fails, what is wrong?" (no code, no error message) Good: > "I get the error Error: object 'pnr' not found - what is missing?" > > r > library(dplyr) > df <- data.frame(PNR = 1:5, age = 20:24) > df %>% filter(pnr > 3) # error here > > > Expected: rows where PNR > 3. Actual: error that 'pnr' is not found. The error: the column is called PNR , the code asks for pnr . R is case-sensitive. Minimal Reproducible Example (Zheer's R Coding Café) works through how to build the fake dataset. How to use AI most effectively for R code AI is good at explaining error messages and suggesting solutions - but you need to give it enough context, and you must verify the answer yourself. Give AI this: 1. The exact error message (including Error: and line number if there is one) 2. The failing code: as little as possible, but enough to reproduce the error 3. What you expected vs. what happened 4. Which packages you are using (e.g. "dplyr and arrow on DST") Example of a good AI question: > "I get Error: Column 'pnr' not found when I run this code with dplyr and arrow on DST. I am using read_register() (fastreg). What is wrong?" > r > bef <- read_register("bef") > bef %>% select(pnr, koen) # error here > Ask for explanation, not just a fix: Write "explain what is wrong and why" rather than just "fix it". If you only get the code corrected without understanding why, the same error will appear again next time. Ask AI to ask questions before answering: Write "ask me questions before you answer if you need information". AI often guesses at context it does not have - this produces better answers if it asks about e.g. your package version, register type or what you actually want to achieve. Always verify the answer: Code examples from AI are starting points - not guarantees. Check that column names, function names and logic match your data with names() , class() and head() . DST has its own AI code tool. Forskermaskinen offers an AI tool for code help → covering R, SAS, SPSS, Stata and Python. It is for code only, the no-data rule above applies in full, and your conversations are not saved when you close it - so treat it as help with syntax, not as a notebook.

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.text: The National Patient Register (Landspatientregisteret, LPR) is where hospital diagnoses, contacts and procedures come from. It holds inpatient contacts from 1977, and outpatient, emergency department and psychiatric contacts from 1995. Private hospitals and clinics report through a separate system, see Private hospitals. Read this page before you write code against LPR. It explains how the register is laid out: the two periods (LPR2 and LPR3), which tables hold what, how the diagnosis codes and diagnosis types work, and the breaks in 1994, 1995 and 2019 that change what a count means. When you are done you know which tables your study period needs and which filters to apply. The code is on the next page, Extract from LPR. In short: LPR changed format in 2019: use LPR2 (up to March 2019) and LPR3 (after) and combine them. All ICD codes carry a D prefix you usually strip, and you choose diagnosis types (A/B for outcomes; G for baseline comorbidity exists only in 1995-2003).

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: LPR is split into two periods
sections.text: In early 2019 LPR changed format, from LPR2 to LPR3. Two dates matter, and they are not the same thing: When the hospitals switched their reporting. Region Hovedstaden, Region Sjælland and Region Midtjylland switched to LPR3 on the weekend of 2-3 February 2019, Region Nordjylland and Region Syddanmark on the weekend of 2-3 March 2019 (Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's data quality report on LPR3, April 2019). Where DST's LPR2 files end. lpr_adm , lpr_diag and the other LPR2 registers at DST end on 31 March 2019 (DST's register overview). A study period that crosses early 2019 needs both systems, combined. LPR2 somatic LPR2 psychiatric LPR3 Period 1977 to 31 March 2019 1995 to 31 March 2019 February or March 2019 and onwards Kinds of contact inpatient only before 1995⁴ all, from 1995 all Contact register lpr_adm t_psyk_adm lpr_a_kontakt Diagnosis register lpr_diag t_psyk_diag lpr_a_diagnose Covers psychiatry No Yes Yes (both combined) Join key recnum recnum ¹ dw_ek_kontakt Date column d_inddto (Date) d_inddto (Date) kont_starttidspunkt (datetime)² pnr column pnr pnr ³ pnr Diagnosis code c_diag c_diag diag_kode Diagnosis type c_diagtype c_diagtype diag_kode_type Contact type c_pattype ( "0" = inpatient) c_pattype kont_type ( "ALCA00" = physical attendance) ¹ ³ These are DST's names. Check whether your variables have been changed during delivery or data preprocessing: in DARTER the join key arrives as k_recnum in t_psyk_adm and v_recnum in t_psyk_diag , and the person column as v_cpr . Check colnames() and rename to recnum and pnr before joining. ² datetime format - convert with as.Date() . ⁴ LPR2 does not hold the same kinds of contact in all years. From 1977 through 1994 it holds inpatient contacts only. Outpatient and emergency department contacts, and contacts at psychiatric departments, are in it from 1995. Some outpatient contacts were reported already in 1994, but not completely (Schmidt et al. 2015; Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's LPR documentation). A study that counts outpatient or emergency contacts therefore cannot start before 1995. This table lists what the registers contain, not what your project was given. Run colnames() on your own extract before you build anything on a column here - c_pattype in particular is often left out (see Patient type).

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: Contact table and diagnosis table: every extract is a join
sections.text: LPR splits each hospital contact into two tables. The contact register (e.g. lpr_adm ) has one row per contact with pnr , dates and hospital, but not the diagnoses. The diagnosis register (e.g. lpr_diag ) has one row per diagnosis with the ICD code, but neither pnr nor a date. One contact can have several diagnoses. You join the two on the contact key ( recnum in LPR2, dw_ek_kontakt in LPR3) to get pnr , date and diagnosis in one table. The recipes in Extract from LPR are built on that join. Operations and procedures work the same way: lpr_sksopr (LPR2) has the SKS code (SKS is the Danish health care classification system) and recnum , but not pnr or date, so it is joined to lpr_adm when you want to find who had an operation and when.

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: Psychiatry: separate tables in LPR2, combined in LPR3
sections.text: Before 2019, contacts at psychiatric departments and their diagnoses (typically F-codes such as dementia and depression) were stored in separate registers ( t_psyk_adm , t_psyk_diag ). The structure resembles somatic LPR2, but column names can differ (see the table footnotes above). LPR3 combines both: somatic and psychiatric contacts and diagnoses are in the same tables, and no separate psychiatric query is needed. Psychiatric data older than 1995 exists but is not part of a standard LPR extract, see Overview of registers.

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: Timeline of the LPR tables
sections.text: The figure shows two breaks that are easy to miss: outpatient, emergency and psychiatric contacts only start in 1995 (footnote 4 above), and the LPR_A files overlap the LPR2 files from 2017 to early 2019 (the callout below). LPR3 is ongoing: its bar stops at November 2026 only because that is when the figure was drawn.

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: LPR3 is delivered in the LPR_A files
sections.text: You access LPR3 through the LPR_A files ( lpr_a_kontakt , lpr_a_diagnose ). Use the LPR_A files, and filter them. Two things, both easy to get wrong. 1. LPR_A, not LPR_F. LPR3 has been delivered as two sets of tables: the older LPR_F ( kontakter , diagnoser , forloeb ) and the current LPR_A ( lpr_a_kontakt , lpr_a_diagnose ). DST released LPR_A in June 2025 and has closed LPR_F for ordering. DST writes that the LPR_A tables largely correspond to the LPR_F tables but hold considerably more variables (LPR_A has 12 tables, LPR_F had 14), and that LPR_A, unlike LPR_F, also holds LPR2 rows from 2017-2019 (DST, Nyt om grunddata, 2nd quarter 2025). Every example on this site uses lpr_a_ . An older project may have both sets in its folder. They hold the same LPR3 contacts, so use one of them: stacking both gives you duplicated rows. 2. LPR_A holds four reporting systems in one table. Besides LPR3 contacts, lpr_a_kontakt and lpr_a_diagnose hold contacts from the older systems that ended in 2017 or later. Every row is tagged by lprindberetningssystem (reporting system): LPR1 , LPR2 , MiniPAS (records from private hospitals) and LPR3 . DST says so in its remark on LPR_A_KONTAKT. That is why the files reach back to 2017, before LPR3 reporting began in early 2019: "LPR3" as a period and "LPR_A" as a file are two different things. Filter both lpr_a_kontakt and lpr_a_diagnose with lprindberetningssystem == "LPR3" , or a contact already counted from lpr_adm gets counted again from its LPR2 -tagged copy in here. The join key does not carry the reporting system, so filtering the contact table alone leaves the diagnosis rows unchecked. The filter can also drop real contacts: if your project's lpr_adm ends before DST's own LPR2 files do (31 March 2019), the LPR2 -tagged rows are the only copy of the contacts in between. And private-hospital contacts (MiniPAS) need a register of their own. Both are explained, with a check to run on your own delivery, in Extract from LPR. Read that before you trust a count that spans 2019. (The LPR_F data model is documented in Vejledning til LPR3_F if you have inherited a project that used it. LPR_A documentation is still incomplete.)

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: ICD codes and the D-prefix
sections.text: ICD-10 (International Classification of Diseases, 10th revision) is the WHO's system for classifying diseases and conditions. Hospital diagnoses in Denmark have been coded with ICD-10 since 1994 (earlier years are ICD-8), e.g. G30 for Alzheimer's disease and F00 for dementia in Alzheimer's. ICD-10 codes in LPR have a prepended "D" : "DG30" (Alzheimer's), "DF00" (dementia), "DI21" (acute myocardial infarction). The D is a Danish addition from SKS, not part of the WHO code. The examples on this site strip the D-prefix before comparing codes, so that a code list reads like the ICD-10 codes in a paper and can be reused across registers: substr(x, start, stop) keeps characters from position start up to and including stop (counted from 1). substr(c_diag, 2, 4) skips position 1 (the D-prefix) and keeps characters 2, 3 and 4: "DG30" → "G30" . Use 2 to 5 for 4-digit codes: "DI219" → "I219" .
sections.code: mutate icd3 substr c_diag dg30 g30 digit code icd4 di219 i219

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: Only the patient registers have the D-prefix
sections.text: The prefix belongs to the patient registers. Other registers store the plain WHO code, and stripping the first character there removes a real one: Register Column What it holds Example LPR2, LPR3, psychiatric LPR c_diag , diag_kode , adiag D-prefixed DE119 Cause of death ( dodsaars , dodsaasg ) c_dod1 , c_dod_1a plain E119 Cancer register c_icd10 plain C509 Run substr(x, 2, 4) on "E119" and you get "119" . It matches nothing, it raises no error, and the result looks like an empty subgroup rather than a bug. A leading D is not always a prefix. ICD-10 has codes of its own that begin with D: D46 (myelodysplastic syndromes) and D32 (benign meningeal tumour) are whole codes. In the cancer register they are stored exactly like that. Strip the "prefix" and D46 becomes 46 .

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: Before 1994 the codes are ICD-8
sections.text: LPR2 starts in 1977, and Denmark did not move to ICD-10 until 1994 (Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's LPR documentation). The early years hold ICD-8: pure digits, no letter and no decimal point, so 446.30 is stored as 44630 . You get no error or warning from this. An ICD-10 code list matches no rows before 1994, and substr(c_diag, 2, 4) on "44630" returns "463" , which is not a code in any classification. A study whose period starts before 1994 reads two classifications out of one column and needs a code list for each. The same applies to dodsaars , which runs from 1970 and changes over in the same year.

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: Diagnosis types
sections.text: LPR2 ( c_diagtype ) has six diagnosis types, and three of them were only in use for some years: Code Meaning In use in LPR2 When to include A Action diagnosis (primary diagnosis) - the main reason for the contact 1977 onwards Yes, for outcomes B Secondary diagnosis - additional condition present 1977 onwards Yes, for outcomes G Underlying condition (grundmorbus), when different from the action diagnosis 1995-2003 Only for baseline comorbidity H Referral diagnosis - given by the referring unit as the reason for referral 1995 onwards Usually not (see below) M Provisional diagnosis - only for ongoing somatic outpatient contacts 1998-2013 Usually not (see below) C Complication 2002-2013 Decide for your study The codes and years are from Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's code sheet for LPR; the explanations of A, H and M follow Schmidt et al. 2015. G was voluntary to record in 1995-2001, was recorded only for psychiatric patients in 2002-2003, and is not used after 2003 (Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's LPR documentation). H and M are usually left out of outcome and comorbidity definitions: a referral diagnosis is what the referring unit suspected, and a provisional diagnosis is not final. That follows from what the two types are; it is not a rule from Sundhedsdatastyrelsen, so say in your methods what you chose. LPR3 ( diag_kode_type ) has only two diagnosis types: action diagnosis (A) and secondary diagnosis (B) (reporting guideline for LPR 2025, section 6.1.3). Keep the type column in your extract. Carry c_diagtype (in LPR3: diag_kode_type ) into your output, not just the diagnosis code. It costs one column and lets you vary the case definition later (main analysis on A + B, sensitivity analysis on A only or including G) without querying LPR again.
sections.code: outcomes exclusion diagnoses filter c_diagtype baseline comorbidity note only exists

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: Patient type: inpatient, outpatient or emergency
sections.text: Some studies need to tell inpatient contacts apart from outpatient and emergency-room visits, for example to count only admissions as an outcome. LPR2 has a field for it, LPR3 does not, so you derive patient type differently in the two. c_pattype and c_indm have to be in your extract. DST documents both for every year of LPR_ADM, but a delivery only contains the variables the project ordered. In the DARTER delivery, for instance, lpr_adm has neither, while t_psyk_adm has both - the same register family, two different extract scopes. Run colnames() on your own lpr_adm first. If the columns are missing, no filtering trick recovers them: you have to ask DST to add them to the delivery. Check the column names and codes below against your own extract with arrow::schema() or colnames() , and look them up in Overview of registers: the column names in LPR_A may differ from the example. The pattern is adapted from the Plana-Ripoll group's code on OSF.

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: Patient type in LPR2: c_pattype
sections.text: Patient type is in c_pattype , but the coding changed twice (Sundhedsdatastyrelsen's LPR documentation, under "Kendte databrud/ændringer", known data breaks): Emergency room, 2014: code "3" was discontinued, and emergency-room visits are from then on registered as "2" (outpatient) with an acute admission mode ( c_indm == "1" ). Part-day patients, 2002: code "1" was discontinued. After that, hospitals registered these patients differently: some as outpatients, some as inpatients. The code below groups "1" with inpatients; whichever you choose, inpatient counts are not directly comparable before and after 2002.
sections.code: dplyr mutate case_when lpr2_type lpr_adm extract patienttype c_pattype inpatient full admitted part day emergency explicit discontinued c_indm became acute outpatient na_character_

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: Patient type in LPR3: derived from duration
sections.text: LPR3 has no c_pattype . The kont_type code ALCA00 means physical attendance (not admission): the patient came in, whether for an outpatient visit or an admission. The other contact types are ALCA01 home or outreach visit, ALCA03 virtual contact, ALCA10 death and ALCA20 a pseudo-contact for reporting diagnoses only (Sundhedsdatastyrelsen, LPR reporting guide, Bilag 1). The prioritet (priority) code ATA1 means acute. The example below derives patient type from the contact's duration plus an emergency-room marker ( skadestue is Danish for emergency room): The 8-hour cut-off is a heuristic, not an official definition. LPR3 has no "inpatient" field. Other cut-offs are in use: DST's hospital statistics report stays under and over 12 hours (DST, documentation of the hospital utilisation statistics). Pick a threshold, write it in your methods, and clarify it with your data manager.

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: Retracted diagnoses in LPR3 (senere_afkraeftet)
sections.text: LPR3 flags diagnoses that were later retracted in the column senere_afkraeftet ("later disproved"). The filter used on this site: The is.na() part is needed. In R, NA != "Ja" returns NA , not TRUE , and filter() drops rows where the condition is NA . filter(senere_afkraeftet != "Ja") alone would therefore remove every diagnosis with an empty flag. With is.na(...) in front, the row is kept if the flag is empty or is not "Ja" . The filter thus assumes that a diagnosis with an empty flag was not retracted.
sections.code: filter is.na senere_afkraeftet

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: Diagnosis counts jump around 2019-2020
sections.text: The move to LPR3's contact-based model also changed how outpatient diagnoses are registered, and this can distort diagnosis counts across the transition. In LPR2, a course of outpatient visits was typically summarised with a single (action) diagnosis for the whole course. In LPR3, each contact can carry its own diagnoses. So a patient with 10 outpatient visits for depression that produced one diagnosis row in LPR2 can produce ten rows in LPR3: the same illness, many more registrations. Count-based analyses are clearly affected. Number of contacts or diagnoses per person per year, healthcare utilisation or recurrence measures, episode counts, or anything comparing volume before and after 2019: the same clinical course can turn into many more registrations, and the apparent "spike" is a registration artifact, not a real change in disease incidence. Whether first/last-diagnosis-date outcomes are also affected is not yet resolved. In principle, fragmentation alone should not change a "first diagnosis of X" date - the earliest matching row is still the earliest row, whether the underlying course produced one registration or ten. But that relies on every row still carrying its true original date across the transition, which is not confirmed. Test this on your own data before relying on it : check whether a first- or last-diagnosis date you compute shows any jump or shift around 2019-2020, the same way you check counts below. The visible effect, for a count-based analysis, is a spike in the number of diagnoses around 2019-2020, present for most diagnoses, and visible even if you restrict to the primary (action) diagnosis. It overlaps with COVID-19 in 2020, which makes the period even harder to interpret.

sections.title: Understand LPR
sections.heading: Check your own diagnoses across the transition
sections.text: There is no single agreed fix, and the problem is largest for analyses that rely only on hospital diagnoses. Count the diagnoses used in your study per calendar year and look at the result: Most diagnoses show the spike. A few are stable across the transition (type 1 diabetes, for example) and make a useful sanity check: if even a stable diagnosis jumps in your data, something else is wrong. For inspiration and for evaluating diagnostic stability across the transition, see Aarhus-Psychiatry-Research/diagnostic-stability-lpr2-lpr3 (methodological inspiration, not code for reuse).

sections.title: IP weighting (IPTW and IPCW)
sections.text: Use this page when you want to control confounding by weighting instead of matching or regression adjustment (IPTW), or to correct for people whose outcome you do not observe (IPCW). You start from the analysis-ready dataset (Phase 12) and end with a weighted estimate, a balance check and robust standard errors. The page does two related jobs, one per part. IP weighting (inverse probability weighting) is one technique with two applications. You model the probability of whatever skews the comparison and weight each person by its inverse . This creates a pseudo-population in which the skew is gone: IPTW (treatment weighting) against confounding : weight by the probability of being exposed . IPCW (censoring weighting) against selection bias from censoring, dropout or missing outcomes: weight by the probability of being observed . Both are handled in the analysis rather than by design. Paths and variable names in the examples are generic - replace them with your own. WeightIt , cobalt , sandwich and lmtest must be installed in your R environment on DST.

sections.title: IP weighting (IPTW and IPCW)
sections.heading: Part 1: IPTW - weighting against confounding
sections.text: Where matching (Phase 10) balances the groups by selecting people, IPTW weights them: each person gets a weight based on their probability of being exposed (the propensity score), so exposed and unexposed become comparable on the measured confounders. Propensity score, three ways - weighting is only one of them The propensity score (each person's probability of being exposed given the confounders) can be used by weighting (IPTW, this page), by matching exposed to unexposed on the score, or by stratifying / adjusting on it. They are alternative routes to the same end, balancing measured confounders, and all share the same positivity diagnostic: poor overlap shows up as extreme weights or as people who cannot be matched. See Hernán & Robins, What If , ch. 15. Three assumptions for IPTW to work (the general identifiability conditions for any causal estimate, introduced in Phase 1): 1. Exchangeability: you have measured and included the main confounders (no substantial unmeasured confounding). 2. Positivity (overlap): within each combination of confounders, both exposed and unexposed must be possible. Very large weights are a warning sign of poor overlap. 3. Consistency: the exposure must be a well-defined intervention, so a "what if everyone were / were not exposed" world makes sense.

sections.title: IP weighting (IPTW and IPCW)
sections.heading: Step 1: estimate the weights
sections.text: The left side of ~ is the exposure (treatment), the right side the confounders - never the outcome. method = "glm" computes the propensity score with logistic regression. estimand = "ATE" weights so both groups come to resemble the whole population.
sections.code: weightit weightit computes weights cobalt bal.tab love.plot check balance readrds path analysis.rds analysis ready dataset one row per person index matched replacement calendar_year as.integer format index_date year exposure age sex education_cat income_cat treatment confounders outcome method glm propensity score via logistic regression estimand ate target average effect whole population

sections.title: IP weighting (IPTW and IPCW)
sections.heading: Step 2: check balance
sections.text: The weights are only good if they actually balance the confounders. Check that before looking at the outcome. bal.tab() / love.plot() show how far each confounder is from being balanced (SMD = standardised difference between the groups) - before and after weighting. The goal is for all of them to sit close to 0 after weighting. If some are still skewed, or a few weights are very large, reconsider the model (more/other confounders) or consider stabilising/trimming the weights.
sections.code: bal.tab standardised differences smd before after weighting love.plot same figure rule thumb

sections.title: IP weighting (IPTW and IPCW)
sections.heading: Step 3: weighted outcome model
sections.text: Once balance is acceptable, fit the outcome model with the weights . Weighting requires robust standard errors (same idea as in Regression). Expected warning. With non-integer weights, glm(..., family = binomial) prints the warning "non-integer #successes in a binomial glm" . It is harmless here and can be ignored: the estimates are correct, and the robust standard errors take care of the uncertainty. (Don't switch to family = quasibinomial to remove it - that changes the model's variance assumption.) The robust standard errors treat the weights as fixed. To account for the weights being estimated too, WeightIt::glm_weightit(outcome ~ exposure, data = df, weightit = W, family = binomial) computes them by M-estimation by default, or you can bootstrap the whole procedure. If the same person is in the data more than once, cluster on pnr as in Regression. The alternative to weighting: standardization (the g-formula) IPTW has a twin for confounding control: standardization (also called g-computation or the parametric g-formula). Instead of weighting, you fit an outcome model and average its predictions over the confounder distribution. It often gives more stable estimates and lets you report marginal risk differences and ratios, not just an odds ratio. The two answer the same causal question and make a good cross-check on each other. See Hernán & Robins, What If , ch. 13 (and §13.4, "IP weighting or standardization?").
sections.code: sandwich vcovhc robust variance lmtest coeftest weights add column model glm outcome exposure weighted just treatment confounders are away family binomial vcov type hc0 standard errors default hc3

sections.title: IP weighting (IPTW and IPCW)
sections.heading: Part 2: IPCW - weighting against censoring and missing outcomes
sections.text: The same machinery can fix a different skew: selection bias from censoring, dropout or missing outcomes. Think of censoring as a "second treatment" : instead of asking "what is the effect of the exposure?" (which requires complete data) you ask "what would the effect be if nobody had been censored? ". This converts selection bias into a confounding problem for censoring, and confounding can be weighted away. Each observed person is weighted by 1/Pr(observed), so they stand in for the similar people who dropped out. This rebuilds the full population. Example (from Hernán & Robins, What If , ch. 8): a randomised trial of wasabi and death. Dropout is highest among precisely the exposed and the sick, so censoring becomes uneven : Completers only N Deaths Risk Exposed 9 4 44% Control 22 11 50% The completer analysis gives RR = 0.89 - wasabi looks protective . But that is an illusion created by the uneven dropout: the exposed who stayed are systematically healthier. Weighted back to the full population, the risk is 57% in both groups, RR = 1.00 - no effect. This code handles an outcome that is missing for some people. For censoring in time-to-event data it is not enough: the probability of staying uncensored changes over follow-up, so the weights must be time-varying, which this page does not cover. The three assumptions apply here too (Hernán & Robins, ch. 8): Exchangeability: the one that fails most often. The predictors in the weight model must contain everything that predicts both dropout AND outcome. We rarely know the true reasons people drop out, and there is no test for whether we caught them all - only substantive judgement. Positivity: everyone must be able to stay observed: Pr(observed) > 0 in every group. If a group is certain to drop out, there is no one left to weight up from. Consistency: a "no censoring" world must be coherent. Fine for loss to follow-up. Not fine for competing events (for example death from another cause), where you cannot remove one cause without touching the others. For missing outcomes, IPCW is an alternative to multiple imputation, see Missing data. Read more Hernán & Robins, Causal Inference: What If - the causal foundation under both halves of this page (free PDF); the relevant chapters are named at each point above.
